p.seg: 《King Chǔ Zhuāng, First》
"When King Zhuāng of Chǔ executed Xià Zhēngshū of Chén,
the Spring and Autumn Annals expressed disapproval in its wording,
not granting him the authority to conduct punitive expeditions;
when King Líng of Chǔ killed Qìng Fēng of Qí,
it directly referred to him as 'the Viscount of Chǔ',
why is this?"
The response:
"King Zhuāng's conduct was virtuous,
and Zhēngshū's crime was grave;
for a virtuous ruler to punish a heavy crime
was commendable in the people's hearts.
If not disapproved,
who would know it deviated from proper principles?
The Spring and Autumn Annals often, where ambiguity might suggest approval,
reveals the lack thereof.
Thus, it did not grant Duke Huán of Qí the right to arbitrarily enfeoff land,
nor Duke Wén of Jìn the right to summon the king to his court,
nor King Zhuāng of Chǔ the right to arbitrarily execute as punishment.
If these three were not granted approval,
then the feudal lords' claims to such rights
would be nearly condemned!
This is why King Líng of Chǔ was referred to as 'Viscount' in his punitive expedition.
The language of the Spring and Autumn Annals often employs analogies,
making its text concise and its principles clear."
The questioner said:
"The disapproval of feudal lords arbitrarily enfiefing
reappears in the case of the destruction of Chén and Cài;
why does the disapproval of arbitrary punitive expeditions
not reappear in the killing of Qìng Fēng?"
The response:
"In the use of language in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
what is already clear is omitted,
what is not yet clear is emphasized.
Now, that feudal lords may not arbitrarily conduct punitive expeditions
is already clear;
but Qìng Fēng's crime had not been explicitly shown,
so it referred to 'the Viscount of Chǔ' to highlight his hegemonic punishment,
emphasizing that his crime deserved death,
to establish a major prohibition for the world.
It says:
In the conduct of a minister,
to demean his lord's position,
to be a minister who throws the state into chaos—
even if he does not usurp or kill,
his crime still deserves death.
Compared to this,
that is what it means."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'Jìn attacked the Xiānyú.'
Why does it condemn Jìn and equate it with the barbarians?"
The response:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals honors ritual and values trust;
trust is more important than land,
ritual is more revered than one's person.
How do we know this is so?
Lady Bó Jī of Sòng feared breaching ritual and died in a fire,
Duke Huán of Qí doubted trust and lost his land—
the Spring and Autumn Annals praises them and cites them,
to set an example for the world.
It says: With ritual and trust,
ritual never goes unanswered,
kindness never goes unrepaid—
this is the way of Heaven.
Now, our ruler and minister, sharing the same surname, came to you,
yet you, without a good heart,
failed to respond with ritual.
If you fear and respect us,
how could you not be like the barbarians?
During the rebellion of Prince Qìngfù,
Lǔ was in peril, nearly lost,
yet Duke Huán of Qí brought it peace;
though not related to them,
he still came to care for us.
How then, sharing the same surname, do you treat us with cruelty and harm?
The Book of Songs says:
'That gentle turtledove,
soars high to the sky.
My heart is full of sorrow,
thinking of those ancestors.
Awake through the dawn, I cannot sleep,
longing for those two.'
All people have this heart.
Now Jìn does not care for us as kin,
but oppresses us with its strength—
our hearts are disappointed.
Hence, the unfavorable wording,
calling it merely 'Jìn',
is a subtle expression of disapproval."
The questioner said:
"Jìn was wicked and not to be befriended;
for the duke to go but not dare to arrive
was merely human sentiment—
why does the gentleman feel shame and say the duke was ill?"
The response:
"If wickedness comes without cause,
the gentleman feels no shame;
introspecting without guilt,
what worry or fear is there?
That is all.
Now, the Spring and Autumn Annals shames him
because Duke Zhāo had brought it upon himself.
Ministers encroaching upon their lord
began in Duke Wén's time and worsened in Duke Zhāo's;
the duke suffered disorder and decline,
yet had no heart of caution or fear,
but recklessly made light plans and rash expeditions,
violated great ritual by taking a wife of the same surname,
engaged in unrighteousness and greatly devalued himself.
People say:
'When the state is well-governed,
neighbors come to congratulate;
when the state is in chaos,
neighbors scatter.'
Thus, Jì Sūn monopolized power,
and no great state corrected him;
he fled for eight years,
and only after death did he return.
He lost his life and endangered his son—
the extremity of hardship.
The gentleman does not shame his hardship,
but shames the reasons for his plight.
Though Duke Zhāo encountered such times,
had he not taken a wife of the same surname,
how could it have come to this?
Even having done so,
had he employed Confucius to assist him,
it still would not have reached this point.
The times were difficult, governance simple;
he acted wrongly without remedy—
this is why he met his plight."
The Spring and Autumn Annals divides the twelve reigns into three categories,
those witnessed,
those heard,
and those transmitted by hearsay.
The witnessed spans three reigns,
the heard spans four reigns,
and the transmitted by hearsay spans five reigns.
Thus, the reigns of Āi, Dìng, and Zhāo
are what the nobleman witnessed.
The reigns of Xiāng, Chéng, Wén, and Xuān
are what the nobleman heard,
and the reigns of Xī, Mǐn, Zhuāng, Huán, and Yǐn
are what the nobleman received by hearsay.
The witnessed covers sixty-one years,
the heard covers eighty-five years,
and the transmitted by hearsay covers ninety-six years.
For the witnessed,
the language is subtle;
for the heard,
the calamities are lamented;
for the transmitted,
the affection is diminished;
all in accordance with the emotional connection.
Hence, when expelling the Jì family, it mentions the rain prayer again,
subtly wording it;
when Zǐchì was killed,
it could not bear to record the date,
lamenting the calamity;
when Zǐbān was killed,
it writes the day Yǐwèi,
diminishing the affection.
The intentions of bending and stretching,
the text's detail and brevity,
all correspond to this.
I observe that it draws near the near and distances the distant, cherishes the intimate and alienates the remote,
and also know that it honors the honorable and disdains the lowly, values the weighty and lightens the trivial,
further understanding that it thickens the thick and thins the thin, praises the good and condemns the evil,
and recognizes that it highlights the bright and obscures the dark, clarifies the white and blackens the black.
All things have their pairs,
pairing and coupling them,
matching and partnering them,
is excellent.
The Book of Songs says:
'Dignified and solemn is the demeanor,
orderly and harmonious the virtuous sound,
without resentment or hatred,
following the multitude of peers.'
This expresses it.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals embodies the greatest righteousness,
grasp one aspect and broadly comprehend it,
observe its rights and wrongs,
to attain its correct principles,
examine its gentle words,
to understand its concealed grievances.
Therefore, externally,
it speaks without explicit display;
internally,
it conceals without complete obscurity;
for the esteemed it is the same;
for the worthy it is the same;
this distinguishes inner from outer, differentiates worthy from unworthy, and grades noble from humble.
Righteousness does not slander superiors,
wisdom does not endanger oneself,
hence the distant are concealed out of righteousness,
the near are cautious out of wisdom,
with caution and righteousness combined,
the closer the era, the more guarded the words.
This is why Dìng and Āi's reigns have subtle language.
Thus, applied, it brings peace to the world;
not applied, it ensures personal safety;
such is the Way of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Way of the Spring and Autumn Annals
reveres Heaven and emulates antiquity.
Thus, though one may have skillful hands,
without applying the compass and square,
one cannot form circles and squares correctly;
though one may have keen ears,
without sounding the six pitch-standards,
one cannot fix the five notes;
though one may have a discerning mind,
without studying the former kings,
one cannot bring peace to the world;
then, the enduring Way of the former kings
is indeed the compass, square, and six pitch-standards for the world!
Therefore, the sage emulates Heaven,
and the worthy emulate the sage,
this is the great principle;
to grasp the great principle brings order,
to lose it brings chaos,
this is the distinction between order and chaos;
it is said that under Heaven there are not two Ways,
thus sages govern differently but follow the same principle,
connecting past and present,
hence the former worthies pass down their methods to later ages.
The Spring and Autumn Annals in dealing with worldly affairs,
approves of restoring antiquity,
criticizes changing constants,
desiring to model on the former kings.
Yet it interjects with a single statement:
"A king must reform institutions."
Those with biased views take this as their argument,
saying:
"If antiquity can be followed,
why not continue the Way of the former kings entirely?"
The world is confused by such words,
doubting the correct Way and believing deviant speech,
which is deeply troubling.
The response is:
"There was a man who heard that the lords performed the archery ritual with the music of 'Lí Shǒu',
so he himself cut off a fox's head,
hung it up and shot at it,
saying:
'Wherein lies the music?'
This is hearing the name without knowing the reality.
Now when we say a new king must reform institutions,
it does not mean changing the Way,
nor altering the principle,
but receiving the mandate from Heaven,
changing the surname and establishing a new king,
not succeeding the previous king to rule;
if one entirely follows the former institutions,
continues the old enterprises,
without any reforms,
then there is no difference from succeeding the previous king.
The king who receives the mandate
is greatly manifested by Heaven;
as one serves a father by following his intentions,
serves a ruler by emulating his will,
so it is in serving Heaven;
now that Heaven has greatly manifested itself,
if things follow the replaced dynasty and are entirely identical,
then it is not manifest and not clear,
contrary to Heaven's will,
thus necessarily moving the capital, changing titles, reforming the calendar, and altering ceremonial colors
for no other reason
than not daring to disobey Heaven's will and to make self-manifestation clear.
As for the great guiding principles, human relations, the Way and principle, governance, education, customs, and cultural meanings remaining entirely as before,
what need is there to change them?
Therefore, the king has the name of reforming institutions,
but not the reality of changing the Way.
Confucius said:
'He who ruled without action,
was it not Shùn!'
Meaning he upheld Yáo's Way, that is all,
is this not evidence of not changing!"
The questioner says:
"When things change and Heaven confers the mandate,
it is manifest,
why must one also create new music?"
The reply:
"Music is different from this.
Institutions are reformed in response to Heaven,
music is created in response to the people.
What they receive the mandate with,
must be what the people collectively enjoy.
Therefore, greatly reforming institutions at the beginning
is to clarify the Mandate of Heaven;
creating new music at the end
is to display Heaven's achievement;
based on what the people of the world newly enjoy, composing the melodies and songs,
both to harmonize governance,
and to promote virtue;
if the world is not universally harmonious,
the king does not vainly create music.
Music is what fills the inner heart and moves to express outwardly,
responding to the time of orderly governance,
establishing rituals and creating music to complete it,
completion means both root and branch, substance and form are fully present.
Thus, those who create music must reflect on what the world began to enjoy under them as the foundation.
In Shùn's time,
the people enjoyed his illuminating Yáo's achievements,
hence the Sháo.
Sháo means to illuminate;
in Yǔ's time,
the people enjoyed the succession of the three sages,
hence the Xià.
Xià means great;
in Tāng's time,
the people enjoyed his rescuing them from calamity,
hence the Hù.
Hù means to rescue;
in King Wén's time,
the people enjoyed his raising armies for campaigns,
hence the Wǔ.
Wǔ means to campaign.
These four were collectively enjoyed by the world,
as one,
but the reasons for their collective enjoyment
could not be the same.
The method of creating music
must reflect the foundation of what is enjoyed.
Since what is enjoyed differs in circumstances,
how can music not vary with the age!
Therefore, Shùn created the Sháo and Yǔ created the Xià,
Tāng created the Hù and King Wén created the Wǔ.
The four musics have different names,
each following what their people began to enjoy under them.
I have seen evidence of this.
The Book of Songs says:
'King Wén received the mandate,
achieved these military feats;
having campaigned against Chóng,
he built a city at Fēng.'
This is the ethos of the music.
It also says:
'The king blazed with anger,
and marshaled his troops.'
At that time,
Zhòu was without the Way,
the lords were in great chaos,
the people enjoyed King Wén's anger and sang of it.
When the Zhōu's virtue had permeated the world,
they reflected on the foundation to create music,
calling it the Great Wǔ,
meaning that what the people began to enjoy was the martial, that is all.
Therefore, all music
is created at the end,
but named after the beginning,
emphasizing the meaning of honoring the foundation.
From this perspective,
the reform of the calendar and ceremonial colors,
and the differentiation in receiving the mandate, responding to Heaven, establishing rituals, and creating music,
are movements of the human heart,
the two aspects separate and reunite,
for the same purpose."
The Jade Cup, Part Two
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes Duke Wén for marrying while in mourning.
A questioner says:
"The rule for mourning
does not exceed three years.
The three-year mourning period
is twenty-five months.
Now examining the Classic,
Duke Wén married only in the forty-first month,
so there was no mourning when he married,
having long exceeded the prescribed period.
Why call it marrying in mourning?"
The response:
"In discussing matters, the Spring and Autumn Annals
values nothing more than intention.
Now, marriage necessarily involves presenting betrothal gifts.
The month of presenting betrothal gifts fell within the mourning period,
hence it is called marrying in mourning.
Moreover, Duke Wén held the Xiá sacrifice in autumn,
and presented betrothal gifts in winter,
both being improperly early.
The Spring and Autumn Annals does not criticize the former
but instead criticizes the latter,
necessarily because the three-year mourning
involves heartfelt emotions.
Even if following custom but unable to complete it,
one should still feel unsettled in heart.
Now, he completely lacked the intention of mourning the departed,
instead thinking about marriage matters.
This is what the Spring and Autumn Annals strongly condemns.
Therefore, it criticizes by not specifying beyond three years at the beginning,
criticizing him for marrying in mourning.
Without distinguishing between before and after,
it condemns his lack of human feeling.
Based on this to discuss ritual,
what ritual values lies in intention.
If the intention is respectful and礼节完备,
then the gentleman acknowledges his understanding of ritual;
if the intention is harmonious and the music elegant,
then the gentleman acknowledges his understanding of music;
if the intention is sorrowful and living austerely,
then the gentleman acknowledges his understanding of mourning.
Hence it is said:
It is not arbitrarily imposed,
but emphasizes intention.
Intention is the substance,
things are the form.
Form attaches to substance;
if substance does not reside in form,
how can form apply to substance?
When both substance and form are complete,
then the ritual is accomplished.
If either substance or form is practiced alone,
one cannot claim to have either.
If both cannot be complete and one must choose,
rather have substance without form.
Though not fully acknowledging his ritual capability,
one still somewhat approves,
as with the case of Jiǎ Gélú's visit.
Having form without substance,
not only is it not acknowledged,
but somewhat condemned,
as with the case of the state ruler's actual visit.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals orders the Way,
prioritizing substance over form,
valuing intention over objects.
Hence it is said:
'Ritual, oh ritual,
does it mean merely jade and silk?'
Extending this forward,
one should also say:
'Court, oh court,
does it mean merely speeches?'
'Music, oh music,
does it mean merely bells and drums?'
Drawing it backward,
one should also say:
'Mourning, oh mourning,
does it mean merely garments?'
Therefore, Confucius established the Way of the new king,
clarifying the value of intention to return to harmony,
showing his love for sincerity to eliminate falsity.
Because there were the弊端 of continuing Zhōu,
it was thus.
The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals:
subordinates follow the ruler,
the ruler follows Heaven.
It says:
According to the hearts of the people and ministers,
they cannot be without a ruler for a single day.
Though they cannot be without a ruler for a day,
yet for three years he is called 'zǐ',
because the ruler's heart is not yet fit to be established.
Is this not subordinates following the ruler?
The heart of a filial son
is not fit for three years.
Though not fit for three years, yet he ascends the throne after the year,
to align with the numbers of Heaven from start to end.
Is this not the ruler following Heaven?
Therefore, subdue the people to elevate the ruler,
subdue the ruler to elevate Heaven,
is the great principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Spring and Autumn Annals discusses events of twelve generations,
where human relationships are thorough and the kingly Way is complete.
Its laws are spread over two hundred and forty-two years,
mutually supporting,
forming literary elegance.
Their arrangement is intricate,
not copying antiquity.
Therefore, those who discuss the Spring and Autumn Annals
combine and penetrate them,
follow and seek them,
group their comparisons,
pair their categories,
examine their threads,
trim their redundancies.
Thus, human relationships are thorough and kingly laws established.
Think it not so?
Now, the Son of Heaven ascends the throne after the year,
feudal lords within their domains are called 'zǐ' for three years.
These are not in the Classic,
yet handling them is no different from what is in the Classic.
Not that there is no distinction,
but having insight, the Classic calmly accepts the redundancy.
Hence, being able to connect categories through comparison, to distinguish and assign redundancy,
is greatly achieving it.
Humans receive mandate from Heaven,
having a nature that loves good and hates evil,
which can be nurtured but not changed,
can be prepared for but not removed,
like the body can be fat or thin,
but cannot be altered.
Therefore, even the most worthy
can tolerate the faults of ruler and parents,
but cannot make ruler and parents faultless.
The Book of Documents says:
"If the sovereign is not sovereign,
leave his presence."
Serving parents is also thus,
all being the utmost loyalty and filial piety.
If not the most worthy, who can be like this?
If the father is not fatherly, the son is not filial;
if the ruler is not ruler-like, the minister is not ministerial.
Duke Wén could not observe mourning,
did not timely perform sacrifices,
reversed order by not completing three years,
and moreover married in mourning,
married from among senior officials,
thereby demeaning the ancestral temple,
confusing his group of ancestors,
and opposing the former dukes.
Not a single minor good,
but four or five major evils;
therefore, feudal lords did not grant him mandate,
senior officials did not serve as envoys.
This is the sign of hating evil, the evidence of not being ministerial.
Insulted abroad,
usurped at home,
he was a ruler without position.
Confucius said:
"Government has been in the hands of senior officials for four generations."
This probably refers to since Duke Wén's time.
The nobleman knows that those in power cannot govern people through force,
therefore they select the Six Arts to provide comprehensive cultivation.
The *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents* give order to one's aspirations,
the *Rites* and *Music* purify one's virtues,
the *Book of Changes* and *Spring and Autumn Annals* illuminate one's wisdom.
All six disciplines are great,
yet each has its own strengths.
The *Book of Songs* expresses aspirations,
thus it excels in substance;
the *Rites* establish regulations,
thus they excel in refinement;
the *Music* celebrates virtue,
thus it excels in influence;
the *Book of Documents* records achievements,
thus it excels in practical matters;
the *Book of Changes* is rooted in heaven and earth,
thus it excels in principles;
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* rectifies right and wrong,
thus it excels in governing people.
One can master all their strengths,
but cannot fully elaborate all their details.
Thus, if a ruler focuses only on major principles, his understanding becomes obscure;
if he seeks excessive breadth, he becomes weary of his tasks.
These two errors differ in nature but are equally condemnable,
and their harm will inevitably arrive.
This cannot escape careful examination.
Therefore, those skilled in teaching
not only beautify their doctrines,
but are also cautious in their conduct.
They regulate timing—early or late,
determine workload—much or little,
adjust pace—fast or slow.
They guide without rushing,
examine without causing distress.
They observe students' actions,
and develop their innate talents.
Thus, effort is not exhausted,
yet personal cultivation is greatly achieved.
This is called sage-like transformation,
and I embrace it.
Does the Spring and Autumn Annals favor subtlety?
It values the underlying intent.
The Spring and Autumn Annals cultivates the principle of root and branch,
expresses responses to changing circumstances,
penetrates the will behind life and death,
and fulfills the ultimate standard of human morality.
Thus, when a ruler is killed and the perpetrator is punished,
it is deemed good and the punishment is recorded;
if no one punishes the culprit,
then the ruler's burial is not recorded,
and the perpetrator does not reappear.
Not recording the burial
signifies the absence of loyal ministers and sons;
the perpetrator not reappearing
indicates they ought to be eradicated.
Now, Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler,
yet four years later,
he reappears on a separate tablet,
which is not the usual phrasing in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Scholars ancient and modern, perplexed, ask,
saying:
"He assassinated his ruler;
why does he reappear?"
"It is as if the perpetrator remains unpunished,
why record the burial?
Asking why the burial is recorded
implies it should not be recorded, yet it is;
asking why he reappears
also implies he should not reappear, yet he does;
these two are of the same thread,
and must correspond.
Zhào Dùn's reappearance
is directly due to addressing the inquiry and clarifying he did not personally commit the murder,
not that he should not be punished;
thus, it must also be said that the recording of Duke Dào's burial
is directly to address the inquiry and clarify it was not a full assassination,
and should not be deemed a crime.
If so, then the doctrine of the Spring and Autumn Annals would be in chaos,
how could it be emulated?"
"Therefore, by linking cases to discuss right and wrong,
though difficult to fully grasp,
the principle is one.
Now, punishing Zhào Dùn is not recorded in the commentary,
not punishing him is not recorded either,
by analogy,
it is a legal judgment;
without analogy to handle it,
is a false statement.
Now, examining the analogy,
both should not die,
why punish them?
The Spring and Autumn Annals addresses hundreds of inquiries,
responds to thousands of questions,
all retained in the Classic,
overturning and drawing comparisons,
to initiate understanding.
Ultimately, no reckless words
are found that receive a response in the commentary;
now, if external perpetrators cannot be punished,
so they all reappear,
and one asks:
'Why does this one reappear?'
No statement is more reckless than this,
how could it receive a response!
Thus, I know the inquiry is not reckless
because it received a response;
because the inquiry is not reckless,
I know Zhào Dùn's case must be examined.
There are those
named as patricides
yet actually exempt from guilt;
also those named as regicides whose crimes go unpunished,
to condemn them directly
is not as good as pondering it gradually.
Moreover, I speak of Zhào Dùn with basis,
the Book of Songs says:
'Others have hearts,
I can measure them.'
This means nothing is without connections;
by examining the exterior,
one can see the interior.
Now, considering Zhào Dùn's actions
and observing his heart,
he was sincere but not punitive,
fitting and trustworthy,
not akin to a usurper or assassin.
Considering Zhào Dùn's cry to heaven,
if inwardly insincere,
how could he be so?
Thus, tracing his beginning and end, he had no intent to assassinate.
Hanging the label of evil schemer
is a fault in not leaving promptly,
a crime in not punishing the perpetrator.
A minister's duty to punish the perpetrator for his ruler
is like a son's duty to taste medicine for his father;
if a son does not taste the medicine,
he is charged with patricide;
if a minister does not punish the perpetrator,
he is charged with regicide.
The principle is the same.
It serves to show the world the abandonment of ministerial and filial integrity,
the enormity of such evil.
Thus, Zhào Dùn's failure to punish the perpetrator
constitutes regicide,
no different from a son not tasting medicine constituting patricide.
Zhào Dùn should not be punished,
based on this reasoning."
The questioner says:
"Calling it regicide,
yet not punishing it,
the argument is hard to understand,
not something the masses can see.
Thus, pardoning the son's crime
is clarified in the commentary;
Zhào Dùn not being punished
lacks commentary,
why?"
The reply:
"In an age of chaos where righteousness is abandoned,
betraying superiors and disloyalty,
usurpations and assassinations overwhelming rulers are numerous,
yet to explicitly punish great evils,
who would speak of such punishment?
Thus, for Jìn's Zhào Dùn and Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Bǐ, both have unpunished records,
but no commentary is made,
not wishing to clarify the intent."
The questioner says:
"Those who assassinate their rulers,
with high ministers present yet unable to punish them,
are not limited to one state.
When Duke Líng was assassinated,
Zhào Dùn was not present.
Not being present versus being present,
the evil differs in severity,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals blames those present who do not punish the perpetrator,
not binding them as ministers and sons;
it blames those not present who do not punish the perpetrator,
then charges them with regicide.
Why blame severe evil lightly and light evil severely?"
The reply:
"The way of the Spring and Autumn Annals
observes what confuses people,
and establishes doctrines to greatly illuminate it.
Now, Zhào Dùn was virtuous but not thorough in principle,
all saw his goodness,
none knew his crime,
so based on his virtue, great evil is added,
binding him with heavy blame,
to make people ponder deeply and reflect to return to the Way,
saying:
'Alas!
The great righteousness of ruler and minister,
the way of father and son,
reach even to this.'
This is why light evil is heavily blamed;
in other states, those who do not punish perpetrators
are petty individuals,
not worth counting.
They are not counted among true men.
This is why severe evil is lightly blamed.
The Commentary says:
'Make light heavy,
make heavy light.'
Is this not what it means?
Thus, Gōngzǐ Bǐ is suspected of being eligible for succession,
Zhào Dùn is suspected of lacking ministerial responsibility,
Xǔ Zhǐ is suspected of lacking filial guilt.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, for those unaware of their evil
and complacent in unpreparedness,
therefore piles on heavy blame,
to rectify a crooked age and straighten it,
for straightening cannot avoid exceeding the norm,
or it cannot be straightened.
Understanding this, the principle is complete."
Bamboo Groves, Third
"The constant phrasing in the Spring and Autumn Annals
denies ritual propriety to the barbarians and grants it to the Central States,
yet at the Battle of Bì,
it abruptly reverses this,
why is this?"
The response:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals employs no fixed terminology,
but shifts according to changing circumstances.
Now Jìn had degenerated into barbarism,
while Chǔ had elevated itself to become a noble state,
hence the phrasing was altered to reflect these facts.
When King Zhuāng of Chǔ spared Zhèng,
he demonstrated praiseworthy virtue,
yet the people of Jìn failed to recognize this goodness
and sought to attack them.
The crisis being already resolved,
to provoke battle
revealed no genuine appreciation for virtue,
but rather contempt for saving the people,
thus they were disparaged
and denied the privilege of ritual recognition among the worthy.
Duke Mù of Qín disregarded Jiǎn Shū's advice and suffered great defeat,
while Duke Wén of Zhèng underestimated his forces and lost his army.
Such is the Spring and Autumn Annals' reverence for the worthy and concern for the people.
Therefore, among the hundreds of recorded
campaigns, invasions, and attacks,
only select few are explicitly documented,
to lament their harm to what is most valued."
The questioner asks:
"It meticulously records warfare,
yet contains no explicit condemnation of it,
why is this?"
The response:
"In assemblies and meetings,
the greater presides over the lesser;
in matters of warfare,
the later-initiated supersedes the first aggressor.
If not disapproving,
why place the instigator in inferior position?
This itself constitutes condemnation of warfare!
Moreover, according to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
during famine years one should not repair old structures,
intending not to burden the people;
burdening the people is already condemned.
How much more so injuring them!
Injuring the people is painful enough,
let alone killing them!
Therefore it is said:
repairing old structures in famine years invites criticism,
establishing new cities is discreetly condemned —
these being lesser harms to the people,
warrant minor disapproval;
greater harms to the people
warrant major condemnation.
Now consider what warfare does to the people —
how immense its harm must be!
Examining the intent and observing the purpose,
what the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns
is relying on force instead of virtue,
driving the people to slaughter and devastation.
What it approves
is establishing military capability without using it,
conquering through benevolence and righteousness.
The Book of Songs says:
'He arrays his civil virtue,
to harmonize these four states.'
This is what the Spring and Autumn Annals praises.
When virtue cannot draw neighbors close,
and civil culture cannot attract distant lands,
yet one stubbornly resorts to warfare —
this is what the Spring and Autumn Annals profoundly detests,
for it is entirely contrary to righteousness."
The objector says:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals records warfare
with both disapproval and approval —
condemning treacherous attacks but approving formal battles,
shaming attacks on mourning states yet honoring revenge.
How can you claim it condemns all warfare as unrighteous?"
The response:
"When the Spring and Autumn Annals records disasters and anomalies,
even a few stalks in a field
are described as 'no wheat seedlings';
now considering the vastness of the realm
across three centuries,
where military campaigns are beyond counting,
with only two instances of just revenge —
how does this differ from calling a field with few stalks 'no wheat seedlings'?
These exceptions cannot refute the principle,
hence we declare there are no righteous wars.
If denying unrighteous wars is unacceptable,
then denying wheat seedlings should be too;
if accepting the absence of wheat seedlings is valid,
then accepting no righteous wars is equally valid.
As for the Annals' treatment of formal battles,
it approves the formality,
not the warfare itself —
evidence confirms this.
The Spring and Autumn Annals cherishes people,
yet warfare kills people —
how can a nobleman possibly approve killing those he cherishes?
Therefore, its treatment of formal battles
resembles its treatment of the Central States:
compared to Lǔ,
they are called external;
compared to barbarians,
they are called internal.
Compared to treacherous warfare,
it is called righteous;
compared to non-warfare,
it is called unrighteous.
Thus alliances are inferior to no alliances,
yet some are called good alliances;
warfare is inferior to no warfare,
yet some are called good warfare.
Unrighteousness contains elements of righteousness,
righteousness contains elements of unrighteousness.
Words cannot fully capture this,
all meaning resides in the intention —
unless one meticulously comprehends the thought,
who can possibly understand it?
The Book of Songs says:
'The cherry tree's flowers,
wave in reverse.
How could I not miss you?
But your dwelling is far away.'
The Master said:
'He is not truly thinking of her,
or what distance would there be?'
From this we see
that those who grasp the intention
do not cling to the words.
Not clinging to the words,
then one may walk the path together."
"Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn, as his lord's envoy,
disregarded his lord's command,
shared intelligence with the enemy,
acceded to their request,
and made peace with Sòng,
thus exercising authority internally and appropriating reputation externally.
Exercising authority diminishes the lord,
appropriating reputation shows disloyalty,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals praises him greatly,
for what reason?"
The response said:
"Because he possessed profound compassion,
he could not bear to let the people of an entire state starve,
forcing them to cannibalize each other.
Extending kindness makes it far-reaching and great,
practicing benevolence naturally makes it beautiful.
Now Zǐfǎn acted from his own heart,
pitying the people of Sòng,
without calculating the implications,
therefore he is praised greatly."
The critic said:
"According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
ministers should not concern themselves with other feudal lords,
governance should not rest with the grand officers.
Zǐfǎn, as a minister of Chǔ, showed compassion for the people of Sòng,
this is concerning himself with other feudal lords;
not reporting back to his lord but making peace with the enemy,
this is governance resting with the grand officers.
At the Júliáng covenant,
when trust was placed in the grand officers,
the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized it,
because it usurped the lord's authority;
peace being made by the grand officers,
also usurps the lord's authority,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals praises it greatly,
this is the contradiction.
Moreover, according to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
it condemns ministers appropriating their lord's good name.
Therefore loyal ministers do not openly remonstrate,
desiring that initiatives come from the lord.
The Book of Documents says:
'When you have good plans and good counsels,
enter and report them to your lord within,
then you should follow them without,
saying:
These plans and these counsels,
are due to the virtue of our lord.'
This is the rule for being a minister.
The good grand officers of old,
all served their lords in this manner.
Now Zǐfǎn, though near his lord, did not return to report,
though he could have seen King Zhuāng, did not inform him,
all because he resolved the difficulties between two states,
considering it unavoidable,
but what about his usurping the lord's good name!
This is what is perplexing."
The response said:
"The Way of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
inherently has constants and variations,
variations apply to changing circumstances,
constants apply to regular situations,
each stops at its proper category,
they do not interfere with each other.
What you various gentlemen cite,
are all universal constants,
the meaning of conventional agreement;
Zǐfǎn's conduct,
was an exceptional variation,
the meaning of principled flexibility.
When the eyes are startled, the body loses its composure,
when the mind is shocked, matters are forgotten,
this is human nature;
those who understand the nature of shock,
take the one good aspect,
without dwelling on all the faults.
The Book of Songs says:
'When gathering the mustard plant and the radish,
do not reject them for their roots.'
This expresses the meaning.
When Zǐfǎn went to inspect Sòng,
heard of people eating each other,
was greatly shocked and pitied them,
never imagining it had come to this,
therefore his heart alarmed and eyes agitated, he violated conventional ritual.
Ritual,
approximates benevolence,
formed through refinement and substance to become complete.
Now causing people to eat each other,
greatly loses benevolence,
how can ritual be established?
While saving the substance,
why worry about the refinement?
Therefore it is said:
'When facing benevolence, do not defer.'
This expresses the meaning.
The phrasing of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
has what is called base,
and what is baser than base.
Where there is what is baser than base,
then there is also what is nobler than noble.
Now deference is what the Spring and Autumn Annals values,
even so,
seeing people eat each other,
shocked at people using each other as fuel,
saving them while forgetting deference,
the Way of the gentleman,
has what is more valuable than deference,
therefore those who explain the Spring and Autumn Annals,
should not use constant principles of peaceful rule,
to doubt the great standards for changing circumstances,
the meaning can almost be understood."
The Spring and Autumn Annals records the successes and failures of the world,
and reveals the reasons behind them.
Profound yet clear,
without commentary yet evident,
it cannot be left unexamined.
Even the greatness of Mount Tài,
if unexamined remains unseen,
how much more so what is subtle and minute!
Therefore, consulting the Spring and Autumn Annals and tracing past events,
exhausting their origins and examining their causes,
successful gentlemen,
joyful people,
cannot but be cautious.
Qí's Duke Qìng was the grandson of Duke Huán of Qí,
his state was vast and its terrain advantageous,
he also inherited the remaining prestige of a hegemon,
and his ambition extended over the feudal lords,
for these reasons,
he was difficult to summon to meetings,
and easily made arrogant and extravagant.
In the nine years since his accession,
harbored anger toward Lǔ and Wèi,
and did not follow the feudal lords to Qīngqiū and Duàndào.
In spring he went to attack Lǔ,
entered its northern suburbs,
then turned back to attack Wèi,
defeating them at Xīnzhù;
at that time,
riding on victory and with expanded ambition,
when a great state came to visit,
he treated its envoys with contempt and disrespect,
angering both Jìn and Lǔ,
who mobilized all their forces internally,
and externally gained allies in Wèi and Cáo,
four states supporting each other,
greatly besieged him at Ān,
captured Duke Qìng of Qí,
and executed Féng Chǒufù.
Tracing deeply the origin of why Duke Qìng suffered great personal humiliation,
nearly lost his state,
and became the laughingstock of the world,
the beginning was his intimidation of Lǔ and victory over Wèi;
attacking Lǔ,
Lǔ dared not come out;
striking Wèi,
greatly defeating them;
thus becoming emboldened and, with no enemy state to cause concern, giving rise to disaster.
Therefore it is said:
success brings joy,
but one cannot be unwary.
This is the proof.
After this,
Duke Qìng became fearful,
ceased listening to music,
refrained from drinking alcohol and eating meat;
internally, he loved the common people,
inquired after the sick and mourned the dead;
externally, he respected the feudal lords,
attended meetings and joined alliances;
until the end of his life,
his household and state were peaceful and secure.
Thus the root of blessing is born from worry,
while calamity arises from joy.
Alas!
The reasons behind things,
how closely they concern humanity,
can they not be reflected upon!
"Féng Chǒufù sacrificed his own life to save his sovereign,
why is he not considered to have understood expediency?
Chǒufù deceived Jìn,
while Jì Zhòng yielded to Sòng,
both distorted righteousness to preserve their sovereigns,
yet what Chǒufù did
was more difficult than Jì Zhòng's action,
Jì Zhòng was praised as worthy,
while Chǒufù was still criticized,
why is this?"
The response said:
"The difficulty in distinguishing right from wrong lies here.
These are cases where the circumstances appear similar but follow different principles,
which must be carefully examined.
To abdicate position and yield to brothers
is highly valued by the gentleman;
to be captured and flee
is deeply despised by the gentleman.
Jì Zhòng placed his sovereign in what people highly value to preserve him,
therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals considered him to understand expediency and praised him;
Chǒufù placed his sovereign in what people deeply despise to preserve him,
the Spring and Autumn Annals considered him not to understand expediency and condemned him.
Though both distorted righteousness to preserve their sovereigns,
appearing similar;
whether they brought honor or disgrace to their sovereign
follows different principles.
Thus whenever people take action,
if they first deviate but later achieve righteousness,
it is called balanced expediency,
even if unsuccessful,
the Spring and Autumn Annals approves it,
as with Lǔ Yǐngōng and Zhèng's Jì Zhòng;
if they begin correctly but later deviate,
it is called wicked path,
even if successful,
the Spring and Autumn Annals does not commend it,
as with Qí Qīnggōng and Féng Chǒufù.
To endure great disgrace to survive,
brings no joy in one's heart,
therefore the worthy person does not do it,
though ordinary people may doubt this,
the Spring and Autumn Annals believes people doubt because they don't understand righteousness,
thus it demonstrates through righteousness,
saying:
'When the state falls,
the sovereign should die with it,
this is correctness.'
Correctness means
aligning with Heaven's endowment of human nature and life,
Heaven's endowment of human nature and life
makes humans practice benevolence and righteousness while ashamed of disgrace,
unlike birds and beasts
who merely seek survival
and profit alone.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals extends Heaven's bestowal and follows human principle,
considering the most honored cannot live through ultimate disgrace,
thus the captured should be cut off;
considering ultimate disgrace cannot be imposed upon the most honored position,
thus even if losing position,
one is no longer sovereign;
even after returning to the state,
and resuming position,
the Spring and Autumn Annals still uses non-sovereign terminology,
let alone when confusedly captured as prisoner!
In terms of righteousness,
he was definitely not sovereign,
if not sovereign,
then how could Chǒufù claim expediency!
Thus deceiving three armies was a great crime against Jìn,
saving Qīnggōng brought disgrace to Qí's ancestral temple,
therefore though difficult, the Spring and Autumn Annals does not commend it.
Chǒufù, in great righteousness,
should have told Qīnggōng:
'You insulted and angered the feudal lords,
this was greatly losing propriety;
now suffering great disgrace but unable to die,
this is shameless;
and would further incur grave offense,
I beg we die together,
not to disgrace the ancestral temple,
not to shame the altars of soil and grain.'
Had he done so,
though sacrificing himself,
he would have preserved an honorable name,
at such moment,
death would be better than life,
thus for the gentleman, living in disgrace
is worse than dying with honor,
this expresses the correct principle.
Judging by standards,
then Chǒufù deceived but missed expediency,
was loyal but missed righteousness,
do you think otherwise?
Reexamine the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Annals' arrangement of terms,
placing the king between spring and correctness,
means not that:
only those serving Heaven's bestowal above and correcting people below
can become kings, and so on!
Now praising good and condemning evil,
loving honor and hating disgrace,
are not things humans generate themselves,
these are Heaven's endowments in humans,
the gentleman judges by Heaven's endowments in humans,
then Chǒufù was not loyal,
Heaven's endowments in humans
give humans sense of shame.
Those with sense of shame
do not live through great disgrace,
no disgrace greater than losing the south-facing throne and being bound captive.
Zēngzǐ said:
'If disgrace can be avoided,
avoid it;
when it cannot be avoided,
the gentleman looks upon death as going home.'
This refers to cases like Qīnggōng."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'Zhèng attacked Xǔ.'
Why condemn Zhèng and treat it as barbarian?"
The response said:
"When Wèi's marquis Sù died,
Zhèng's army invaded them,
this was attacking mourners;
Zhèng made covenant with feudal lords at Shǔ,
having covenanted then dismissed the lords,
whereupon Zhèng attacked,
this was betraying the covenant.
Attacking mourners lacks righteousness,
betraying covenant lacks trustworthiness,
lacking trust and righteousness,
therefore it was greatly condemned."
The questioner said:
"Here the sovereign died,
his son not yet past the mourning year,
he is called earl rather than viscount,
what crime does this terminology indicate?"
The response said:
"According to ancient kings' system,
those with great mourning
should not be summoned for three years,
respecting that their mind is not on affairs.
The Book of Documents says:
'Emperor Gāozōng in mourning hut,
did not speak for three years.'
This is the meaning of mourning observance.
Now even if unable to do exactly this,
how could he raise troops in mourning
before his father's death passed a year?
The Spring and Autumn Annals, for his shallow kindness
and losing his son's heart,
thus no longer calls him viscount,
calling him Earl of Zhèng instead,
to disgrace him.
Moreover, his predecessor Duke Xiāng attacked mourners and betrayed covenants,
offending the feudal lords,
their anger not yet subsided,
their hatred not ended,
his successor
should strive for goodness to redeem it,
yet now he repeated it,
hence attacking others during mourning;
the father attacked others in mourning,
the son attacked others while in mourning;
the father added unrighteousness to others,
the son showed lack of filial duty to his parent,
thereby offending the central states;
thus the father bore old faults ahead,
he himself raised great faults behind.
The feudal lords indeed angrily hated him,
united and came together,
planning joint attack against him,
Zhèng then feared,
left Chǔ and made the Gǔláo covenant.
Chǔ and the central states pressed and attacked him,
Zhèng became exhausted and endangered,
终生忧愁不幸。
We trace its origin,
defeated by lack of righteousness,
due to such careless mind.
Confucius said:
'To govern a state of thousand chariots,
handle affairs respectfully and keep trust.'
Knowing this greatly affects gain and loss,
thus handle it respectfully and carefully.
Now the Earl of Zhèng, lacking son's kindness,
and not deliberating carefully,
once raising troops inappropriately,
suffered endless troubles,
brought it upon himself.
Therefore living he is not called viscount,
losing his righteous status;
dead he is not recorded buried,
showing his desperation.
It is said:
rulers of states observe this,
if conducting oneself without following righteousness,
undertaking affairs without examining timing,
what else could result but this?"
"The Fourth Chapter of Jade Blossoms"
states that the Primordial Unity
is the Great Beginning.
Understanding the record of the inaugural year
is valued by the noble,
but neglected by the petty.
Hence, the foundation of governing a state lies in rectifying names.
When names are rectified,
five generations prosper,
and beyond five transmissions,
good and evil become manifest,
which can be said to grasp the truth,
something beyond Zǐlù's perception.
Assuming a position not rightfully one's own,
even if received from a former ruler,
the Spring and Autumn Annals regards it as perilous,
as with Duke Mù of Sòng;
not rightfully one's position,
not received from a former ruler,
yet seizing it personally,
the Spring and Autumn Annals regards it as perilous,
as with King Liáo of Wú;
nevertheless,
if one can practice goodness and win the people's support,
the Spring and Autumn Annals does not deem it perilous,
as with Marquis Jìn of Wèi being recorded as buried with legitimacy.
Though both were unfit to stand,
Duke Mù of Sòng, receiving it from a former ruler, was deemed perilous,
while Duke Xuān of Wèi, not receiving it from a former ruler, was not deemed perilous,
showing that winning the people's hearts is paramount for security.
Thus Duke Huán of Qí not only did not receive it from a former ruler,
but also led those unfit to be rulers to stand,
his offense being grave indeed.
However, knowing fear and caution,
he promoted worthy men to cover his faults,
and did not betray key covenants to cleanse himself,
thus becoming a worthy ruler,
and hegemon among the feudal lords;
had Duke Huán of Qí borne evil without this virtue,
escaping execution or destruction would have been fortunate enough,
let alone achieving hegemony!
Duke Huán of Lǔ forgot his worries,
and disaster befell him;
Duke Huán of Qí worried over his worries,
and achieved merit and fame.
Extending this broadly,
all who have worries but do not know to worry meet misfortune,
while those who have worries and deeply concern themselves with them meet good fortune.
The Book of Changes says:
'Returning to the proper path,
what blame is there?'
This refers to this idea.
For a commoner to reverse course to eliminate blame is still difficult,
for a ruler to reverse course to eliminate blame is very easy.
The Book of Songs says:
'Virtue is as light as a hair.'
Meaning it is easy.
"The duke watched fish at Táng;
what was wrong with that?"
"By human nature,
none do not uphold righteousness,
yet those who fail to act righteously
are led astray by profit;
thus the nobleman speaks all day without mentioning profit,
wishing only to shame them by silence,
shaming them to block the source.
Those in positions influencing customs and transformation,
merely uttering the name of profit,
still detest it,
let alone seeking profit!
Thus when the Son of Heaven sent men to seek funeral gifts or gold,
both were recorded as great wrongs.
Now, not only sending others,
but personally seeking it,
is an even greater wrong.
Why criticize by saying 'watched fish'?
It is like saying 'watched the community sacrifice,'
both being euphemisms for great wrongs."
The Spring and Autumn Annals has constant rites,
and adaptive rites.
Those that calm nature and pacify the mind are constant rites;
there are those that,
though unsettling to nature,
and disturbing to the mind,
cannot be altered in principle,
these are adaptive rites.
Thus, in marriage rites not naming the host
is a constant rite;
when words are exhausted and none can be named,
naming the host
is an adaptive rite.
The Son of Heaven being called king only after three years
is a constant rite;
if there are exigencies,
then being called king before three years
is an adaptive rite.
Women not leaving the state
is a constant rite;
a mother fetching a wife for her son,
or rushing to mourn her parents,
are adaptive rites.
Understanding constant and adaptive matters,
one then knows the distinction between light and heavy,
and can adapt to expediency.
A critic asks:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals uses the same wording for similar events.
These four are all adaptive rites,
yet some align with constant rites,
others do not align with constant rites,
why?"
Reply:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals orders all things,
distinguishes categories,
clarifies subtleties,
and cultivates roots and branches.
Thus, falling stars are called 'falling,'
locusts falling are called 'rain,'
their origins differ,
some descending from heaven,
some arising from earth,
their wording cannot be the same.
Now these four are all adaptive rites alike,
but their origins also differ,
some arising from men,
some from women,
their wording cannot be the same.
Thus some align with the constant,
some align with the adaptive."
Duke Huán's intent showed no king,
thus 'king' was not recorded;
his intent was to assume the throne,
thus 'ascending the throne' was recorded.
Recording 'ascending the throne'
indicates his murder of his elder brother the ruler;
not recording 'king'
shows his defiance of the Son of Heaven.
Hence, for Duke Yǐn not saying 'correct,'
and for Duke Huán not saying 'king,'
both follow their intents to reveal their deeds.
Following the intent of the worthy
to express their righteousness;
following the intent of the unworthy
to highlight their evil.
From this perspective,
what the Spring and Autumn Annals praises is good,
what it does not praise is not good,
one must reflect on both.
"The Classic states:
'Sòng Dū assassinated his ruler Yǔyí.'
The Commentary says:
'It was Zhuāng Gōng Féng who killed him.'
This is not recorded in the Classic,
why is that?"
The response is:
"It is not that it could not have been recorded in the Classic,
but the connection is subtle,
insufficient to categorize and link it,
hence it is difficult to know.
The Commentary says:
'Zāngsūn Xǔ and Jìn Xì Kè at the same time visited Qí on diplomatic missions.'
Checking the Classic, there is no record of this,
is it not subtle indeed!
Not recording their going
is because there was avoidance.
Now this Commentary mentions Zhuāng Gōng Féng,
but it is not written in the Classic,
also because there is reason to avoid it.
Therefore, not recording the visit to Qí
avoids what is shameful;
not recording Zhuāng Gōng Féng's killing
avoids what is good.
Thus, yielding is what the Spring and Autumn Annals praises.
Duke Xuān did not pass the throne to his son but to his younger brother,
and his younger brother also did not pass it to his own son but returned it to his elder brother's son.
Although this did not conform to the law,
both acts embodied the virtue of yielding,
which cannot be discarded.
Therefore, the nobleman conceals it.
Not adhering to the proper succession is called avoidance, as later it leads to disorder;
shifting the blame to Sòng Dū
preserves the good intention.
This is also the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
that no good deed is left unacknowledged.
If it directly recorded the usurpation,
then the noble acts of Duke Xuān and Duke Mù would be obliterated,
and the good would not be visible."
The questioner says:
"Concealing for the sake of the worthy is always spoken of;
concealing for Duke Xuān and Duke Mù,
why is it not mentioned?"
The response is:
"Because they did not achieve the status of worthies.
Their good deeds were not according to the law,
neither acceptable
nor discardable.
To discard them would be to discard good intentions;
to accept them would harm the king's law.
Therefore, they are neither discarded nor recorded,
but only hinted at.
If the intention is toward benevolence,
there is no evil.
This is what it means."
"That vessels follow their names and lands follow their masters is called regulation,
the beginning of weighing circumstances,
which must not be overlooked.
Although weighing circumstances may contradict the classics,
it must lie within the permissible realm.
If it is not within the permissible realm,
then even facing death,
one ultimately must not do it,
as with Gōngzǐ Mùyí.
Therefore, when feudal lords' fathers, sons, or brothers are installed improperly,
the Spring and Autumn Annals views their state as no different from one with a properly installed ruler;
these all lie within the permissible realm.
As for Zēng being taken by Jǔ,
considering them as co-residents,
it is recorded as 'the Jǔ people destroyed Zēng,'
this is not within the permissible realm.
Thus, feudal lords outside the permissible realm
are said to possess great virtue;
great virtue does not overstep bounds,
called upholding the classics.
Feudal lords within the permissible realm
are said to possess minor virtue;
minor virtue may allow some flexibility.
Weighing circumstances and stratagems
still ultimately return to uphold the great classics.
Therefore, the way of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is broad yet essential,
detailed yet returning to unity,
all one.
Gōngzǐ Mùyí restored his ruler
but ultimately did not take the state;
Jì Zhòng initially gave it
but later changed it;
Jìn Xún Xī died without virtue;
Wèi Màngū resisted and did not admit the ruler.
These four ministers' actions differed but their hearts were the same,
their righteousness one.
Mùyí not taking the state
valued the ancestral temple;
Jì Zhòng giving it
also valued the ancestral temple;
Xún Xī dying for it
honored the former ruler's command;
Màngū resisting it
also honored the former ruler's command.
Though their actions were opposite,
their purpose was the same,
all to value the ancestral temple and honor the former ruler's command."
The questioner says:
"What Gōngzǐ Mùyí and Jì Zhòng did
both preserved their service to the ruler,
so it is good to praise them;
but Xún Xī and Màngū had no such deeds,
and those they supported
were all improperly installed,
how can they be recorded as righteous?"
The response is:
"The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is:
if a ruler installs someone improperly,
it is not recorded;
if a minister installs,
it is recorded.
Recording it
does not approve of the minister installing someone improper;
not recording it
approves of the ruler's installation.
For a ruler to install someone improper
is wrong;
once installed,
if the minister serves him,
it is right;
this is the righteousness of Xún Xī and Màngū."
The critic questioned Jì Jì, saying:
"According to the methods of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
senior officials should not cede territory.
It also says:
nobles should not have the principle of leaving their state.
It further states:
the noble man does not avoid external calamities.
Jì Jì violated these three principles,
how can he be considered virtuous!
Would a virtuous minister indeed steal land to appease the enemy,
and abandon his ruler to avoid disaster?"
The response was:
"The virtuous do not act in this manner.
Therefore, attributing virtue to Jì Jì
serves to show what Jì did not do;
that Jì Jì did not act thus, yet the Marquis of Jì sent him, makes this clear.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, in recording events,
sometimes conceals the truth,
to avoid certain implications;
in recording people,
it sometimes alters names,
to practice concealment.
Thus, it concealed the truth about Duke Wén of Jìn achieving his ambition,
to avoid mentioning his summoning the king;
it referred to the ruler of Jǔ as a commoner,
to conceal Duke Yǐn;
it changed Qìngfǔ's name to Zhòngsūn;
altered Shèng to Chéng,
to conceal great evils.
Therefore, those who interpret the Spring and Autumn Annals
must penetrate these deceptive expressions,
follow their intricacies,
and only then grasp the meaning.
Now Jì Jì received orders from his ruler, yet the classic records it as his own initiative,
without a single word of praise yet the text presents him as virtuous,
these are all deceptive expressions,
which must be carefully examined.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, regarding those it considers virtuous,
consistently follows their intentions and unifies the narrative,
highlighting their righteousness and praising their goodness.
Now the Marquis of Jì is esteemed by the Spring and Autumn Annals,
hence it accedes to his intention to enter Qí,
but transfers the expression of submitting to guilt
to Jì Jì.
Thus, the one who sought grain from Qí
was actually Duke Zhuāng who did it,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals alters the account,
attributing it to Zāngsūn Chén;
the one who offered Xī to Qí
was actually the Marquis of Jì who did it,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals alters the account,
attributing it to Jì Jì;
though the methods of alteration differ,
the essence is the same."
The critic asked:
"Those who possess states and families,
if others wish to establish them,
should firmly refuse entirely;
if the state is destroyed,
the ruler should die for it,
that is correct;
why then consider the Marquis of Jì virtuous?"
The response was:
"Qí was about to seek revenge,
the Marquis of Jì knew his strength was insufficient,
yet intended to resist it,
so he told his younger brother:
'I am the master of our ancestral temple,
I cannot but die,
you take Xī and go,
submit to Qí,
requesting to establish the five temples,
so that our former rulers may have a place to rely on during seasonal sacrifices.'
Leading the multitude of the entire state,
to defend the temple of nine generations of rulers,
Duke Xiāng drove them away but they did not leave,
sought them but they did not yield,
high and low were united in heart and all died together,
therefore it is called the great departure.
The Spring and Autumn Annals considers dying for righteousness virtuous,
and he also gained the people's hearts,
hence it conceals the destruction.
By concealing for him,
it shows his virtue.
Because he is considered virtuous,
it reveals his embodiment of benevolence and righteousness."
Essence and Flower, Fifth
The Spring and Autumn Annals is cautious in wording,
meticulous in naming relationships and classifying things.
Therefore, minor barbarians are said to be attacked but not said to fight,
major barbarians are said to fight but not said to be captured,
central states are said to be captured but not said to be seized,
each has its specific terminology.
There are cases where minor barbarians avoid major barbarians and thus cannot be said to fight,
major barbarians avoid central states and thus cannot be said to be captured,
central states avoid the Son of Heaven and thus cannot be said to be seized,
the naming of relationships does not grant,
implying expressions of subservience.
Therefore, great and small do not exceed their ranks,
noble and base correspond to their relationships,
this is the correctness of righteousness.
What is the Great Rain Sacrifice?
It is a sacrifice during drought.
The critic asked:
"During great drought, the Rain Sacrifice is performed to pray for rain,
during great flood, drums are beaten to attack the earth altar,
these are acts of heaven and earth,
arising from yin and yang,
why sometimes pray and sometimes show anger?"
The response was:
"Great drought is yang extinguishing yin,
yang extinguishing yin means
the noble suppressing the base,
which is inherently righteous,
even if severe,
one only bows and prays,
daring not to add anything more.
Great flood is yin extinguishing yang,
yin extinguishing yang means
the base overcoming the noble,
solar eclipses are similar,
all are cases of inferiors offending superiors, the base harming the noble,
which is rebellious conduct,
hence drums are beaten to attack it,
red threads are used to coerce it,
because it is unrighteous,
this also shows the Spring and Autumn Annals' fearlessness of the strong.
Thus, to change the positions of heaven and earth,
correct the sequence of yin and yang,
directly practice the Way,
without forgetting the difficulties,
is the ultimate righteousness.
Therefore, coercing the solemn earth altar is not disrespectful to the spirits,
expelling the Heavenly King is not dishonoring the superior,
refusing a father's command is not disobedient to the parent,
severing maternal ties is not unfilial or unkind,
this is righteousness indeed!"
The critic asked:
"According to the methods of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
senior officials should not act on their own initiative.
It also says:
beyond the borders, if there is something that can secure the altars of soil and grain and benefit the state,
then taking initiative is permissible.
It further states:
when senior officials go out on the ruler's orders,
advance or retreat is up to the senior official.
It also says:
upon hearing of mourning, proceed slowly but do not return.
Now, it says not to act on one's own initiative,
yet also says taking initiative is permissible.
It says advance or retreat is up to the senior official,
yet also says proceed slowly and do not return.
They seem contradictory,
what does this mean?"
The response was:
"These four each have their appropriate context,
if the context is right,
then all are correct;
if the context is wrong,
then all are incorrect.
The Spring and Autumn Annals has constant principles,
but also responds to changing circumstances.
'Not acting on one's own initiative'
refers to times of peace and stability;
'taking initiative is permissible'
refers to rescuing danger and eliminating disasters;
'advance or retreat is up to the senior official'
refers to generals commanding troops;
'proceed slowly and do not return'
means not letting kinship harm honor,
not letting private matters hinder public duty;
this is called grasping the subtleties,
understanding the intent.
Thus, when Gōngzǐ Jié received orders to escort a bride to Jì for a Chén man,
he initiated matters along the way,
forming an alliance with Duke Huán of Qí,
the Spring and Autumn Annals does not condemn this,
considering it saved Duke Zhuāng from danger.
When Gōngzǐ Suì received orders to go to the capital,
he initiated matters along the way,
going to Jìn,
the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns this,
considering that at that time Duke Xī was secure without danger needing rescue.
Therefore, having danger but not taking initiative to rescue
is called disloyalty;
having no danger but presumptuously initiating matters
is belittling the ruler.
Thus, these two ministers both initiated matters,
the Spring and Autumn Annals approves one and disapproves the other,
such is the meaning of righteousness."
Duke Huán of Qí, possessing the capability of a virtuous minister,
and utilizing the resources of a major state,
five years after his accession,
was unable to summon even one feudal lord.
At the covenant of Kē,
he demonstrated his great trustworthiness,
and within a year,
the rulers of nearby states all arrived,
as seen in the meetings of Juàn and Yōu.
In the following twenty years,
which was quite a long time,
he still had not managed to assemble the feudal lords extensively.
It was only with the events of rescuing Xíng and Wèi,
where he displayed the principle of preserving the perishing and continuing the severed lines,
that the next year,
the rulers of distant states all arrived,
as in the meetings of Guànzé and Yánggǔ.
Hence it is said:
"To draw the near, one does not rely on words;
to summon the distant, one does not rely on envoys."
This is the evidence of it.
Later, he boasted of his achievements,
became arrogant and self-satisfied,
and no longer cultivated virtue.
Thus, when the people of Chǔ extinguished Xián, he showed no concern,
and when Jiāng and Huáng attacked Chén, he did not go to rescue them.
He harmed other states
and detained their high officials.
He did not save Chén from its distress,
yet blamed Chén for not breaking away.
He did not restore peace to Zhèng,
but insisted on pressuring them with military force.
Before his achievements were fully accomplished,
his ambition had already become complacent.
Therefore, it is said:
"How small was Guǎn Zhòng's capacity!"
This refers to this.
From then on, he declined daily,
and nine states rebelled.
The Spring and Autumn Annals in hearing legal cases
must base them on the facts and trace the intent.
Those with evil intent
need not wait for the act to be completed;
the chief culprits
are punished especially heavily;
those whose basis is upright
are judged lightly.
Thus, Féng Chǒufù deserved beheading,
but Yuán Táotú should not have been detained;
Jìzǐ of Lǔ pursued Qìngfù,
while Jìzǐ of Wú released Hélú.
In these four cases,
the crimes were similar but the judgments differed,
because their fundamental motives varied.
Both deceived the three armies,
yet one died and the other did not;
both assassinated their rulers,
yet one was punished and the other was not.
In hearing lawsuits and deciding cases,
can one not be careful?
Thus, if a case is decided correctly,
the principle becomes clearer,
and teachings are better implemented;
if a case is decided incorrectly,
it obscures principles and confuses the masses,
conflicting with teachings.
Teachings are the root of governance,
legal cases are the branch of governance.
Their domains differ,
but their function is the same.
They must not be inconsistent,
hence the gentleman values them.
One who questions the Jìn affair said:
"The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is to refer to a ruler who has not passed the first year as 'zǐ',
which reflects the correct sentiment of people.
Yet when Lì Kē killed Xī Qí,
it avoided this proper term and called him 'the ruler's son'.
Why is that?"
The response was:
"It is said that the Odes have no fixed interpretation,
the Changes have no fixed divination,
the Spring and Autumn Annals have no fixed terminology.
Follow the changes and follow righteousness,
unifying all to serve humanity.
A benevolent person records the calamity of those of the same surname,
and thus should change the approach.
Jìn was of the same surname as the Spring and Autumn Annals.
With one scheme of Lí Jī,
three rulers died because of it,
a sorrow shared by all under heaven.
Tracing the reason for their actions,
they were blinded by their desire to obtain the throne,
and did not see the difficulties.
The Spring and Autumn Annals detest this blindness,
so it removed the term of rank,
merely calling him 'the ruler's son'.
As if saying to Xī Qí:
'Alas!
Being the son of a great state's ruler,
you had enough wealth and honor;
why did you desire to occupy your elder brother's position,
leading to this outcome?'
It records the words of sorrow.
Thus, within sorrow there is sorrow:
those who were innocent yet suffered death,
such as Shēn Shēng, Xī Qí, and Zhuō Zǐ;
within evil there is evil:
one who established himself,
and then killed himself,
not like other ministers who assassinated their rulers,
such as Prince Shāng Rén of Qí.
Therefore, the calamity of Jìn is sorrowful, while that of Qí is grave.
The Spring and Autumn Annals grieve for the sorrowful and emphasize the grave,
hence it deprives the Jìn son of the term for succession
and grants the Qí son the title of accomplished ruler,
showing this in detail."
The ancients had a saying:
"If you do not know the future,
look to the past."
Now, the study of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is about elucidating the past to illuminate the future.
However, its wording embodies the subtlety of Heaven,
so it is difficult to understand.
If one cannot discern it,
it seems silent and nonexistent;
if one can discern it,
nothing is beyond its scope.
Therefore, those who study the Spring and Autumn Annals
grasp one thread and connect it widely,
see one point and penetrate it comprehensively,
then all under heaven is encompassed.
Duke Xī of Lǔ ascended the throne amidst turmoil,
yet knew to closely rely on Jìzǐ.
While Jìzǐ was unharmed,
there was no internal disorder among ministers,
no external troubles from feudal lords.
This lasted twenty years,
with the state peaceful and stable;
after Jìzǐ's death,
Lǔ could not withstand the troubles from neighboring states,
and simply begged for troops from Chǔ.
Duke Xī's situation was not due to sudden incompetence,
yet the state declined and became more endangered.
Why?
Because there was no Jìzǐ.
Seeing that the people of Lǔ were like this,
one knows that other states are all like this.
Knowing that other states are all like this,
one knows that all under heaven is like this.
This is called connecting and penetrating,
so even though all under heaven is vast,
and past and present are long,
it is determined by this.
Employing the worthy
leads to the ruler's honor and the state's security.
Employing the unworthy
leads to the ruler's humiliation and the state's danger.
This is inevitable for all ages,
without any doubt.
As the Changes say:
"The cauldron's legs break,
overturning the duke's meal."
The breaking of the cauldron's legs
means employing the unworthy;
overturning the duke's meal
means the state topples.
Therefore, employing the unworthy without the state toppling
has never been heard of from ancient times to the present.
Thus, I examine the Spring and Autumn Annals to observe success and failure,
and deeply grieve over the rise and fall of past generations.
Employing worthy ministers
leads to the state's prosperity.
If one's wisdom is insufficient to recognize the worthy,
there is no alternative;
but knowing them yet not employing them
leads in major cases to death and loss,
in minor cases to chaos and danger.
How should one deal with this?
Did Duke Zhuāng not know that Jìzǐ was worthy?
Why, knowing he was ill and near death, did he summon him and entrust him with the state?
Did Duke Shāng not know that Kǒng Fù was worthy?
Why, knowing that if Kǒng Fù died he would surely die, did he rush to save him?
Both rulers had sufficient wisdom to recognize the worthy,
yet were indecisive,
and could not employ them.
Thus, Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ faced danger,
and Duke Shāng of Sòng was assassinated.
If Duke Zhuāng had employed Jìzǐ earlier,
and Duke Shāng had consistently employed Kǒng Fù,
they might have prospered and even influenced neighboring states,
let alone merely avoiding assassination!
This is what I deeply grieve and lament.
The Kingly Way, Part Six
Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals value the term "origin" and speak of it?
The origin is the beginning,
signifying that the foundation is correct;
the Way is the Way of the True King;
the king is the beginning of humanity.
When the king is correct,
then the primordial energy is harmonious, winds and rains come in season, auspicious stars appear, and yellow dragons descend;
when the king is not correct,
then changes occur in the heavens above,
and baleful energies appear together.
Under the rule of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
no one in the world dared to possess [excess],
the hearts of rulers and people [were aligned],
with a tax of one-tenth.
They were taught with love,
employed with loyalty,
respected the elders,
cherished their kin and honored the honorable,
did not rob the people of their farming seasons,
and required labor from the people no more than three days a year,
so that households were well-supplied and people had enough,
without the troubles of resentment and anger, or conflicts between the strong and weak,
without slanderous, harmful, envious, or hateful individuals,
the people cultivated virtue and were virtuous and fine,
roaming with loose hair and food in their mouths,
not coveting wealth and honor,
ashamed of evil and not committing it,
fathers did not weep for sons,
elder brothers did not weep for younger brothers,
venomous insects did not sting,
fierce beasts did not attack,
and horned creatures did not gore,
therefore heaven sent down sweet dew for them,
vermilion grass grew,
sweet springs emerged,
winds and rains were timely,
bountiful grain flourished,
phoenixes and qílín roamed the suburbs,
prisons were empty,
and even with symbolic penalties painted on clothing, the people did not offend,
the four barbarian tribes came through interpreters to pay homage,
the people's nature was utterly simple and unadorned,
they sacrificed to heaven at the border and to earth,
ordered the mountains and rivers,
and in due time proceeded to fēng-sacrifice on Tài Shān and shàn-sacrifice on Liángfù.
They established the Bright Hall,
reverently sacrificed to the former emperors,
matching ancestors with heaven,
and all the feudal lords under heaven came to sacrifice according to their duties.
They offered the products of their lands,
first presenting them in the ancestral temple,
then, wearing formal caps and robes, they appeared before their ancestors.
The repayment of virtuous grace
is the response to honoring the origin.
Jié and Zhòu were both descendants of sage kings,
yet they became arrogant and acted recklessly.
They built extravagant palaces,
expanded parks and preserves,
exhausted the variations of the five colors,
pushed the craft of ornate materials to the extreme,
trapped the feet of wild beasts,
drained the benefits of mountains and marshes,
and ate vicious animals of all kinds.
They seized the people's wealth and food,
elevated the spectacle of carved and engraved decorations,
exhausted the craftsmanship of gold, jade, bone, and ivory,
abounded in ornaments of feathered creatures,
and pursued every variation of white and black,
imposed harsh punishments and wanton killings to oppress those below,
listened to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
indulged the desires of their leaning palaces,
and kept rare animals like líng, tiger, sì, and those with patterned hides,
for the thrill of novelty,
rewarding flatterers and bestowing gifts on slanderers.
They made mounds of dregs,
and ponds of wine,
yet did not care for the orphaned and poor,
killed sages and worthies and split their hearts,
burned people alive to smell their odor,
cut open pregnant women to observe the transformation,
chopped off the feet of morning waders to examine their toes,
killed Méi Bó to make minced meat,
and executed Guǐ Hóu's daughter to take her rings.
Their demands for confiscation were endless,
leaving the world empty and depleted,
ministers feared and trembled,
none dared to be fully loyal,
and Zhòu grew even more self-righteous.
When Zhōu raised troops,
without prior arrangement, eight hundred feudal lords
gathered at the banks of Mèng Jīn,
together to punish Zhòu,
and he greatly lost the world.
The Spring and Autumn Annals takes this as a warning,
recording the disaster at the Bó Shè.
When the Zhōu declined,
the Son of Heaven became weak,
feudal lords governed by force,
great ministers monopolized the state,
officers monopolized cities,
and they could not practice the rituals of measured laws and patterned culture.
Feudal lords turned traitorous,
none upheld tributes or missions,
or presented offerings to the Son of Heaven.
Ministers assassinated their rulers,
sons killed their fathers,
and illegitimate sons murdered their clan heads,
unable to maintain order,
they attacked each other to expand their territories.
Using strength to coerce,
they could not control their subordinates.
The strong swallowed the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
the rich employed the poor,
and annexations knew no end.
Ministers exceeded their positions from below,
and this could not be stopped.
The sun underwent eclipses,
stars fell like rain,
locusts rained down,
Shà Lù collapsed,
summer brought great floods,
winter brought heavy snow,
five meteorites fell in Sòng,
six yì birds flew backward,
frost fell but did not kill the grass,
plum and apricot trees bore fruit,
no rain fell from the first month
until the seventh month of autumn,
earthquakes occurred,
Liáng Shān collapsed,
blocking the river,
which did not flow for three days,
daylight turned dark,
a comet appeared in the east,
and a broom star was seen in Dà Chén.
Quails came to nest,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded these as anomalies,
