thereby revealing the signs of turmoil and disorder.
Confucius clarified gains and losses,
distinguished the noble and the base,
and returned to the root of the Kingly Way.
He criticized the heavenly king to promote great peace.
Censuring evil and reproving the subtle,
he omitted nothing, great or small,
no good, however minor, was left unraised,
no evil, however minor, was left unremoved,
promoting the good and punishing the evil,
he cut them off at the root.
The Heavenly King sent Zǎi Xuān to present funeral gifts for Huì Gōng and Zhòngzǐ,
criticizing the delay in performing duties;
the Heavenly King attacked Zhèng,
reproaching his personal involvement;
meeting with the royal heir,
censuring the demeaning act;
Jì Gōng came to welcome the queen,
condemning the breach of ritual.
Criticizing Jiā Fù for requesting chariots,
Wǔ Shì and Máo Bó for seeking funeral contributions,
the king's men rescuing Wèi.
The royal army was defeated at Mào Róng,
the Heavenly King failed in his duties,
fled to reside in Zhèng,
killed his own brothers,
the royal house fell into chaos,
unable to extend influence beyond,
splitting into Eastern and Western Zhōu,
losing the means to lead the world,
summoning the marquis of Wèi,
unable to secure his compliance;
sending Zǐ Tū to campaign against Wèi,
unable to cut ties;
attacking Zhèng,
unable to secure obedience;
Wú Hài destroyed Jí,
yet unable to punish him.
The feudal lords thus engaged in great turmoil,
usurpations and regicides ceaseless,
ministers oppressing superiors,
arrogating themselves to the Son of Heaven;
the powerful feudal lords exerted authority,
small states were destroyed;
Jìn advanced to invade Zhōu three times,
battled the Heavenly King at Mào Róng,
and severely defeated him;
the Róng captured Fán Bó at Chǔ Qiū,
and took him away;
the feudal lords, harboring resentment and following evil,
launched armies to destroy each other,
annihilating ancestral temples and altars of state,
unable to maintain order;
ministers grew strong,
to the point of assassinating their rulers and fathers;
laws and institutions were abandoned,
and not reinstated,
authority and power severed,
and not restored.
Hence, Zhèng and Lǔ exchanged territories,
Jìn Wén twice summoned the Son of Heaven,
Qí Huán met with the royal heir,
arbitrarily enfeoffed Xíng, Wèi, and Qǐ,
rampaged across the Central States,
intending to rule the world,
Lǔ performed the eight-row dance,
sacrificed to Mount Tài in the north,
offered suburban sacrifices to heaven and earth,
acting as the Son of Heaven would.
Because of this,
thirty-two rulers were assassinated,
fifty-two states perished,
all resulting from the persistence of minor evils.
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" establishes principles:
the Son of Heaven sacrifices to heaven and earth,
feudal lords sacrifice to the altars of state,
mountains and rivers outside their domains are not to be sacrificed to.
While the Son of Heaven exists,
feudal lords may not arbitrarily possess land,
may not arbitrarily enfeoff,
may not detain the Son of Heaven's high officials,
may not perform the Son of Heaven's music,
may not levy the Son of Heaven's taxes,
may not assume the Son of Heaven's honors.
Toward one's ruler and parents, no thought of harm,
if such thoughts arise, they must be punished;
high officials may not hold hereditary posts,
high officials may not annul or alter the ruler's commands.
Establish the heir,
by age not by worth,
establish sons by nobility not by age.
Establish the wife by status not by concubinage,
the Son of Heaven does not treat the maternal relatives as subjects,
draw near to attract the distant,
thus none have ever attracted the distant without first drawing near.
Therefore, regard one's own state as internal and the Central States as external,
regard the Central States as internal and the barbarians as external,
meaning to start from the near.
Feudal lords who come to court are praised,
Zhūlóu Yífù is referred to by his courtesy name,
Téng and Xuē are called marquises,
Jīng is acknowledged as human,
Jiè Gélú is recorded by name;
from within, terms like "arrive" are used,
feudal lords coming is called "court",
high officials coming is called "visit",
this reflects the intent of the kingly way.
In punishing evil, none may be omitted, great or small,
feudal lords may not raise armies for a commoner's cause,
may not detain the Son of Heaven's high officials,
detaining the Son of Heaven's high officials
incurs the same guilt as attacking a state,
capturing Fán Bó is termed an attack;
presenting the eight-row dance,
euphemized as six rows;
Zhèng and Lǔ exchanging territories,
euphemized as borrowing;
Jìn Wén twice summoning the Son of Heaven,
euphemized as a hunt;
Huán Gōng preserving Xíng, Wèi, and Qǐ,
not recorded in the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
inwardly approving his actions,
but legally rejecting and not endorsing them,
as a way to stop chaos,
not what feudal lords should do.
The principle of the "Spring and Autumn Annals":
a minister who does not punish a regicide,
is no minister;
a son who does not avenge a wrong,
is no son;
thus Zhào Dùn was condemned, for the regicide was not punished,
his burial not recorded,
as condemnation by ministers and sons;
Xǔ's heir, Zhǐ, not tasting the medicine,
was condemned as patricide;
Chǔ's prince Bǐ, forced onto the throne,
could not escape death;
Qí Huán and Jìn Wén arbitrarily enfeoffed,
summoned the Son of Heaven,
punished the extinct, restored the severed, preserved the perishing,
invaded, campaigned, met, and assembled,
often acting as the central authority,
saying:
Huán Gōng saved the Central States,
repelled the barbarians,
ultimately subdued Chǔ,
performing deeds fit for a king;
Jìn Wén twice summoning the Son of Heaven,
both were spared punishment,
praised for shepherding the feudal lords,
presenting tribute to the Son of Heaven and restoring the Zhōu house,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" acknowledged them as hegemons,
meaning to condemn intent rather than words.
When Duke Yǐn of Lǔ acted as regent for Duke Huán's succession,
and when Jì Zhòng exiled Duke Hū to install Duke Tuī,
the martyrdom of Qiú Mù, Kǒng Fù, and Xún Xī,
and how Mùyí, the prince of Sòng, refused to yield the state of Chǔ,
all these exemplify upholding authority to preserve the state,
practicing righteousness to rectify the age,
and maintaining sincere devotion.
The Spring and Autumn Annals praises their righteous spirit,
thus recording them all,
which is called restoring correctness.
The barbarian tribes of Zhūlóu, Móu, and Gé
were condemned for conducting diplomatic visits after the heavenly king's demise,
this being their punishment.
The killing of a crown prince or maternal brothers
is directly attributed to the ruler,
revealing the loss of familial affection.
Jìzǐ of Lǔ being exonerated,
and Jìzǐ of Wú declining the throne,
illuminate the kindness of cherishing kin.
The eunuch assassinating Yújì, king of Wú,
shows that punished criminals should not be kept close.
The death of Duke Kūnwán of Zhèng at a meeting,
concealed as a natural death,
laments the powerful minister controlling the lord,
preventing the ruler from doing good.
The people of Wèi killing Zhōuyū,
and the people of Qí killing Wúzhī,
clarify the duty between ruler and subject,
upholding the state's integrity.
The people of Wèi establishing Jìn as ruler,
praises gaining popular support.
The ruler leading troops is not explicitly stated,
emphasizing the ruler's dignity.
In the first month,
with the duke in Chǔ,
ministers and sons longing for their lord,
expresses the sentiment of not a day passing without a ruler.
Punishing those accepting orders,
and recalling Wèi's guardians,
rectifies judicial fairness.
Mentioning the siege of Chéng,
and the military sacrifice on Jiǎwǔ day,
distinguishes crimes of coercion,
a method of punishing intentions.
Constructing the south gate,
carving rafters,
painting pillars red,
building the Pheasant Gate and twin towers,
erecting three terraces,
and renovating the extended stables,
criticize extravagance without caring for the people.
Hence Zāng Sūnchén requesting grain from Qí,
prompted Confucius to say:
"A gentleman governing a state
must have three years' reserves;
one poor harvest
leads to begging for grain,
failing the ruler's duty."
Punishing initial offenders,
reducing penalties to eradicate evil,
targets the root of problems.
Ministers swearing covenants at Chányuān,
satirizes their usurpation of power.
When feudal lords assembled,
the virtuous presided,
honoring worthiness.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records even minor faults,
returning to the kingly way,
valuing ancient sincerity,
settling matters with words alone,
without animal sacrifices or covenants to seal agreements,
hence it is said:
"The marquises of Qí and Wèi exchanged promises at Pú."
The Commentary states:
"In ancient times, they did not swear covenants,
but concluded with words and departed."
Bójī of Sòng said:
"A woman going out at night,
without her governess present,
should not descend the hall."
It is said:
"When Duke Zhōu campaigned east,
the western states lamented."
Duke Huán declared:
"Do not hoard grain,
do not block valleys,
do not change the appointed heir,
do not make a concubine the wife."
Duke Xiāng of Sòng said:
"Do not attack those not in formation,
do not trap the enemy."
King Zhuāng stated:
"In ancient times, if shields weren't pierced,
nor leather armor worm-eaten,
they did not go to war."
The gentleman holds fast to ritual,
and scorns profit;
seeks the people's allegiance,
not their land;
punishing those who submit after warning is inauspicious;
it brings misfortune;
the strong should not bully the weak.
Duke Qìng of Qí mourned the dead and visited the sick;
Kǒng Fù stood solemnly at court,
so none dared offend or bring harm to his lord;
Guó Zuǒ of Qí fulfilled his mission without disgracing his ruler,
and honored the marquis of Qí;
this reflects the Spring and Autumn Annals correcting refinement with substance.
Correcting refinement with substance
shows how some feudal lords lost their states:
The ruler of Lù sought to adopt Central States' rituals,
distancing from barbarian customs,
yet not fully integrating,
leading to his downfall.
King Fūchāi of Wú oppressed Yuè,
enslaving its ruler,
taking his wife as concubine,
ultimately causing his own destruction,
ancestral temples razed,
altars of state destroyed.
How lamentable!
A long-reigning king met his death,
Alas!
Is it not grievous!
Duke Líng of Jìn acted without propriety,
stationed on a tower,
pelting his ministers,
dismembering and discarding his cook;
he leaked Yáng Chǔfǔ's plan,
causing Yáng Chǔfǔ's death;
resentful of Zhào Dùn's remonstrance,
he sought to kill him,
but was ultimately slain by Zhào Chuān.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn acted against reason,
killing his crown prince Shēnshēng,
installing Xī Qí and Zhuō Zǐ through Lí Jī,
all of whom were killed,
plunging the state into chaos,
stabilized only after four generations,
nearly leading to annexation by Qín,
all stemming from Lí Jī.
King Píng of Chǔ acted without restraint,
killing Wǔ Zǐxū's father and brother;
when Duke Zhāo of Cài paid homage,
he demanded his fur coat,
which Duke Zhāo refused;
the king of Wú condemned this,
launched an attack on Chǔ,
and defeated it severely,
occupying the royal palace,
and ministers' residences,
even taking the mother of the king of Chǔ as wife,
all resulting from greed and tyranny.
Duke Lì of Jìn practiced brutal rule,
executing innocent people,
killing three high ministers in one day;
the following year,
his subordinates, fearful,
killed him in Jìn.
Duke Tuó of Chén debauched in Cài,
and the people of Cài slew him.
In ancient times, feudal lords leaving their borders were fully attended,
with a full division,
to prepare for contingencies.
But Duke Tuó indulged in moving alone among the people,
meeting his end by a commoner in the alleys,
far unbefitting a ruler's conduct.
Duke Mǐn of Sòng, proud of his woman and inwardly jealous,
gambled with his minister Wàn.
Wàn praised Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ, saying:
"Among all feudal lords under heaven,
only the marquis of Lǔ is fit to be ruler."
Duke Mǐn, jealous of his words,
retorted:
"You are a captive.
As a captive,
how could you know the merits or faults of the marquis of Lǔ?"
Wàn of Sòng, enraged,
attacked Duke Mǐn,
and broke his neck,
all due to the error of gambling with a minister.
In ancient times, the ruler stood in the shade,
ministers in the sun,
to distinguish positions,
and clarify nobility and baseness.
Gambling face-to-face with a minister,
with women by his side,
this blurs the distinction between ruler and subject;
thus, Wàn praised another state,
belittling Duke Mǐn,
who, in turn, humiliated Wàn,
gambling with him personally,
lowering himself as ruler,
shamed in the women's quarters,
and, in his pride over women,
alone met the fate of being killed.
The Spring and Autumn Commentary states:
"Ministers do not approach the ruler closely."
To avoid such pressure.
The state of Liáng endlessly conscripted its people for labor,
until the people could bear it no longer.
It organized them into groups of five households,
stipulating that if one household fled,
the other five would be executed.
The people lamented:
"Those who flee first gain rewards,
those who flee later face punishment."
A ruler should guide his people
to be filial to their parents,
respectful to elders,
guard their ancestral graves,
maintain the ancestral temples,
and perpetually worship their forebears.
Yet now, when resources prove insufficient,
punishments are imposed as if they could never be severe enough,
slaughter is carried out like butchering animals,
treating the people as enemies.
The state rotted from within like decaying fish and perished,
leaving the capital completely empty.
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"Liáng perished."
Its destruction was self-inflicted,
not caused by others.
Duke Yú, driven by greed,
disregarded the impending danger,
seeking only pleasure for his ears and eyes.
He accepted the jade from Jìn and the horses from Qūchǎn,
granting the Jìn army passage through his territory,
only to bring about his own ruin.
His ancestral temples were destroyed,
the state altars left without sacrifices,
and his body lay unburied after death—
all consequences of his greed.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals demonstrates that nothing comes without cause,
and treasures do not emerge without reason.
What originates from within
cannot proceed without partnership;
what comes from outside
cannot settle without a host.
This is its manifestation.
King Líng of Chǔ exerted his strength against Chén and Cài,
expanding his ambition through force,
heedless of his conduct;
obsessed with what pleased him,
he exhausted his people internally.
At Gānxī there was a stone maiden,
visible when the water receded,
and hidden when the water rose.
King Líng mobilized the entire state for labor,
continuing without cease for three years,
causing great resentment in Chǔ.
Acting with violent intent,
he killed the innocent minister Chéng Rán,
plunging Chǔ into deep discontent.
Prince Qìjí eventually compelled King Líng and his son to take their own lives,
seizing the state for himself.
Had the fish not left the marshes,
or the farmers not abandoned their fields,
the people would have lived in mutual affection.
Was this not the error of overindulging one's desires?
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ loved palaces,
building three towers in a single year.
His consort committed adultery with two brothers,
leading to mutual killings among brothers, sons, and father,
until the lineage was severed with no heir,
and the state was preserved only by Qí.
This was the fault of the consort's licentiousness.
In choosing consorts and noble concubines,
must one not be cautious!
These all exemplify self-assertion
leading to ruin by following one's heart.
Witnessing the downfall from self-assertion,
if proper remonstrance is still ignored,
the end is inevitable destruction.
Cáo Jī advised his lord, saying:
"The Róng are numerous and without righteousness;
do not go to them, my lord."
The lord did not listen,
and indeed died at the hands of the Róng invaders.
Wǔ Zǐxū counseled the King of Wú,
arguing that Yuè must be conquered,
but the King of Wú disregarded him.
After Wǔ Zǐxū's death,
within nine years,
Yuè indeed annihilated the state of Wú.
When Duke Mù of Qín planned to launch a surprise attack on Zhèng,
Bǎilǐ and Jiǎn Shū admonished him:
"Those who attack others from a thousand lǐ away
never avoid destruction."
Duke Mù ignored them,
and the army was decisively defeated at Xiáo,
without a single horse or chariot wheel returning.
Jìn sought passage through Yú,
and Duke Yú agreed.
Gōng Zhīqí advised:
"With lips gone, the teeth feel cold.
Yú and Guó should save each other,
not bestow favors.
I beg you, my lord, not to consent."
Duke Yú did not listen,
and later Yú indeed perished at the hands of Jìn.
The Spring and Autumn Annals clarifies these principles of survival and destruction for observation:
Observing the Shrine of Bó,
one learns the penalty for arrogance and excess;
observing the Field of Xǔ,
one understands that feudal lords may not arbitrarily enfeoff;
observing Duke Huán of Qí, Duke Wén of Jìn, Duke Xiāng of Sòng, and King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
one comprehends the merits of employing the worthy and serving the superior;
observing Duke Yǐn of Lǔ, Jì Zhòng, Shū Wǔ, Kǒng Fù, Xún Xī, Qiú Mù, Jìzǐ of Wú, and Prince Mùyí,
one recognizes the loyalty of devoted ministers;
observing Prince Bǐ of Chǔ,
one grasps the way of ministers and sons,
and the duty of sacrificing one's life;
observing the Earl of Lù,
one realizes the downfall of having no support and self-imprecation;
observing the duke's presence in Chǔ,
one appreciates the gratitude of ministers and sons;
observing careless speech,
one sees the severance of loyal paths;
observing the offering of six rows of dancers,
one discerns the distinctions between high and low;
observing Bó Jī of Sòng,
one understands the faithfulness of chaste women;
observing King Fūchāi of Wú,
one knows the strong bullying the weak;
observing Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
one recognizes the fault of defying reason and indulging in lust;
observing King Zhāo of Chǔ's attack on Cài,
one learns the repercussions of unrighteousness;
observing Duke Lì of Jìn's indiscriminate killing of the innocent,
one sees the retribution for violent acts;
observing Chén Tuó and Duke Mǐn of Sòng,
one understands the errors of jealousy and licentiousness;
observing Duke Yú and the fall of Liáng,
one grasps the extremity of greed and perversion of law;
observing King Líng of Chǔ,
one knows the harm of oppressing the people;
observing Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ's tower-building,
one comprehends the failures of pride, extravagance, and debauchery;
observing Marquis Shuò of Wèi,
one learns the crime of not responding to summons;
observing the capture of Fán Bó,
one understands the law against offending superiors;
observing Xì Quē of Jìn's attack on Zhūlóu,
one realizes the punishment for ministers usurping authority;
observing Prince Huī,
one discerns ministers spying on the ruler's intent;
observing hereditary ministers,
one sees the ruin of shifting power.
Thus, the enlightened king sees the unseen,
listens to the soundless,
under heaven's canopy and earth's support,
ensuring all states under heaven dutifully and reverently accept their mandates,
without revealing the extent of his knowledge to his ministers.
For when the way is the same, none can take precedence;
when sentiments align, none can command another.
This is the teaching.
From this perspective,
no one who relinquishes a ruler's authority
can control its power;
no one who eliminates distinctions between noble and base
can preserve their position intact.
Hence, the noble person is cautious in this regard.
On the Destruction of States, Part One
A king is one whom the people turn to,
a ruler is one who does not lose his followers;
thus, one who can make the myriad people turn to him,
and gain the allegiance of all under heaven,
is invincible in the world.
Thirty-one rulers lost their states,
fifty-two rulers saw their states perish,
because small states with shallow virtue did not pay court visits,
large states did not join the gatherings of feudal lords,
they stood isolated without mutual support,
dwelling alone without sharing community,
and when disaster struck, none came to rescue them—
this is why they perished.
Not only dukes, marquises, and great men are like this;
those born between heaven and earth,
with weak roots,
cannot withstand great winds and heavy rains,
and quickly wither and fade.
Marquis Shuò of Wèi stubbornly served Duke Xiāng of Qí,
yet the world worried about him;
Yú and Guó joined forces,
and Duke Xiàn of Jìn found it troublesome.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn was but a single man,
without an inch of land,
without a single follower,
yet Duke Líng, relying on the remnant dignity of a hegemon king,
wished to execute him;
exhausting schemes and extreme deceit,
when deceit was spent and strength drained,
great calamity reached his person.
Considering Zhào Dùn's heart,
bearing the position of a small state,
who could have destroyed him?
Thus Wǔ Zǐxū, a single man,
left Chǔ,
sought out Hé Lǘ,
and achieved success in Wú—
if one's reliance is truly fitting,
how can it be withstood?
King Kūn of Chǔ entrusted his state to Zǐ Yù (Dé Chén),
and the world feared him;
Duke of Yú entrusted his state to Gōng Zhī Qí,
and Duke Xiàn of Jìn worried about it;
when King Kūn killed Dé Chén,
the world despised him;
when the Duke of Yú did not employ Gōng Zhī Qí,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed him.
The signs of survival and ruin
cannot be unknown.
When feudal lords saw armies attacking them,
they fled and ran,
reaching destruction with none to save them—
their lifelong conduct is thus revealed.
Duke Yīn replaced Duke Huán's position,
what is called barely surviving;
he sent Wú Hài to lead troops and destroy Jí,
with no remonstrating ministers inside,
and no rescue from feudal lords outside;
this was also the case for Zài:
Sòng, Cài, and Wèi attacked it,
and Zhèng seized it using their strength—
this is no different from leaving heavy treasures on the road unguarded,
for passersby to pick up.
Dèng and Gǔ lost their lands and paid court to Duke Huán of Lǔ—
Dèng and Gǔ losing their lands,
was it not fitting?
《On the Fall of States, Part II》
The reason for the destruction of the Marquis of Jì
was a feud spanning nine generations;
a single day's words
endangered a lineage of a hundred generations,
hence it is called "the great departure."
The people of Wèi invaded Chéng,
Zhèng entered Chéng,
and when the Qí army besieged Chéng,
it suffered three major attacks,
ultimately perishing
with none to save it—
where was its reliance?
Duke Huán of Qí wished to practice hegemonic rule,
but Tán defied his orders,
so it was destroyed and fled to Jǔ,
serving the small instead of the great.
The reason the Earl of Cáo died fighting in his position
was that no feudal lords aided him in his distress.
At the Yōu gathering,
Duke Huán of Qí repeatedly assembled the feudal lords;
Cáo, being small,
did not attend;
Lǔ, a large state,
at the Yōu gathering,
Duke Zhuāng did not go,
so the Róng people then showed military force west of the Jǐ River,
seeing that Lǔ stood alone with none to rescue it.
At this time, great ministers disregarded their ruler's commands,
solely rescuing the endangered.
In the 27th year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ,
Duke Huán of Qí held the Yōu gathering,
and the people of Wèi did not come.
The next year,
Duke Huán, angered, heavily defeated them;
and when attacking the Shān Róng,
he displayed flags and arrayed spoils to boast to the feudal lords.
Thereupon, Lǔ built towers three times in one year,
rebellious ministers arose three times within,
and Yí-Dí armies repeatedly attacked from without;
the beginning of Wèi's destruction
lay in missing the Yōu gathering;
the root of chaos
rests in clinging to kinship and internal obscurity.
Xíng never attended Duke Huán of Qí's gatherings,
and its attachment to Jìn was weak;
the Marquis of Jìn was captured at Hán and turned his back—
this was the case at the Huái gathering.
When Duke Huán of Qí died,
the chaos of Shù Diāo and Yì Yá erupted.
Xíng joined the Dí in attacking its own surname state,
and seized it—
with conduct like this,
even if they are your kin,
how could they remain close to you?
This ruler,
destroyed by his own surname—
as when Marquis Huǐ of Wèi destroyed Xíng.
Duke Huán of Qí held the Yōu gathering,
Wèi did not attend,
Duke Huán, angered, attacked it;
the Dí destroyed it,
and Duke Huán, concerned, reestablished it.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ made the Kē covenant,
seized Wènyáng,
Lǔ was cut off,
and Duke Huán reestablished it.
Xíng and Qǐ never paid court visits,
Duke Huán of Qí saw them destroyed,
led the feudal lords, and reestablished them—
with such intent,
how could he not become hegemon?
Thus, he was entrusted with the worries of the world.
《Following the Roots of Rise and Decline, Part IX》
When Yán Yuān died,
the Master said:
"Heaven is destroying me."
When Zǐlù died,
the Master said:
"Heaven is cursing me."
When the unicorn was captured during the western hunt,
he said:
"My way is exhausted,
my way is exhausted."
Three years later,
he followed in death.
From this perspective,
the mandate of heaven, success or failure,
the sage knows it,
yet there are things he cannot save—
such is fate!
Before the death of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Duke Huán of Qí held the Kuíqiū assembly,
twice convening the gatherings.
One year before the death of Duke Xiào of Qí,
Duke Xǐ of Lǔ requested troops to capture Gǔ,
demonstrating the authority of Duke Wén of Jìn,
with the Son of Heaven twice acknowledging him.
One year before his death,
Duke Xǐ of Lǔ's loyalty was divided as he served Qí,
while Duke Wén did not serve Jìn.
One year before the death of Marquis Pān of Qí,
Duke Wén went to Jìn,
with the Marquises of Wèi and Zhèng arriving unexpectedly.
After the Marquis of Qí had died,
the feudal lords indeed met with the senior officials of Jìn at Xīnchéng.
Because Duke Zhāo of Lǔ served Chǔ,
the people of Jìn did not enter,
while Chǔ grew strong and triumphant,
convening the feudal lords twice in one year,
attacking the powerful Wú,
executing the rebellious ministers for Qí,
and subsequently destroying Lì.
Lǔ leveraged this influence to annihilate Zēng,
and the following year went to Jìn,
avoiding the disaster at Héshàng.
One year before the death of Duke Zhāo of Jìn,
there was no calamity.
Chǔ experienced internal strife,
with ministers assassinating their ruler,
and the feudal lords gathered at Píngqiū,
plotting to punish Chǔ's rebellious ministers.
Duke Zhāo was unable to join the covenant,
and his senior officials were detained.
Wú heavily defeated Chǔ's six allied states at Jīfù,
and when the duke went to Jìn, he suffered great humiliation.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* concealed this,
stating he was ill.
From this, it is evident
that one's actions cannot be fully relied upon,
and one must be cautious in whom one serves.
This is crucial to survival, honor, or disgrace.
Three years before the death of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
Jìn destroyed the Red Dí tribes of Lùshì and Jiǎshì Liúxū.
Three years before the death of Chǔ's ruler Shěn,
Zhèng submitted at Xiāoyú.
One year after the death of Marquis Zhōu of Jìn,
and two years before the death of Chǔ's ruler Zhāo,
they allied with Chén and Cài to attack Zhèng and achieved a great victory.
The following year,
Qū Jiàn of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords and expanded the Central States' influence.
Three years after his death,
the rulers of the various Xià states paid court to Chǔ.
Chǔ's ruler Juǎn succeeded him,
dying after four years,
yet his state was neither invaded nor usurped,
but instead grew prosperous and powerful.
The Central States did not recover for over a year—
why was this?
Chǔ's ruler Zhāo was perhaps acceptable to the feudal lords,
and those under heaven who hated their rulers
all rose in complaint and took advantage.
Troops were dispatched four or five times,
often using many to attack few,
and concentrated forces to strike the dispersed,
exhausting righteousness.
Four or five years before his death,
the Central States were internally divided,
with the armies of Qí, Jìn, Lǔ, and Wèi separately guarding,
large states attacking small ones.
The various Xià states twice gathered at Chényí,
but Qí refused to attend.
With Wú to the south,
two of its rulers were killed,
and the Central States to the north
saw Qí and Wèi slay their rulers.
Qìng Fēng seized his ruler and threw the state into chaos,
while followers of Shí È gathered and formed factions.
Wèi's Yǎn occupied Chényí and practiced deception,
and Lín Fǔ held Qī and rebelled.
The Duke of Sòng killed his heir,
and Lǔ suffered a great famine.
The conduct of the Central States
bore the marks of doomed states,
similar to the era of Dukes Wén and Xuān,
when the rulers of the Central States
saw five rulers killed within five years.
With the conduct of Duke Líng of Jìn,
he stationed a senior official at Fěilín,
who, with a mere gesture,
made the feudal lords dare not refuse to emerge—
this is like a marsh having its banks.
**Alliance Assemblies Essential, Tenth**
Though the ultimate meaning is difficult to comprehend,
the sage values eliminating the troubles of the world.
Valuing the elimination of the world's troubles,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* thus earnestly records the world's troubles comprehensively,
aiming to reveal the root causes of the world's afflictions.
Its intent is to eliminate the world's troubles—
what does this mean?
When the world is free of troubles,
then human nature can become good;
when human nature can become good,
then the influence of purity and integrity spreads;
when the influence of purity and integrity spreads,
then the Kingly Way is established,
and rites and music flourish—
its heart lies herein.
The *Tradition* states:
"The feudal lords gathered to form covenants."
The nobleman governing the state
said:
"Is this the work of commanders?"
Thus, the nobleman worries about the world,
and troubles reached the point of thirty-one regicides
and fifty-two lost states,
all resulting from unceasing minor evils.
The message is already clear,
hence it is said:
Establish righteousness to clarify the distinction between noble and base;
strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches to clarify the duties of great and small;
distinguish suspicious conduct
to illuminate the principle of rectifying the age;
adopt conveyed intentions
to correct improper rites;
promote no good as too small,
and eliminate no evil as too minor,
to purify its beauty;
distinguish the worthy from the unworthy
to clarify honor;
draw near to attract the distant,
accommodating the world through one's own state;
classify relationships and categorize things
without losing their principles;
judge right and wrong with a public heart,
rewarding good and punishing evil,
so the king's grace permeates.
It begins with eliminating troubles,
rectifying the one to prepare all things—
thus it is said:
How great is its designation,
with two words encompassing the world!
This refers to that.
**Correct Penetration, Eleventh**
The Spring and Autumn Annals
is the foundation of great righteousness!
The six categories
refer to the six essential principles,
then by drawing upon heavenly beginnings,
spreading the flow of things,
and penetrating their principles,
the events and changes are expressed through its words.
Thus it records the origins of success and failure,
and then distinguishes the beginnings of nobility and baseness;
discusses crimes to determine punishments based on their severity,
then severs connections with distinctions;
establishes righteousness to fix the sequence of respect and humility,
and then the duties of ruler and minister become clear;
records the worthy methods of the world,
manifesting where humility and righteousness reside,
then restoration of correctness becomes visible;
the obscure and hidden do not transgress each other,
and approaching them makes them intimate,
then the responses of all things become endless,
thus their application to humans can be implemented,
without contradicting their proper relationships.
Therefore, one must understand the system in its proper application,
thus knowing its energy,
then one can nourish its will;
knowing its sound,
then one can support its essence;
knowing its actions,
then one can fulfill its form;
knowing its nature,
then one can distinguish its circumstances;
thus when leading, the people harmonize,
when acting, the people follow,
this shows understanding of guiding by innate preferences,
and restraining what emotions dislike.
Thus, though words be concise,
their meaning must spread;
though affairs be small,
their achievement must be great;
the resonance of prosperous transformation moves through things,
dispersing into principles;
virtue resides between heaven and earth,
divine spirits beautifully gather,
operating together without exhaustion,
filling the four seas with songs of praise.
The Book of Documents says:
"The eight tones achieve harmony,
none interfere with their proper order,
spirits and humans are in harmony."
This is what it means,
thus only by understanding human nature
can one discuss governance,
otherwise,
though laboring without achievement,
awake day and night,
with wearied heart from thinking,
still unable to perceive,
thus the world has those who err.
Three demonstrations hit the mark,
what Confucius called wrong,
how could they understand penetration!
The Twelve Essential Principles
The Spring and Autumn Annals' text covering 242 years,
with the vastness of the world,
the breadth of events and changes,
leaves nothing unrecorded,
nevertheless,
its main essentials have ten principles.
The ten principles
are what matters hinge upon,
the means through which kingly transformation flows.
Raising events and changes,
revealing what deserves emphasis,
is one principle;
observing where events and changes lead,
is one principle;
treating according to what caused them to occur,
is one principle;
strengthening the trunk and weakening branches,
enlarging the root and reducing ends,
is one principle;
distinguishing suspicions,
differentiating categories,
is one principle;
discussing the meaning of worthy talent,
distinguishing their capable strengths,
is one principle;
drawing near those close and attracting those distant,
uniting with what the people desire,
is one principle;
inheriting Zhou's refinement and returning to substance,
is one principle;
fire represents summer,
heaven's beginning,
is one principle;
criticizing what deserves punishment,
examining where anomalies are added,
heaven's beginning,
is one principle.
Raising events and changes,
revealing what deserves emphasis,
then the common people are peaceful;
observing where events and changes lead,
then success and failure are clear;
treating according to what caused them to occur,
then the foundation of affairs is corrected;
strengthening the trunk and weakening branches,
enlarging the root and reducing ends,
then the distinction between ruler and minister is clear;
distinguishing suspicions,
differentiating categories,
then right and wrong become evident;
discussing the meaning of worthy talent,
distinguishing their capable strengths,
then all officials are properly ordered;
inheriting Zhou's refinement and returning to substance,
then the focus of transformation is established;
drawing near those close and attracting those distant,
uniting with what the people desire,
then benevolent grace reaches everywhere;
wood generates fire,
fire represents summer,
then the principles of yin-yang and four seasons mutually receive and sequence properly;
criticizing what deserves punishment,
examining where anomalies are added,
then what heaven desires is implemented.
Unifying these and raising them up,
benevolence goes forth and righteousness comes,
virtuous influence spreads wide,
overflowing to the four seas,
yin and yang harmoniously adjusted,
all things without exception obtain their proper principle.
Those who explain the Spring and Autumn Annals all use this,
this is their method.
Emphasizing Governance Chapter Thirteen
Only the sage can connect all things as one,
and tie them to the origin,
never reaching the root source to inherit it,
cannot accomplish its work.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals change "one" calling it "origin",
origin meaning source,
its meaning follows heaven and earth's beginning and end,
thus humans only have beginning and end,
yet life doesn't necessarily correspond to the four seasons' changes,
thus the origin is the root of all things,
and human origin resides there.
Where does it reside?
It exists before heaven and earth,
thus though humans are born of heavenly energy and serve heavenly energy,
they cannot share heaven's original root, heaven's original mandate, and jointly oppose what it does.
Therefore the first month of spring
inherits what heaven and earth have done,
continuing heaven's work and completing it,
its way mutually shares achievements and maintains endeavors.
How can one speak of being heaven and earth's origin?
Why would heaven and earth's origin here impose evil upon humans?
This greatly manifests the principle of inheriting meaning.
Those who can discourse on the categories of birds and beasts
are not what the sage wishes to discuss;
what the sage wishes to discuss
lies in expounding benevolence and righteousness and ordering them,
knowing their divisions and classifications,
connecting what is attached,
clarifying the principles by which they are examined,
and preventing ambiguity—
this is what the sage values and nothing more.
Otherwise,
transmitting numerous sayings,
observing myriad things,
discussing non-urgent words,
and thereby confusing later learners
is what the noble person deeply detests.
What use is it!
The sage ponders and reflects,
not wearying by day,
continuing through the night,
and only then does he discern all things through benevolence and righteousness.
From this perspective,
how could one attain it on one's own?
Hence it is said:
Alas!
Those who serve as teachers
must not be cautious?
Righteousness originates from the classics,
the classics and commentaries are the great foundation;
abandoning effort and laboring the mind,
suffering the will and exhausting emotions,
until the head turns white and teeth fall out,
still may not suffice for self-recording.
Humans are born with a great destiny,
which is their substance;
there is also a changing destiny within it,
which is governance.
If governance is uneven,
people will harbor resentful and angry intentions,
as if about to impose perilous difficulties,
and there are times when followers and encounters occur,
connections with the divine,
signs of severed links.
There are also changes within it,
causing such imbalance,
which must be examined;
examining it emphasizes the root of governance.
Gathering them into one,
advancing righteousness and punishing evil,
the root of severance,
and implementing it—
this shares similarities with Tāng and Wǔ but differs;
Tāng and Wǔ employed it
to govern with benevolence.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* clarify gains and losses,
distinguish noble and base,
rooted in heaven.
What caused the king to lose the empire
was allowing the feudal lords to greatly disrupt it;
discussing it and then guiding and reversing it,
hence it is said:
broad and clear,
incisive and profound.
"The Images of Attire Regulations: Fourteenth"
Heaven and earth produce the myriad things to nourish humans,
so what is edible
is used to nourish the body;
what inspires awe
serves as attire and adornment;
this is why rites arise.
The sword on the left
symbolizes the Azure Dragon;
the blade on the right
symbolizes the White Tiger;
the hook in front
symbolizes the Red Bird;
the crown on the head
symbolizes the Dark Warrior;
these four are the grand adornments of humans.
Only those who comprehend past and present,
distinguish right from wrong,
can wear these.
The Dark Warrior
is the most stern and awe-inspiring in appearance;
its image is on the right,
yet its attire is conversely on the head,
signifying the ultimate in martial virtue unused.
The sage transcends effortlessly;
even if one wishes to follow,
there is no way to do so.
Those who must grasp armor to repel enemies
are not what the sage values;
the noble person manifests it in attire,
so the brave and martial dissolve their will in appearance.
Thus, civil virtue is esteemed,
and martial prowess is secondary,
this is how the world achieves eternal wholeness.
How is this stated in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*?
Kǒng Fù's righteousness manifested in his countenance,
and treacherous ministers dared not harbor evil;
Yú had Gōng Zhī Qí,
and Duke Xiàn could not sleep because of it;
with Jìn Lì's strength,
the central states suffered continuous corpses and bloodshed.
Thus, when King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he wore ceremonial robes and inserted the tablet,
and tiger warriors discoursed on swords—
how can it be that only through martial ferocity and killing can awe be established?
Therefore, what the noble person wears is paramount,
so that their dignified appearance
is already ultimate;
how can one not examine this?
"The Two Origins: Fifteenth"
The profound meaning of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* has two origins;
without understanding where these two origins arise,
one cannot discuss portents and anomalies,
which distinguish small from large, subtle from manifest.
Seeking the subtle in limitless places,
truly knowing the small will become large,
the subtle will become manifest,
with fortune and misfortune not yet formed,
is where the sage stands alone;
even if one wishes to follow,
there is no way to do so,
this refers to that.
Thus, when the king receives the mandate,
he rectifies the calendar,
not following the old numbers forward,
but necessarily welcoming the new and receiving it,
which is the principle of transmission.
Hence, the sage can connect his heart to the subtle and extend it to the manifest.
Therefore, the way of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
uses the depth of the origin
to rectify heaven's beginning,
uses heaven's beginning
to rectify the king's governance,
uses the king's governance
to rectify the feudal lords' accession,
uses the feudal lords' accession
to rectify the governance within the borders.
When these five are all rectified,
transformation spreads greatly.
Yet it records solar eclipses, meteor falls, ghost moths, mountain collapses, earthquakes, heavy summer rains, heavy winter snows,
frost that does not kill grass,
no rain from the first month until the seventh month of autumn,
and magpies nesting—
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* treats these as anomalies,
using them to reveal signs of disorder.
This shows that the small cannot become large,
the subtle cannot become manifest;
even if extremely minor,
they are still one origin.
Confucius used this to demonstrate,
which is why I value the subtle and emphasize beginnings,
disliking those who push portents and anomalies forward
and only then plan for safety, danger, and chaos afterward—
this is not highly valued in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Yet the *Spring and Autumn Annals* raises it as one origin
to encourage reflection on heaven's reproof and fear of heaven's majesty,
stirring inwardly in heart and mind,
manifesting outwardly in affairs and circumstances,
cultivating the self and examining one's own,
clarifying a good heart to return to the way.
Is this not valuing the subtle, emphasizing beginnings, cautioning ends, and inferring effects?
"Auspicious Omens: Sixteenth"
There are things that cannot be achieved by force but come spontaneously,
such as capturing the qílín while hunting in the west—
this is the omen of receiving the mandate.
Then, relying on the *Spring and Autumn Annals* between correctness and incorrectness,
it clarifies the principle of institutional reform,
unifying under the Son of Heaven,
and increasing concern for the world's worries,
striving to eliminate what the world suffers from,
seeking to connect upward to the Five Emperors,
downward to the Three Kings,
to penetrate the way of all kings,
and follow heaven's beginnings and ends,
broadly examining the effects of gains and losses,
and investigating the actions of destiny and signs,
exhausting principle to fulfill the appropriateness of nature and disposition,
then heaven's countenance is achieved.
All officials gaze together from different paths;
unifying them lies with the ruler,
leading them lies with the minister.
"Preface to Responses: Seventeenth"
When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he sought above to rectify the heavenly foundation and the positions of kings and lords,
addressing the desires of the myriad people,
and below to illuminate gains and losses,
promote worthy talents,
awaiting later sages.
Thus he drew from historical records,
organized past events,
corrected right and wrong,
and revealed the conduct of kings and lords.
Among the records of the twelve dukes,
all were matters from decadent times,
so his disciples were perplexed.
Confucius said:
"I base my work on actual events,
and apply the mind of a king to them,
believing that empty words are not as broad,
profound, and clear as actual events."
Therefore, Zǐgòng, Mǐnzǐ, and Gōngjiānzǐ spoke of its relevance to governing the state and worthiness.
Its relevance
extends to regicide and the fall of states,
fleeing and being unable to protect the altars of soil and grain.
The reason for this
is all due to not understanding the Way,
and not studying the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Thus Wèi Zǐxià said:
"Those who possess states
must study the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Without studying it,
they cannot see the dangers from all sides,
nor understand the great authority of the state and the heavy responsibility of the ruler."
Thus some were coerced into poverty, lost their states,
or were assassinated in their positions,
all happening in a single day.
If one can follow the methods of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and practice its Way,
how could it merely avert disasters?
It would be the virtue of Yáo and Shùn."
Therefore, the heir said:
"Merit extends to descendants,
glory shines for a hundred generations.
The virtue of sage kings
has none greater than forbearance."
Thus I first said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals details oneself but simplifies others,
accommodating the world through its own state."
The Way of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
greatly attained leads to kingship,
slightly attained leads to hegemony.
Thus Zēngzǐ and Zǐshí praised Duke Qí,
pacified the lords,
and honored the Son of Heaven.
The Way of hegemony and kingship
is rooted in benevolence.
Benevolence is the heart of Heaven,
hence it follows with the heart of Heaven.
The greatest in loving others
is none greater than considering troubles and preventing them.
Thus when Cài gained advantage over Wú,
and Lǔ gained advantage over Qí,
the Spring and Autumn Annals did not record it.
Hence it follows with saying:
"Do not approach those who resent you,
do not be familiar with enemy states,
do not allow states of plunder and theft to remain close long,"
all meaning to prevent troubles and remove them for the people.
The gradual lack of love for the people
leads to death and destruction.
Thus it speaks of King Chǔ Líng and Duke Jìn Lì being killed in their positions,
resulting from their lack of benevolence.
Therefore, it praises Duke Sòng Xiāng for not putting others in distress,
stating that winning through unjust means
is worse than losing through just means.
The Spring and Autumn Annals honors this,
intending to transform customs
and achieve kingly transformation.
Thus Zǐxià said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals values people,
all its criticisms are based on this.
Some were extravagant, causing resentment,
some were tyrannical, harming others,
all ultimately bringing disaster upon themselves."
Thus Zǐchí said:
"Duke Lǔ Zhuāng built towers,
with red pillars and carved rafters;
Duke Jìn Lì's punishments were excessively harsh;
both failed to die of old age."
Being extravagant above,
and harsh in punishments,
neither practiced internal forbearance,
demanding perfection from others.
Hence it follows with the Spring and Autumn Annals,
considering human feelings,
pardoning minor faults,
and the Commentary clarifies this, saying:
"This is the language of a gentleman."
Confucius illuminated gains and losses,
revealed success and failure,
deplored the lack of benevolence in his time,
and the loss of the essence of the kingly Way.
Thus, considering human feelings,
he pardoned minor faults,
and the Commentary again clarifies this, saying:
"This is the language of a gentleman."
Confucius said:
"I base my work on actual events,
and apply my kingly mind to them."
He borrowed titles and positions
to rectify human relationships,
using their successes and failures
to clarify obedience and rebellion.
Thus, what he praised,
such as the deeds of Huán and Wén, led to success;
what he condemned,
when practiced by chaotic states, ended in failure.
Hence it begins with major evils,
regicide and the fall of states,
and ends with pardoning minor faults,
starting with the coarse
and ending with the subtle,
with education and transformation spreading,
virtuous influence greatly permeating,
so that all under heaven,
each person possesses the conduct of a scholar-gentleman,
and has few faults.
This also conveys the meaning of criticizing double names.
The Eighteenth: The Root of Separation and Union
Heaven places itself high but bestows its gifts lowly,
hides its form but reveals its light;
placing itself high
is for the sake of dignity,
bestowing lowly
is for the sake of benevolence,
hiding its form
is for the sake of divinity,
revealing its light
is for the sake of brightness.
Thus, being dignified yet bestowing benevolence,
hiding divinity yet revealing light,
is the action of Heaven.
Therefore, the ruler of men
should emulate Heaven's actions.
Thus, deeply hidden within,
he becomes divine;
broadly observing without,
he becomes bright;
employing all the worthy,
he receives their accomplishments;
not laboring personally in affairs,
he maintains dignity;
universally loving all beings,
not using personal joy or anger for reward and punishment,
he practices benevolence.
Therefore, the ruler of men
takes non-action as his Way,
and non-partiality as his treasure.
He occupies a position of non-action,
yet utilizes fully equipped officials.
His feet do not move,
yet ushers guide him forward;
his mouth does not speak,
yet attendants voice his words;
his mind does not ponder,
yet all ministers offer their appropriate services.
Thus, none see him acting,
yet achievements are accomplished.
This is how the ruler of men emulates Heaven's actions.
As for the minister of men,
he should emulate the way of Earth,
exposing his form,
revealing his nature to others.
High or low, dangerous or easy,
hard or soft, firm or yielding,
plump or lean, beautiful or ugly,
all can be assessed and utilized.
Thus, whether his form is suitable or not,
can be determined and utilized.
The minister of men,
compared to Earth, values trustworthiness,
and fully reveals his nature to the ruler.
The ruler can then assess and utilize him.
Thus, the kingly Way remains authoritative without loss.
The minister of men always exhausts his feelings and efforts,
revealing his strengths and weaknesses,
enabling the ruler to employ him appropriately.
Just as Earth exhaustively reveals its nature,
thus his suitability can be assessed and utilized.
The Nineteenth: Establishing the Original Spirit
The ruler is the foundation of the state.
His words and actions
are the pivot of all things.
The movement of this pivot
initiates honor and disgrace.
If it errs by a hair's breadth,
a team of four horses cannot overtake it.
Therefore, the ruler
carefully attends to the root and examines beginnings,
revering the small and cautioning the subtle.
His will should be like dying embers,
his form like draped garments.
He quiets his essence and nurtures his spirit,
solitary and inactive,
resting his form without casting a shadow,
muffling his voice without emitting a sound.
With a humble heart, he treats worthies with respect,
observes the future and examines the past,
consults with the multitude of worthies,
and investigates the common people.
He grasps their hearts,
comprehensively perceives their sentiments,
examines their likes and dislikes,
to discern loyalty and flattery.
He studies their past conduct,
testing it against the present.
He calculates their accumulated merits,
inheriting from former worthies.
He releases grudges and enmities,
observes their conflicts,
distinguishes their factions and clans,
relying on them as a standard.
Occupying his position to govern the people,
what should he use to establish his reputation?
With daily accumulation over time,
what achievement cannot be accomplished?
He can thereby understand the external from the internal,
infer the great from the small.
He must know the reality,
which is the art of opening and closing.
The ruler is the root of the state.
In governing a state,
no transformation is greater than honoring the root.
Honoring the root, the ruler's transformation is like that of spirits;
not honoring the root, the ruler has no means to unite people.
Without the means to unite people,
even with severe punishments and heavy penalties,
the people will not follow.
This is what is called driving the state to abandon it.
What calamity could be greater!
What is meant by the root?
It is said:
Heaven, Earth, and Humanity are the roots of all things.
Heaven gives them birth,
Earth nourishes them,
Humanity completes them.
Heaven gives them birth through filial and fraternal devotion,
Earth nourishes them with clothing and food,
Humanity completes them with rites and music.
These three are like hands and feet to each other,
combining to form a whole,
none can be missing.
Without filial and fraternal devotion,
they lose the means of birth;
without clothing and food,
they lose the means of nourishment;
without rites and music,
they lose the means of completion.
If all three are lost,
the people become like deer,
each following their own desires,
each household forming its own customs.
Fathers cannot command sons,
rulers cannot command ministers.
Even with walled cities,
they are called empty towns.
In such a case,
the ruler lies prostrate with a clod for a pillow,
though no one endangers him, he endangers himself;
though no one destroys him, he destroys himself.
This is called the punishment of nature.
When the punishment of nature arrives,
even wrapped in stone chambers,
separated by barriers and obstacles,
one cannot escape it.
Enlightened rulers and worthy sovereigns
are necessarily faithful to this.
Therefore, they solemnly honor the three roots:
offering sacrifices in the suburbs to show reverence,
serving ancestors with shared duties,
promoting and displaying filial and fraternal devotion,
distinguishing and honoring filial conduct,
thereby serving the root of Heaven;
holding the plow to personally till,
picking mulberry leaves and tending silkworms themselves,
clearing grasslands and growing grains,
opening wastelands to ensure sufficient clothing and food,
thereby serving the root of Earth;
establishing schools and academies,
cultivating filial devotion, fraternal duty, respect, and deference,
enlightening through education,
influencing with rites and music,
thereby serving the root of Humanity.
When all three are served,
the people become like younger brothers and sons,
not daring to act on their own authority.
The state becomes like parents;
without awaiting kindness, they love it;
without requiring strictness, they obey it.
Even dwelling in the wilds and露宿ing outdoors,
they feel more secure than in palaces.
In such a case,
the ruler rests peacefully on his pillow,
though no one assists him, he strengthens himself;
though no one pacifies him, he secures himself.
This is called the reward of nature.
When the reward of nature arrives,
even if he humbly retreats and abdicates the state to leave,
the people will carry their children on their backs,
following to make him their ruler,
and the ruler cannot leave them either.
Therefore, a state governed by virtue
is sweeter than syrup and honey,
firmer than glue and lacquer.
Thus, sages and worthies strive to honor the root,
not daring to lose it.
The ruler is the evidence of the state.
He must not initiate first,
but respond after being moved.
Thus, he occupies the position of initiator
without exercising the force of initiation;
he does not hold the duty of harmony,
yet makes harmony his virtue.
Constantly yielding to those below,
he is thereby able to be above them.
The way to embody the state
lies in honoring the spiritual.
Honor is what upholds governance;
the spiritual is what accomplishes transformation.
Therefore, without honor there is no awe,
without the spiritual there is no transformation.
To achieve honor,
one must rely on appointing the worthy;
to achieve the spiritual,
one must achieve unity of heart.
When worthies serve as limbs and aides,
the ruler is honored and secure, and the state is peaceful;
when hearts are united in succession,
transformation occurs as if by spirits.
None see what he does,
yet merit and virtue are accomplished.
This is called honoring the spiritual.
Heaven accumulates all essences to strengthen itself,
the sage accumulates all worthies to empower himself;
Heaven arranges the sun, moon, and stars to illuminate itself,
the sage arranges ranks and emoluments to enlighten himself;
The reason Heaven is strong
is not due to the power of a single essence,
the reason the sage is powerful
is not due to the virtue of a single worthy.
Thus, the Way of Heaven strives to make its essences abundant,
the sage strives to make his worthies numerous;
making its essences abundant unifies its yang,
making his worthies numerous unifies their hearts;
unifying its yang,
then it can attain its spirit;
unifying their hearts,
then it can achieve its merit;
Therefore, the method of establishing governance
values obtaining worthies and uniting hearts.
For the ruler of men,
the essential lies in valuing spirit,
spirit is something that cannot be seen,
cannot be heard;
Hence, looking, one does not see its form,
listening, one does not hear its sound;
Not hearing its sound,
thus none can grasp its echo,
not seeing its form,
thus none can grasp its shadow;
Unable to grasp its shadow,
then there is no means to judge its straight or crooked,
unable to grasp its echo,
then there is no means to discern its clear or murky;
Without means to judge straight or crooked,
then his achievements cannot be undermined;
without means to discern clear or murky,
then his name cannot be measured.
What is called not seeing its form
does not mean not seeing the form of its advances and halts,
but that the reasons for its advances and halts cannot be seen;
What is called not hearing its sound
does not mean not hearing the sound of its commands,
but that the reasons for its commands cannot be heard;
Not seeing and not hearing,
this is called obscure darkness,
able to be obscure then enlightened,
able to be dark then illustrious,
able to be obscure and able to be dark,
this is called spirit.
The ruler values dwelling in obscurity while illuminating his position,
residing in the shade while facing the light,
disliking others seeing his true feelings,
yet desiring to know people's hearts.
Therefore, the ruler of men
holds considerations without source,
performs deeds without beginning,
uses not seeking to take,
uses not asking to inquire;
I, by not seeking, take,
then I gain advantage;
They, by not emerging, emerge,
then they incur cost;
I, by not asking, inquire,
then I become spiritual,
they, by not answering, answer,
then they reveal their feelings.
Thus, asking all day,
they do not know what to respond;
taking all day,
they do not know where it comes from.
I then become enlightened,
while they do not know what they have lost.
Therefore, ministers reside in the light yet act as the dark,
the ruler resides in the dark yet acts as the light.
The way of the dark values form and reveals feelings,
the way of the light has no beginning and values spirit.
"Preserving Position and Authority, Chapter Twenty"
If the people have no desires,
the ruler has no means to exercise authority;
if the people have no aversions,
the ruler has nothing to instill fear with;
without means to exercise authority,
and nothing to instill fear,
then the ruler has no way to impose control;
without means to impose control,
subjects become equals in power,
and there is no basis for honoring the ruler.
Therefore, when a sage governs the state,
he follows the natural dispositions of heaven and earth and the benefits of the senses,
to establish a system of hierarchy,
to differentiate between noble and humble,
setting up government offices, ranks, and emoluments,
enriching the five flavors,
enhancing the five colors,
and harmonizing the five sounds,
to entice their ears and eyes;
making clear distinctions between purity and impurity,
and sharply contrasting honor and disgrace,
to stir their hearts;
striving to ensure the people have desires,
for having desires
allows them to be encouraged,
hence setting rewards to motivate them.
Having desires
necessarily entails having aversions,
and having aversions
allows them to be feared,
hence setting punishments to intimidate them;
with both motivation
and intimidation,
they can then be controlled;
to control them
means regulating their desires,
so rewards for encouragement should not be excessive;
regulating their aversions
means punishments for intimidation should not be overly severe;
if desires are excessive,
it leads to arbitrary favor;
if aversions are too severe,
it results in arbitrary power;
arbitrary power causes the ruler to lose authority,
and the world to resent each other;
arbitrary favor causes the ruler to lose virtue,
and the world to harm one another.
Thus, the sage's way of controlling the people
is to give them desires,
but not beyond moderation;
to make them sincere and simple,
yet not without desires;
whether without desires or with desires,
each finds satisfaction,
and the way of the ruler is achieved.
What makes a state a state
is virtue;
what makes a ruler a ruler
is authority.
Therefore, virtue cannot be shared,
nor authority divided,
for sharing virtue loses kindness,
and dividing authority loses power.
Losing power makes the ruler despised,
losing kindness causes the people to scatter,
the people scattering leads to state chaos,
and the ruler being despised results in ministers rebelling.
Hence, as a ruler,
one must firmly uphold virtue
to win the people's allegiance;
firmly grasp authority
to correct the ministers.
Sounds have compliance and opposition,
necessarily with clarity and murkiness;
forms have goodness and evil,
necessarily with straightness and crookedness;
so the sage, upon hearing a sound,
distinguishes its clarity or murkiness;
upon seeing a form,
differentiates its straightness or crookedness.
Within murkiness,
he must discern clarity;
within clarity,
he must detect murkiness;
within crookedness,
he must perceive straightness;
within straightness,
he must identify crookedness.
No sound is too faint to heed,
no form too small to notice,
not letting the obvious obscure the subtle,
nor the many overshadow the few,
each corresponding to its affair,
to bring about due recompense.
With black and white clearly distinguished,
the people then know what to follow and avoid;
the people knowing what to follow and avoid,
then governance can be achieved,
this is the model to emulate.
As a ruler,
reside in a position of non-action,
practice wordless teaching,
silent and soundless,
tranquil and formless,
holding to the one without bias,
serving as the source for the state,
taking the state as one's body,
the ministers as one's heart,
using the ministers' words as sounds,
their actions as forms;
where there is sound, there must be an echo,
where there is form, there must be a shadow;
sound emanates from within,
echo responds from without;
form stands above,
shadow mirrors below;
echoes have clarity and murkiness,
shadows have straightness and crookedness;
the echo responds
not to a single sound;
the shadow mirrors
not to a single form.
Therefore, as a ruler,
maintain an open mind and calm demeanor,
attentively listening to the echoes,
clearly observing the shadows,
to implement the semblance of rewards and punishments.
In executing rewards and punishments,
if the echo is clear, those who produce clarity are honored;
if the echo is murky, those who produce murkiness are disgraced;
if the shadow is straight, those who produce straightness are advanced;
if the shadow is crooked, those who produce crookedness are demoted;
examining names and assessing substance,
to verify the reality.
Rewards are not given arbitrarily,
punishments are not meted out without cause.
Thus, ministers fulfill their duties and govern,
each respectful and diligent in their tasks,
striving to achieve merits,
expanding their reputations,
while the ruler presides over it all,
this is the art of natural exertion.
The sage follows this,
so achievements come from the ministers,
and fame归于 the ruler.
"Examining Merits and Reputations, Chapter Twenty-One"
The method of assessing achievements
examines what has been accumulated.
The Way of Heaven accumulates numerous essences to form light;
the sage accumulates numerous virtues to achieve merit;
thus, the brightness of the sun and moon
is not the light of a single essence;
the sage bringing about great peace
is not the merit of a single virtue.
The source from which brightness arises
cannot be pinpointed as a single origin,
the source from which goodness emerges
cannot be identified as a single beginning,
one must measure circumstances to establish authority,
and adapt principles according to events.
Therefore, when the sage promotes benefits for the world,
it is like the spring air giving life to grass,
each according to its growth, whether small or large,
and measuring its quantity;
when eliminating harms for the world,
it is like rivers flowing into the sea,
each following its natural inclination,
yet directed north or south;
thus, though the paths differ, they arrive at the same end,
though the methods vary, their virtue is equal,
their aim to promote benefits and eliminate harms is one.
Hence, the key to promoting benefits
lies in achieving them,
not in their quantity;
the key to eliminating harms
lies in removing them,
not in their direction.
Assess achievements for demotion or promotion,
evaluate affairs to abolish or retain,
what is beneficial is called public good,
what is not beneficial is called troublesome.
Examine names and demand reality,
allowing no empty words,
reward those with merit,
punish those with crimes,
abundant merit receives conspicuous reward,
numerous crimes incur heavy punishment.
If one cannot achieve merit,
even with a reputation for worthiness,
they shall not be rewarded;
if one's official duties are not neglected,
even with a reputation for foolishness,
they shall not be punished.
Rewards and punishments are based on reality,
not on reputation,
worthiness or foolishness lies in substance,
not in appearance,
thus right and wrong cannot be confused,
joy and anger cannot sway,
treachery and deceit cannot manipulate,
all things attain their true nature,
then officials are encouraged in their duties,
striving to advance their merits.
The method of examination:
for major matters, be gradual,
for minor matters, be urgent;
for the noble, be relaxed,
for the lowly, be prompt.
Feudal lords examine their states monthly,
regional chiefs examine their districts seasonally,
four examinations constitute one assessment,
the Son of Heaven examines the empire annually,
three examinations constitute one assessment,
after three assessments, demotion or promotion is decided,
this is called accounting.
The method of examination:
combine their ranks and emoluments,
aggregate their salaries,
accumulate their days of service,
present their actual achievements,
calculate merits and measure offenses,
offsetting fewer with more,
to determine names based on reality,
first internally rank them,
initially comparing two or three parts,
categorizing as upper, middle, and lower,
to assess advancement or regression,
then externally compile,
collectively termed advancement or regression,
increases or decreases in quantity,
with ratios for grades,
nine parts divided into three sets of three,
also with upper, middle, and lower,
one being the highest,
five being the middle,
nine being the lowest.
Surplus is attributed to the middle,
above middle gains credit,
below middle incurs deficit,
those with little gain
have one added,
up to four,
those with much deficit
have four subtracted,
down to one,
all in reverse order,
three times four makes twelve,
completing the accounting,
those reaching full account are demoted or promoted.
Subsequent accounts each time,
follow their respective grades,
to tally the incoming numbers.
The first secondary account,
the next secondary account,
each retaining its previous grade,
and also reaching full account for demotion or promotion.
The first secondary account,
refers to the second upper,
the next secondary account,
refers to the third upper,
nine years form one grade,
two nines make eighteen,
remove six of them,
setting three grades,
six sixes equal,
set two,
combining middles yields three,
remove them all,
combine three threes in account,
yielding six,
combine for one account,
yielding six,
this constitutes four accounts.
Demotion follows the same principle.
"Governing the State and Cultivating the Self: Chapter Twenty-Two"
The pure in qì are essence,
the pure among people are worthy,
those who cultivate the self regard
accumulating essence as treasure,
those who govern the state regard accumulating worthies as the Way.
The self takes the heart as its foundation,
the state takes the ruler as its master;
when essence accumulates at its foundation,
then blood and qì mutually sustain;
when worthies accumulate around the ruler,
then superiors and subordinates mutually control and direct;
when blood and qì mutually sustain,
then the body suffers no ailment;
when superiors and subordinates mutually control and direct,
then all officials fulfill their roles;
when the body suffers no ailment,
then the self can attain peace;
when all officials fulfill their roles,
then the state can be maintained.
Those who wish to attract essence
must empty and calm their form;
those who wish to attract worthies
must humble and modest their person.
Those with calm form and empty will
are where essential qì gathers;
those who honor humility and lower themselves
are whom benevolent worthies serve.
Therefore, those who cultivate the self
must firmly hold emptiness and calm to attract essence;
those who govern the state
must exhaust humility and modesty to attract worthies;
being able to attract essence,
then one merges with brightness and attains longevity;
benevolence able to attract worthies,
then virtuous influence spreads and the state achieves great peace.
"The Three Dynasties' Reforms of Institutions and Substance and Refinement: Chapter Twenty-Three"
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"The King's First Month."
The Commentary explains:
"To which king does this refer?
It refers to King Wén.
Why does it mention 'king' before 'first month'?
Because it is the king's first month."
Why is it called the king's first month?
It is said:
A king must receive the Mandate before he can rule.
The king must reform the calendar,
change the colors of vestments,
establish rituals and music,
unify all under Heaven,
thereby demonstrating the change of surname,
not succeeding another person,
but receiving it directly from Heaven.
When a king receives the Mandate and rules,
he institutes this month to respond to change,
thus creating regulations to serve Heaven and Earth,
therefore it is called the king's first month.
How does a king reform institutions and create regulations?
It is said:
Corresponding to the twelve colors,
each calendar follows its method and correct color,
counting back three and repeating.
Setting aside the three before,
called the Five Emperors,
each emperor beginning with one color,
counting forward five and repeating,
rituals and music each follow their method imitating what is appropriate.
Counting forward four and repeating.
All create state names,
move capitals,
change official titles,
establish rituals and create music.
Thus Tāng received the Mandate and ruled,
responding to Heaven changed Xià,
created the name Yīn,
at that time adopting the White System,
honoring Xià thus Yú,
setting aside Táng calling him Emperor Yáo,
taking Shénnóng as the Red Emperor.
Built a capital south of the Luò River,
named the minister's palace Yǐn.
Created the Huò Music,
established simple rituals to serve Heaven.
King Wén received the Mandate and ruled,
responding to Heaven changed Yīn creating the name Zhōu,
at that time adopting the Red System.
Honoring Yīn thus Xià,
setting aside Yú calling him Emperor Shùn,
Xuānyuán called the Yellow Emperor,
elevating Shénnóng as the Nine Sovereigns,
built a capital at Fēng,
named the minister's palace Zǎi,
created the Wǔ Music, established refined rituals to serve Heaven.
King Wǔ received the Mandate,
built a capital at Hào,
established five ranks of nobility,
created the Xiàng Music,
succeeded Wén to serve Heaven.
Duke Zhōu assisted King Chéng in receiving the Mandate,
built a capital at Luòyáng,
completed the institutions of Wén and Wǔ,
created the Zhuó Music to serve Heaven.
After Yīn Tāng it was called a city,
showing Heaven's change returning the Mandate,
thus the Son of Heaven's mandate is not constant,
only virtue is rewarded.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals responds to Heaven creating affairs of the new king,
at that time adopting the Black System,
ruling through Lǔ,
honoring black,
setting aside Xià,
honoring Zhōu,
thus Sòng.
Music should honor Zhāo Wǔ,
thus using Yú records for honor,
music institution should follow Shāng,
combining Bó, Zǐ, and Nán into one rank.
How then to summarize this?
It is said:
The Three Systems begin with the Black System,
aligning the sun, moon, and new moon at Yíngshì,
the Dipper points to Yín.
Heaven's system energy begins transforming things,
things show sprouting growth,
their color is black.
Thus court ceremonies use black garments,
headwear with black ornaments,
main carriage plain black,
horses black,
major insignia ribbons and headbands honor black,
flags black,
great precious jade black,
sacrificial animals black,
sacrificial animals with small horns.
Capping ceremony at the eastern steps,
wedding ceremony meets in the courtyard,
funeral ceremony encoffins above the eastern steps.
Sacrificial animals black males,
offerings honor liver.
Musical instruments black material.
Law does not punish those pregnant or newly delivered,
this month no killing.
First day audience suspends punishments promotes virtue,
fully preserving two former kings' descendants.
Honoring the Red System,
thus day division at dawn,
dawn court audience.
How about the White System?
It is said:
The White System,
aligning the sun, moon, and new moon at Xū,
the Dipper points to Chǒu.
Heaven's system energy begins shedding transformations,
things begin to bud,
their color is white,
thus court ceremonies use white garments,
headwear with white ornaments,
main carriage plain white,
horses white,
major insignia ribbons and headbands honor white,
flags white,
great precious jade white,
sacrificial animals white,
sacrificial animals with small horns.
Capping ceremony in the hall,
wedding ceremony meets in the hall,
funeral ceremony encoffins between pillars,
sacrificial animals white males,
offerings honor lungs.
Musical instruments white material.
Law does not punish those pregnant,
this month no killing,
First day audience suspends punishments promotes virtue,
fully preserving two former kings' descendants,
honoring the Black System,
thus day division at cockcrow,
cockcrow court audience.
How about the Red System?
It is said:
The Red System,
aligning the sun, moon, and new moon at Qiānniú,
the Dipper points to Zǐ.
Heaven's system energy begins extending transformations,
things begin to move,
their color is red,
thus court ceremonies use red garments,
headwear with red ornaments,
main carriage plain red,
horses red,
major insignia ribbons,
headbands honor red,
flags red,
great precious jade red,
sacrificial animals red,
sacrificial animals with small horns,
Capping ceremony in the side room,
wedding ceremony meets at the door,
funeral ceremony encoffins above the western steps,
sacrificial animals red males,
offerings honor heart.
Musical instruments red material.
Law does not punish those pregnant,
emphasizing nurturing to cultivate subtlety,
this month no killing,
First day audience suspends punishments promotes virtue,
fully preserving two former kings' descendants.
Honoring the White System,
thus day division at midnight,
midnight court audience.
The meaning of calendar reform,
begins with honoring the origin,
ancient kings receiving the Mandate and ruling,
reforming institutions naming the first month,
vestment colors determined,
then sacrificing to Heaven, Earth and all spirits,
remotely tracing ancestors,
then proclaiming to all under Heaven.
Feudal lords receive it in temples,
announcing to soil and grain, ancestral temples, mountains and rivers,
then responses unite their offices,
the change of Three Systems,
nearby barbarians and distant lands have none who kill,
only the Central Kingdom,
thus the Three Dynasties' calendar reform,
must use the Three Systems throughout the world.
It is said:
Three Systems and Five Beginnings,
are the foundation for transforming the four directions,
Heaven begins abolishing and begins bestowing,
Earth must await the center,
therefore the Three Dynasties must reside in the Central Kingdom.
Imitating Heaven honoring the foundation,
grasping essentials to rule the world,
receiving feudal lords in audience.
Therefore the meaning of court audience,
the Son of Heaven wears pure system-colored garments,
The feudal lords wore dark robes with crimson hems and ties,
the high ministers and scholars wore caps with three distinctions,
the nearby barbarians wore ribbons,
and distant regions each wore their own attire when attending court,
all to illuminate the principle of the heavenly mandate.
As for what is meant by unifying the three correct beginnings,
it is said:
"Correct" means to rectify,
the mandate brings forth the vital force,
and all things respond and become upright;
when the mandate is correct,
all else follows in correctness.
The essence of the year
lies in the first month.
The way of modeling correctness
rectifies the root so the branches respond,
rectifies the inner so the outer responds;
in every action and movement,
none fail to transform and follow—
this may be called modeling correctness.
Hence the noble person says:
"King Wǔ indeed took the first month as correct."
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"The Earl of Qǐ came to court."
The descendants of a king are called "Duke,"
so why is Qǐ referred to as "Earl"?
The Spring and Autumn Annals elevates by demoting the Xià
and preserves the Zhōu below,
treating the Spring and Autumn Annals as the new king to be implemented.
How does the Spring and Autumn Annals serve as the new king?
It is said:
The method of a king must rectify titles,
demoting a "king" to be called "emperor,"
enfeoffing his descendants with a small state
to continue his sacrifices;
preserving the two preceding kings' lines with large states below,
having them wear their own attire,
practice their rituals and music,
