two concubines each,
and one tutor for the heir apparent.
The Shì who guard the ruler in residence,
are ranked equal to Senior Ministers,
with one Junior Minister,
and the numbers for higher and lower ranks each follow their respective standards.
The tutor of the heir apparent,
has five historians each for higher and lower ranks.
Five good ones of lower rank.
Those known as virtuous,
are granted land half the size of the ruler's territory.
Nine halves,
subtracting one-fourth,
yields definitively three territories of ten lǐ square,
with a fixed ratio supporting seventy-two hundred people.
One steward for the heir apparent,
equivalent to two hundred shí today.
Lower four halves, three halves, twenty-five.
Subtracting one-third,
yields definitively one territory of ten lǐ square,
and fifty of one lǐ square,
with a fixed ratio supporting three thousand six hundred people.
One steward for the heir apparent,
equivalent to one hundred shí today,
with five historians,
for the wives of the clan, guards in service, and ministers of the heir apparent.
"The Methods of Benevolence and Righteousness, Chapter Twenty-Nine"
What the Spring and Autumn Annals governs
are others and oneself;
the means to govern others and oneself
are benevolence and righteousness;
using benevolence to comfort others,
using righteousness to rectify oneself;
thus the term benevolence refers to others,
the term righteousness refers to oneself,
these terms are distinguished by their names.
Benevolence toward others,
righteousness toward oneself,
must not go unexamined.
If the multitude does not examine this,
they instead use benevolence to indulge themselves,
and use righteousness to demand of others.
To distort their positions and violate this principle
seldom fails to cause disorder.
Therefore, though none desire disorder,
generally there is constant disorder.
All because they are blind to the distinction between others and self,
and do not understand where benevolence and righteousness lie.
Hence, the Spring and Autumn Annals establishes the model for benevolence and righteousness.
The model of benevolence lies in loving others,
not in loving oneself;
the model of righteousness lies in rectifying oneself,
not in rectifying others;
if I do not rectify myself,
even if I can rectify others,
it is not deemed righteousness.
If others do not receive one's love,
even if one deeply loves oneself,
it is not deemed benevolence.
In the past,
Duke Líng of Jìn killed his chef to improve his meals,
and shot his officials to amuse himself,
not that he did not deeply love himself,
yet he could not be considered a good man,
because he did not love others.
In essence, loving the people,
extending down to birds, beasts, and insects, there is none not loved.
Without such love,
how can it be called benevolence!
Benevolence is the name for loving others;
Xī,
the Commentary does not use terms that magnify it.
Acting on one's own to pursue,
then it praises his concern for the distant.
If troops have already attacked,
and only then goes to rescue,
it is not praised.
If prepared before arrival,
then it is praised,
commending his preventing harm beforehand.
To rescue early and preempt,
then harm has no way to arise,
and the world is free from harm.
Thus, observing the movements of things,
and perceiving their sprouts in advance,
cutting off disorder and blocking harm before they occur and are put into action,
is the intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
its clarity is utmost,
without the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn,
knowing the root of rites,
who could match this?
Therefore, to prevent harm with foreknowledge,
is clarity.
The duke's concern for the distant,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals praising him,
detailing his intention to care for the distant,
then between heaven and earth, his benevolence becomes satisfying.
Without the virtue of the Three Sovereigns,
the essence of selecting the worthy,
who could achieve this?
Hence, knowledge brings clarity first,
and benevolence extends kindness afar.
Those who care for the distant are more worthy, and those who care for the near are less so,
is about love;
thus, a true king's love reaches the four barbarians,
a hegemon's love reaches the feudal lords,
a secure ruler's love reaches within his borders,
an endangered ruler's love reaches his immediate circle,
a doomed ruler's love reaches only his own person.
One who loves only himself,
even if occupying the position of Son of Heaven or feudal lord,
is merely a solitary individual,
with no use of ministers or people.
Such a person,
though none destroy him, destroys himself.
The Spring and Autumn Annals does not speak of attacking Liáng,
but says Liáng perished,
because its ruler loved only his own person.
Therefore it is said:
The benevolent love others,
not in loving themselves,
this is its model.
Righteousness means,
not rectifying others,
but rectifying oneself.
Even in chaotic times or under corrupt superiors,
none do not wish to rectify others.
How can that be called righteousness!
In the past,
King Líng of Chǔ punished the offenders of Chén and Cài,
Duke Huán of Qí held Yuántāotú accountable for his crime,
not that they could not rectify others,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals does not grant them,
deeming it not righteousness,
because they did not rectify themselves.
Hélǘ could rectify the troubles of Chǔ and Cài,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals denies him the term righteous,
because he himself was not upright.
The ruler of Lù among the feudal lords,
could rectify nothing,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals grants him righteousness,
because he himself was upright,
and acted for benefit.
Therefore it is said:
Righteousness lies in rectifying oneself,
not in rectifying others,
this is its model.
To demand of others what I lack,
or to criticize others for what I possess,
is what others cannot accept.
This principle is perverse!
How can it be called righteousness?
Righteousness means what is appropriate in me.
What is appropriate in me,
then can be called righteousness.
Thus, speaking of righteousness,
combines self and appropriateness,
into one concept.
By this standard,
righteousness as a term refers to the self,
hence it is said:
Those who act and attain righteousness,
are called self-attained;
those who act and lose righteousness,
are called self-lost.
Those who favor righteousness,
are called self-favoring;
those who do not favor righteousness,
are called not self-favoring.
By this comparison,
righteousness is the self,
is clear.
Thus, righteousness and benevolence differ.
Benevolence refers to going outward,
righteousness refers to turning inward.
Benevolence emphasizes the distant,
righteousness emphasizes the near.
Love directed at others is called benevolence,
righteousness directed at oneself is called righteousness.
Benevolence focuses on others,
righteousness focuses on oneself.
Therefore it is said:
Benevolence is for others,
righteousness is for oneself,
this is what it means.
The noble person seeks the distinction between benevolence and righteousness,
to order the space between others and self,
then discerns the division between internal and external,
and clarifies the place of compliance and opposition.
Thus, internal governance returns to principle to rectify the self,
relying on blessings to encourage prosperity.
External governance extends kindness to broaden generosity,
with lenient control to accommodate the multitude.
Confucius said to Rǎnzǐ:
"In governing the people, first enrich them,
then add education."
He told Fánchí:
"In governing oneself, first endure hardship, then seek gain."
This means that governing oneself and governing the people
have different priorities.
The Book of Songs says:
"Give them drink, give them food,
teach them, instruct them."
First food and drink, then teaching and instruction,
refers to governing others.
It also says:
"Kǎnkǎn cutting spokes,
that noble person,
does not eat without labor!"
First the task,
then the meal,
refers to governing oneself.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes the faults of superiors,
and pities the suffering of inferiors;
minor faults in others it does not record,
but in oneself it records and censures;
all these six points,
use benevolence to govern others,
righteousness to govern oneself,
being strict with oneself and lenient in blaming others,
this is what it means.
Moreover, the Analects have already shown this,
yet people do not examine it,
saying:
The noble person attacks his own faults,
not the faults of others.
Not attacking the faults of others,
Is this not the breadth of benevolence?
Attacking one's own faults,
is this not the completeness of righteousness?
This is called benevolence shaping others,
righteousness shaping oneself,
how do they differ?
Therefore, speaking of one's own faults is called sincerity,
speaking of others' faults is called malice;
demanding from oneself is called generosity,
demanding from others is called harshness;
holding oneself fully accountable is called wisdom.
Holding others fully accountable is called confusion.
Thus, to govern others with the standard of self-discipline,
is to lack tolerance in high position;
to discipline oneself with the measure of governing others,
is to lack reverence in practicing ritual.
Lacking reverence in practicing ritual,
then it harms conduct and the people will not respect;
lacking tolerance in high position,
then it harms generosity and the people will not draw close.
Not drawing close then not trusting,
not respecting then not revering.
When these two principles are distorted above,
and perverse actions are performed, there will be criticism below;
how can the application of benevolence and righteousness not be discussed!
If the eyes do not look,
they do not see;
if the mind does not deliberate,
it does not comprehend;
although there may be the finest flavors under heaven,
if not chewed,
one does not know their taste;
although there may be the supreme Way of the sages,
if not deliberated,
one does not understand its meaning.
"The Thirtieth: Necessity of Benevolence and Wisdom"
Nothing is closer than benevolence,
nothing more urgent than wisdom.
To have courage, strength, wealth, or talent without benevolence,
is like being mad and wielding a sharp weapon;
to be eloquent, clever, and quick-witted without wisdom,
is like being lost and riding a fine horse.
Thus, having talent without benevolence or wisdom,
one will use that talent to assist their depraved and mad mind,
and abet their perverse and contrary actions,
only sufficient to magnify their errors and worsen their faults.
Their strength is enough to cover up mistakes,
their resistance enough to commit fraud,
their cleverness enough to deceive the foolish,
their eloquence enough to gloss over faults,
their firmness enough to justify wickedness,
their severity enough to reject advice.
This is not for lack of talent,
but because it is applied improperly and exercised unrighteously.
Those with a wicked heart,
should not be given convenient power;
those with a dull nature should not be given sharp tools.
What the "Analects" calls "not knowing people",
fears failing to distinguish such types.
Benevolent but not wise,
then loves without distinction;
wise but not benevolent,
then knows but does not act.
Thus, the benevolent are those who love humanity,
the wise are those who remove its harms.
What is called benevolence?
The benevolent are compassionately loving towards people,
cautious and harmonious, not contentious,
their likes and dislikes guided by ethics,
without a heart that injures or hates,
without intentions of hidden jealousy,
without an aura of envy,
without desires of resentment and sorrow,
without treacherous and biased affairs,
without perverse and contrary conduct.
Therefore their heart is at ease,
their will calm,
their energy harmonious,
their desires moderated,
their affairs straightforward,
their path principled,
thus able to be even-tempered, harmonious, and reasonable without strife,
such a one is called benevolent.
What is called wisdom?
Speaking first and then proving appropriate.
Whenever people wish to act,
they all use their wisdom to plan first and then act.
Those whose plans are correct,
their actions succeed,
their undertakings are appropriate,
their conduct is accomplished,
their name is honored,
they themselves benefit without calamity,
blessings reach their descendants,
virtue is bestowed upon the myriad people,
Tāng and Wǔ were such.
Those whose plans are wrong,
their actions do not succeed in their affairs,
their undertakings are inappropriate,
their conduct is unfulfilled,
their name is disgraced,
harm befalls themselves,
their line cut off without continuation,
such are the destroyers of kindred, extinguishers of clans, and ruiners of states.
Therefore it is said:
Nothing is more urgent than wisdom.
The wise see fortune and misfortune from afar,
they know advantage and harm early,
when things move they know their transformation,
when affairs arise they know their outcome,
seeing the beginning they know the end,
speaking without daring to be frivolous,
establishing what cannot be abolished,
adopting what cannot be discarded,
without contradiction between before and after,
consistent from start to finish,
thoughtful and capable of repetition,
approached yet not tiresome.
Their words are few yet sufficient,
concise yet illustrative,
simple yet penetrating,
economical yet complete,
few yet cannot be added to,
many yet cannot be reduced,
their actions hit the mark of principle,
their words address what is essential.
Such a one is called wise.
In general categories,
when things of heaven and earth have unusual changes,
they are called anomalies,
minor ones are called disasters.
Disasters often come first and anomalies follow.
Disasters are heaven's warnings,
anomalies are heaven's awe.
If warned and unaware,
then awe is used to instill fear.
The "Book of Songs" says:
"I fear the awe of Heaven."
This probably refers to this.
The root of all disasters and anomalies,
stems entirely from the failures of the state.
When the state's failures first sprout,
heaven sends disasters to warn it;
warned yet not changing,
then anomalies appear to startle it;
startled yet still not fearful,
then calamity and misfortune arrive.
From this, heaven's benevolent intent is seen, not wishing to ruin people.
Carefully considered:
Disasters and anomalies reveal heaven's intent.
Heaven's intent has what it desires and what it does not desire,
what it desires and what it does not desire,
people should inwardly reflect,
and ought to feel admonished in their hearts;
outwardly observe events,
and ought to see verification in the state.
Thus, those who perceive heaven's intent regarding disasters and anomalies,
fear them but do not resent them,
believing heaven wishes to correct our faults,
rescue us from errors,
therefore using these to repay us.
The method of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
when above changing the ancient and altering the constant,
and correspondingly having heavenly disasters,
is called a fortunate state.
Confucius said:
"What heaven favors,
may do wrong yet repeatedly reach extremes."
And King Zhuāng said:
"Heaven shows no disaster,
earth shows no calamity."
Then prayed to the mountains and rivers,
saying:
"Is heaven about to destroy me!
It does not point out my faults,
it is punishing my crimes to the extreme."
From this perspective,
heavenly disasters correspond to faults and arrive,
anomalies are clearly manifest and fearsome.
This is what heaven desires to save,
what the "Spring and Autumn Annals" uniquely consider fortunate,
what King Zhuāng prayed and requested.
Even sage rulers and worthy lords gladly accept loyal ministers' remonstrance,
how much more should they accept heaven's warnings?
"The Thirty-First: Self-Cultivation's Importance Over Righteousness"
When Heaven gives birth to humans,
it endows them with righteousness and benefit.
Benefit serves to nourish their bodies,
righteousness serves to nourish their hearts.
The heart cannot find joy without righteousness,
the body cannot find peace without benefit.
Righteousness is the nourishment of the heart,
benefit is the nourishment of the body.
The body is not more precious than the heart,
therefore nourishment is not more important than righteousness,
righteousness's nourishment of human life is greater than benefit.
How do we know this?
Now there are people with great righteousness but little benefit,
though poor and humble,
they still maintain their conduct,
taking pride in themselves and finding joy in life,
such as Yuán Xiàn, Zēng Shēn, and Mǐn Sǔn.
There are people with great benefit but little righteousness,
though very wealthy,
they suffer great shame and disgrace.
Their wickedness deep,
their calamities heavy,
if not immediately dying for their crimes,
they quickly suffer injury and sorrow,
unable to enjoy life and complete their natural lifespan,
such are the people punished, executed, or dying prematurely.
Those who possess righteousness,
though poor, can find joy in themselves;
while those greatly lacking righteousness,
though wealthy, cannot preserve themselves.
I therefore verify that righteousness's nourishment of human life
is greater than benefit and more substantial than wealth.
The people cannot understand this,
and often act contrary,
all forgetting righteousness and pursuing benefit,
abandoning principle and running toward evil,
thus harming themselves and bringing disaster to their families.
This is not because they are insincere in their own planning,
but because their understanding cannot comprehend it.
Now if you hold a date and a gold coin,
and show them to an infant,
the infant will certainly take the date and not the gold.
Hold a catty of gold and a priceless pearl,
and show them to a rustic,
the rustic will certainly take the gold and not the pearl.
Thus, among things for humans,
the smaller ones are easily understood,
while the larger ones are difficult to perceive.
Now benefit is small for humans while righteousness is large,
no wonder the people all rush toward benefit and not righteousness,
this is indeed because they are in the dark.
The sage attends to illuminating righteousness,
to shine light on their darkness,
thus the people do not fall into error.
The Book of Songs says:
"Show me illustrious virtuous conduct."
This refers to this.
The ancient kings displayed virtue to show the people,
the people rejoiced and sang of it, making it into poetry,
delighted and transformed, making it into custom.
Thus, without orders, they act spontaneously,
without prohibitions, they stop naturally,
following the will of those above,
without awaiting commands,
as if by nature.
Therefore it is said:
The sage moves heaven and earth and transforms the four seasons,
not for any other reason,
but because he sees righteousness as great, thus he can move,
moving thus he can transform,
transforming thus he can greatly prevail,
with transformation greatly prevailing, laws are not violated,
laws not violated, punishments are not used,
punishments not used—this is the merit and virtue of Yáo and Shùn.
This is the way of great order,
handed down by former sages and restored.
Therefore Confucius said:
"Who can go out without using the door?
Why does no one follow this way!"
Now if illustrious virtuous conduct is not shown,
the people are in the dark about righteousness,
unable to be illuminated;
confused about the way, unable to be freed,
and then attempting to correct them with great severity and harshness,
merely harms the people and diminishes the ruler's virtue,
such measures cannot succeed.
Zhòngní said:
"When the state has the Way,
even if punishments are added,
there are no punishments.
When the state is without the Way,
even if people are killed,
it cannot be overcome."
What he called having the Way or lacking the Way
refers to whether illustrious virtuous conduct is shown or not.
Response to Prince Jiāoxī: Why Yuè's Great Officers Cannot Be Considered Benevolent, Number Thirty-Two
The command to the chancellor said:
"Great officers Lǐ, Zhǒng, Yōng, Gāo, and Chē Chéng,
the King of Yuè plotted with these five great officers to attack Wú,
and subsequently destroyed it,
avenging the shame of Kuàijī,
finally becoming hegemon.
Fàn Lǐ left him,
Zhǒng died for him.
I consider these two great officers both worthy.
Confucius said:
'Yīn had three benevolent men.'
Now considering the worth of the King of Yuè,
and the ability of Lǐ and Zhǒng,
these three men,
I also consider Yuè to have three benevolent men.
What does the lord think?"
Duke Huán resolved doubts with Guǎn Zhòng,
I resolve doubts with you."
Zhòngshū bowed twice, prostrating on the ground,
and replied:
"Zhòngshū's knowledge is narrow and learning shallow,
insufficient to decide this.
Nevertheless,
when the ruler questions his minister,
the minister dare not fail to respond fully,
as is proper.
Your minister Zhòngshū has heard:
In former times,
the ruler of Lǔ asked Liǔxià Huì:
'I wish to attack Qí,
what about it?'
Liǔxià Huì replied:
'It cannot be done.'
Withdrawing, he wore a troubled expression,
saying:
'I have heard that
those who plot to attack states
do not consult benevolent men.
Why then has this come to me?'
Merely being asked, he still felt ashamed,
how much more so actually engaging in deceit to attack Wú!
That it is inappropriate is clear.
From this perspective,
Yuè originally had not one benevolent man,
how could it have three!
A benevolent man
corrects his way without scheming for benefit,
cultivates his principle without hastening for achievement,
arrives at non-action while customs are greatly transformed,
he may be called benevolent and sage.
The Three Kings were such.
The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals
values trustworthiness and disdains deceit.
To defeat others through deceit,
even if successful,
the noble man does not do it.
Therefore, in Confucius's school,
even a child of five feet
speaks ashamed to praise the Five Hegemons.
Because they used deceit to achieve success,
acting merely expediently,
thus they are unworthy of praise in the great noble man's school.
The Five Hegemons,
compared to other feudal lords were worthy,
but compared to benevolent worthies,
what worthiness do they have?
They are like fake jade compared to beautiful jade.
Your minister Zhòngshū bows twice, prostrating on the ground, to report this."
Observing Virtue, Number Thirty-Three
Heaven and Earth are
the origin of all things and the source from which ancestors arise.
Vast and boundless,
their virtue shines brightly,
their years are numerous,
eternal and without end.
Heaven produces the utmost brightness,
a category for all beings,
and nothing it overshadows is left unilluminated.
Earth produces the utmost obscurity,
yet with stars and the sun providing light,
it dares not remain dark.
The principles of ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife are derived from this.
At the end of the grand rites,
ministers and sons dare not assume authority for three years.
Even when they do,
they must refer to the former ruler,
they must refer to their ancestors,
daring not to covet the highest honor.
The honors of all rites
are arranged by month,
months are arranged by season,
seasons are arranged by the ruler,
and the ruler is arranged by Heaven.
Those whom Heaven abandons,
the world does not protect,
as with Jié and Zhòu;
those whom the Son of Heaven executes and cuts off,
ministers and sons cannot establish,
as with the Crown Prince of Cài and Féng Chǒufù;
those whom the royal father or father cuts off,
sons and grandsons cannot continue,
as with Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ being unable to remember his mother,
and Wèi Zhé refusing his father's command.
Thus, receiving the mandate, the world follows them,
like the multitude of stars surrounding the North Star,
or flowing waters revering the vast sea.
How much more for those living between Heaven and Earth,
emulating the appearance of the great ancestor and forebears,
then their utmost virtue takes form,
and all titles honor them,
this is why the sage is held in high esteem.
Tàibó's virtue matched that of Heaven and Earth,
so God set aside the rightful heir, changed the surname, and treated him as a son.
Yielding his utmost virtue,
the world cherished and returned to him.
Tàibó declined three times and dared not take the throne.
Bó Yìkǎo's followers had divided loyalties,
so he withdrew and stirred himself,
to comply with the divine spirits.
With utmost virtue, he received the mandate,
and heroes, outstanding and wise men gathered and returned to him.
The highest were ranked as dukes and marquises,
down to ministers and grandees,
how splendidly arrayed!
All were ordered by virtue.
Thus, Wú and Lǔ shared the same surname,
yet at the meeting of Zhōnglí, they could not be ranked and addressed as lord,
treating Lǔ differently in the assembly,
because of their barbaric behavior.
At the battle of Jīfù,
Wú could not participate in the rites of the Central States.
As for the journeys to Bójǔ and Huángchí,
they changed and returned to the Way,
thus were granted ranks without distinction.
At the meeting of Shàolíng,
the lord of Lǔ was present but could not act as host,
yielding to Qí Huán.
In the thirteenth year of Lǔ Huán's reign,
Qí, Sòng, Wèi, and Yān raised an army to march east,
while Jì, Zhèng, and Lǔ joined forces to retaliate.
Later, on that day,
because Lǔ could not fully participate,
they yielded to Marquis Jì and Duke Lì of Zhèng.
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" consistently state
that barbarians cannot partake in the rites of the Central States.
By the time of the battle of Bì,
the barbarians rebelled,
and the Central States could not engage in rites with them,
yielding to Chǔ Zhuāng.
Xíng and Wèi
shared the same surname as Lǔ,
yet when the Dí people destroyed them,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" concealed it,
to yield to Qí Huán.
In such cases,
only virtue is cherished,
and all prioritize their kin.
Thus, among the descendants of Zhōu,
their kinship is equal,
yet King Wén is foremost.
The four seasons are equal,
yet spring is foremost.
The twelve months are equal,
yet the first month is foremost.
When virtue is equal,
then kinship is prioritized.
The twelve dukes of Lǔ are equal,
yet Dìng and Āi are most honored.
Wèi was among the Xià states,
yet at the meeting of Shàndào,
it alone was prioritized internally,
because it shared the same surname with us.
Wú was among the barbarians,
yet at the meeting of Zhā,
it alone was prioritized internally,
because it shared the same surname with us.
Over fifteen states were destroyed,
yet the Xià states were prioritized first.
Lǔ and Jìn were both Xià states,
yet when criticizing double names,
they were the first to be mentioned.
Shèng Bó and Gào Zǐ both deserved to be cut off,
yet only they were not named,
because they were our brothers of the same surname.
Many were sent away,
but those sent away as maternal brothers
were uniquely condemned,
for abandoning their mother and betraying their kin.
Among destroyers of states, none were cut off,
yet only Duke Huǐ of Wèi, who destroyed a state of the same surname, was cut off,
for dishonoring his ancestors and forgetting his origins.
Kinship priority begins with the closest,
establishing the heir by seniority,
and the mother honored through her son first.
On Jiǎxū and Jǐchǒu,
Marquis Bào of Chén died,
recorded as seen,
without mentioning the obscurity.
Five meteorites fell in Sòng,
six fish hawks flew backward,
heard and recorded by ear,
seen and written by eye,
whether gradual or detailed,
all were ordered by what first connected with us.
The same applies to the rites of meetings, audiences, and visits.
Many feudal lords participated in alliances,
yet only Yífù gradually advanced.
Duke Xī of Zhèng came to meet us but was killed on the way,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" conveyed the intent,
calling it "as if meeting."
The ruler of Lù left the barbarians and returned,
his faction able to rise,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" called him "zǐ,"
to acknowledge his intent.
At the meetings of Bāolái, Shǒudài, Huángchí, Jiàntǔ, and Cāo,
Chén and Zhèng left us,
called "fleeing back";
Zhèng stayed and did not come,
called "begging for an alliance";
the Marquis of Chén arrived late,
called "as if meeting";
the people of Jǔ doubted us,
demoted and called "people."
Many feudal lords paid court to Lǔ,
yet only Téng and Xuē were called marquises.
The Duke of Zhōu transformed us,
stripped of rank and without title.
Wú and Chǔ, being the first to visit us, were seen as virtuous;
at the battles of Qūjí and Ān,
those who first worried for us were seen as virtuous.
"Honoring the Root, Chapter Thirty-Four"
Rites are what
connect Heaven and Earth, embody yin and yang,
carefully distinguish between host and guest,
order the positions of noble and humble, high and low, great and small,
and differentiate the ranks of outer and inner, distant and near, new and old,
taking abundant virtue as their model.
All things take breadth, vastness, multitude, and long-lasting years as their model.
In Heaven, what serves as the model of Heaven
is nothing greater than the sun and moon,
which continue the light and brilliance of Heaven and Earth,
illuminating everything without exception.
Among stars, none are greater than the Great Chén,
the constant stars of the Northern Dipper.
The constant stars of the Northern Dipper
comprise three hundred ministerial stars,
and three thousand guard stars.
The Great Fire has twenty-six stars,
the Punishment constellation has thirteen stars,
the Northern Dipper has seven stars,
there are five constant stars,
and twenty-eight lunar mansions.
The most numerous are the twenty-eight or twenty-nine mansions.
This is like the hundred-stemmed yarrow sharing a single root,
or the thousand-year-old tortoise being treasured by people.
Therefore, the Three Dynasties passed down decisions for resolving doubts.
What obtains the substance of Earth
is nothing like mountains and mounds.
Among humans, those who obtain Heaven and the multitude
are none other than the Mandated Son of Heaven.
Descending to dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons,
the hearts of all within the seas are suspended upon the Son of Heaven,
and the people within the borders are governed by the feudal lords.
Solar and lunar eclipses
are both announcements of calamity,
not due to their regular motion.
When a comet appears in the east,
at the Great Chén,
enters the Northern Dipper,
constant stars become invisible,
earthquakes occur,
Mount Liáng and Shālù collapse,
disasters strike Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng,
and kings, dukes, and senior ministers are usurped and assassinated,
the Spring and Autumn Annals records all these as major anomalies,
but does not mention comets entering among numerous stars, or meteor showers,
or low-lying marshes collapsing,
or the deaths of common people in a single state,
nor does it resolve doubts by consulting common plants and trees.
Only in the designation of fields and towns,
the more numerous ones determine the master's name.
The ruler does not mention his ministers,
ministers do not mention their armies,
when the king is pacified or the ruler captured,
the army's defeat is not mentioned.
Confucius said:
"Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself upon it."
Modeling upon it
means greatness.
"How majestic were his achievements!"
refers to his respect and greatness in achieving success.
Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn did not respect the Zhōu court,
thus they could not become hegemons;
the sages of the Three Dynasties did not model themselves on Heaven and Earth,
thus they could not attain true kingship.
From this perspective,
one can understand the nobility of Heaven and Earth.
Deep-flowing waters are immeasurable,
and the highest respect is boundless.
Therefore, what Heaven imposes,
even if it brings disasters,
should still be received and magnified,
with reverence being endless,
as in the case of the temple of Yí Bó being struck by lightning.
Heaven has no erroneous disasters,
while Earth has anomalies of shaking and movement.
Those whom the Son of Heaven executes or eliminates,
and the armies he defeats,
even if not following the right path,
the Spring and Autumn Annals dares not omit,
recording them with care.
Thus, there have been many military expeditions,
yet returns are rarely mentioned.
When our army and the Qí army besieged Chéng,
and Chéng surrendered to the Qí army,
only then was the return mentioned.
Their ruler was coerced externally,
with no alternative,
thus it could be directly stated.
As for other armies,
all were following their rulers' commands,
so it is said not to be the army's fault.
This means ministers do not accept blame for their rulers,
and no crime is greater than that of disloyal ministers.
The most brilliant
shines boundlessly;
the darkest
is obscurely boundless.
Now the Spring and Autumn Annals uses Lǔ to express kingly righteousness,
treats Yǐn and Huán as remote ancestors,
honors Dìng and Āi as parents,
making them supremely noble and lofty,
extremely illustrious and bright.
The foundation it adds to the soil,
the moisture and grace it spreads,
are endlessly extensive.
Previously, this was a constant principle,
neighbors for ten years,
secluded people draw near their graves yet remain lofty and bright.
Great states like Qí and Sòng,
when separated, do not mention meetings.
Rulers of minor states,
in death and burial rites,
are recorded with elaborate language.
Rulers of distant barbarians,
are included internally rather than externally.
At this time,
Lǔ had no despised borders,
and all feudal lords attacking Āi were recorded as "us."
Zhūlóu Shùqí, Bíwǒ,
ministers of Zhūlóu.
Though they had no kinship with us,
due to proximity,
they gained prominence.
Yǐn and Huán,
close ancestors in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
when Yìshī died, the date was not recorded;
at the meeting of Jì,
it mentions completing the disorder of Sòng,
to connect with external affairs.
At the meeting of Huángchí,
using the language of two hegemons,
it states not treating it as external,
but as drawing near internally.
Deep Examination of Names and Designations - Thirty-Fifth
The foundation of governing the world,
lies in examining and distinguishing the great.
The foundation of distinguishing the great,
lies in deeply investigating names and titles.
Names are the foremost chapter of the great principle.
By recording the meaning of this foremost chapter,
to glimpse into the affairs within,
then right and wrong can be known,
obedience and defiance naturally become evident,
and its subtleties penetrate through heaven and earth.
The correctness of right and wrong,
is derived from obedience and defiance;
the correctness of obedience and defiance,
is derived from names and titles;
the correctness of names and titles,
is derived from heaven and earth;
heaven and earth are the great meaning of names and titles.
The ancient sages,
cried out and imitated heaven and earth, which is called a title,
sounded forth and bestowed commands, which is called a name.
A name speaks of sounding and commanding,
a title speaks of crying out and imitating,
crying out and imitating heaven and earth is a title,
sounding forth and commanding is a name.
Names and titles differ in sound but share the same root,
both are expressions that convey the will of heaven.
Heaven does not speak,
but lets humans express its will;
it does not act,
but lets humans carry out its principles.
Names are the expressions of heaven's will by the sages,
which must be deeply contemplated.
The ruler who receives the mandate,
is bestowed by the will of heaven.
Thus, one titled as the Son of Heaven,
should regard heaven as a father,
and serve heaven with the way of filial piety;
those titled as feudal lords,
should carefully attend to the Son of Heaven they serve;
those titled as grand masters,
should deepen their loyalty and trustworthiness,
strengthen their ritual and righteousness,
making their goodness exceed the righteousness of common men,
sufficient to transform others;
shì means to serve,
mín means the unenlightened;
shì do not reach the level of transformation,
but can be made to uphold duties and follow superiors.
The five titles each praise,
each has its division.
Within divisions are specifics,
and specifics have names.
Names are more numerous than titles,
titles encompass the whole.
Names,
designate distinctions and separations.
Titles are general and broad,
names are detailed and specific.
Specifics mean comprehensively distinguishing affairs,
general means highlighting the major matters.
The title for offering to spirits and deities,
is called jì.
The specific names of jì,
in spring is called cí,
in summer is called yuè,
in autumn is called cháng,
in winter is called zhēng.
The title for hunting animals,
is called tián.
The specific names of tián,
in spring is miáo,
in autumn is sōu,
in winter is shòu,
in summer is xiǎn.
There is none that does not align with the will of heaven.
All things have general titles,
all titles have specific names like this.
Thus, affairs each follow names,
names each follow heaven.
The connection between heaven and humanity,
merges into one.
Unified and sharing the same principle,
acting and benefiting each other,
obeying and receiving mutually,
is called the virtuous way.
The Shī says:
"Only by these titles and words,
there is order and trace."
This refers to it.
Deeply investigating the great meaning of the title "king",
it contains five categories:
Huáng category, Fāng category, Kuāng category, Huáng category, Wǎng category.
Combining these five categories into one word is called "king".
King means huáng (magnificent),
king means fāng (upright),
king means kuāng (corrective),
king means huáng (yellow/central),
king means wǎng (to go/to attract).
Therefore, if the king's intention is not universally great and magnificent,
then the way cannot be straight and upright;
if the way cannot be straight and upright,
then virtue cannot correct and circulate universally;
if virtue cannot correct and circulate universally,
then beauty cannot be yellow (central);
if beauty cannot be yellow,
then the four directions cannot come;
if the four directions cannot come,
then it is incomplete as a king.
Hence it is said:
Heaven covers without exclusion,
earth carries with universal love,
wind blows commands and unifies its authority,
rain spreads and equalizes its virtue.
This is called the king's method.
Deeply investigating the great meaning of the title "lord",
it also contains five categories:
Yuán category, Yuán category, Quán category, Wēn category, Qún category.
Combining these five categories into one word is called "lord".
Lord means yuán (origin),
lord means yuán (source),
lord means quán (authority),
lord means wēn (gentle),
lord means qún (community).
Therefore, if the lord's intention does not align with the origin,
then actions lose their foundation;
if actions lose their foundation,
then endeavors cannot be established;
if endeavors cannot be established,
then they are not effective at the source;
if not effective at the source,
then one abandons oneself;
if one abandons oneself,
then transformation cannot be carried out;
using authority in change,
then loses the appropriateness of balance;
if the appropriateness of balance is lost,
then the way is not level and virtue is not gentle;
if the way is not level and virtue is not gentle,
then the masses are not intimate and peaceful;
if the masses are not intimate and peaceful,
then they scatter and do not form a community;
if scattered and not forming a community,
then it is incomplete as a lord.
Names arise from truth;
if not truthful,
they should not be used as names.
Names are what the sage uses to truthfully represent things.
The term "name" means truth.
Therefore, all things obscure and murky,
when each returns to its truth,
then the murky becomes clear again.
To examine straightness and crookedness,
nothing is better than using a plumb line;
to examine right and wrong,
nothing is better than using names.
The examination of right and wrong through names
is like the examination of straightness and crookedness through a plumb line.
Questioning their names and realities,
observing their matches and mismatches,
then the true nature of right and wrong cannot be distorted.
Nowadays, people are confused about human nature,
and those who speak of it differ;
why not try to return to the name of nature?
Is the name of nature not "birth"?
That which is the natural endowment of life is called nature.
Nature is substance;
questioning the substance of nature against the name of goodness,
can it match?
Since it cannot match,
yet still calling the substance good,
why is that?
The name of nature cannot be separated from substance.
If separated from substance even by a hair,
then it is no longer nature,
and this must be carefully considered.
The Spring and Autumn Annals discern the principles of things
to correct their names.
Naming things according to their truth,
not missing even the tip of an autumn hair.
Hence, naming falling stones,
they mention five later;
speaking of retreating swallows,
they mention six first.
This is how carefully the sage rectifies names.
The noble person, in speech,
is never careless,
as seen in the phrasing of "five stones" and "six swallows."
To restrain all evils within,
preventing them from manifesting outwardly,
is the mind's role,
hence the mind is named "restrainer."
If humans received qi without any evil,
what would the mind restrain?
I infer from the name of the mind the sincerity of humans;
human sincerity includes both greed and benevolence,
with both benevolent and greedy qi present in the body.
The name of the body is derived from heaven,
as heaven has the dual application of yīn and yáng,
so the body has the dual nature of greed and benevolence.
Heaven has prohibitions on yīn,
the body has restraints on desires,
aligning with the way of heaven.
Thus, the movement of yīn must not interfere with spring and summer,
and the moon's dark side is often overshadowed by sunlight.
Sometimes full, sometimes damaged,
such is heaven's prohibition on yīn;
how can one not reduce desires and restrain emotions to correspond to heaven?
What heaven prohibits,
the body prohibits,
hence it is said the body is like heaven.
Prohibiting what heaven prohibits
is not prohibiting heaven itself.
One must know that heavenly nature, without education,
ultimately cannot be restrained.
Examine reality to assign names;
without education,
how could nature be as such?
Thus, nature is compared to grain,
goodness to rice;
rice comes from grain,
but grain cannot wholly be called rice;
goodness comes from nature,
but nature cannot wholly be called good.
Goodness and rice
are what humans inherit from heaven and complete externally,
not within heaven's direct doing.
What heaven does
has its limits and stops,
what stops within is called heavenly nature,
what stops outside is called human effort.
Effort lies outside nature,
yet nature must be formed into virtue.
The term for the people
is derived from "drowsiness";
if nature were already good,
why use "drowsiness" as a label?
Speaking of the dormant,
without support,
they would fall into chaos and madness;
how could they be good?
Nature is like the eyes;
eyes closed in darkness and drowsy,
await awakening to see.
When not yet awake,
one can say they have the substance of sight,
but cannot say they see.
Now, the nature of the myriad people,
has the substance but not yet awakened,
like the drowsy awaiting awakening,
becoming good only after education.
When not yet awakened,
one can say they have the substance,
but cannot call it good,
similar to the eyes' drowsiness and awakening,
a parallel comparison.
Calm the mind and observe slowly,
and these words become evident.
Nature is like drowsiness before awakening,
done by heaven.
Imitating heaven's doing,
creating a name for it,
hence called "people."
The term "people"
indeed means drowsy;
follow the name and label to understand its principle,
and you will grasp it.
Thus, rectifying names and labels based on heaven and earth,
what heaven and earth produce
is called nature and emotion.
Nature and emotion together form a single drowsiness.
Emotion is also nature;
if nature is said to be already good,
what about emotion?
Therefore, the sage never claimed nature is good,
to avoid burdening the name.
The body having nature and emotion
is like heaven having yīn and yáng.
To speak of human substance without emotion
is like speaking of heaven's yáng without its yīn.
Those who argue exhaustively
are never accepted.
Naming nature,
not by the highest,
not by the lowest,
but by the nature of the average people.
Like a cocoon or an egg,
an egg needs incubation to become a chick,
a cocoon needs reeling to become silk,
nature needs education to become good.
This is called true heaven.
Heaven endows people's nature with the substance of goodness but not yet good,
thus establishing kings to make it good,
this is heaven's intent.
People receive from heaven a nature not yet good,
and subsequently receive from the king education to complete nature.
The king upholds heaven's intent,
tasked with completing people's nature.
Now, to judge by true substance and claim people's nature is already good
is to lose heaven's intent and abandon the king's responsibility.
If the nature of the myriad people were already good,
what task would the king have upon receiving the mandate?
Setting people's nature incorrectly,
thus abandoning heavy responsibility and违背ing the great mandate,
is not the language of law.
The phrasing of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
for internal matters awaiting external influence,
speaks from the external perspective.
Now, the nature of the myriad people
awaits external education to become good;
goodness should be attributed to education,
not to nature.
Attributing it to nature leads to burdens and lack of refinement,
self-achievement without sages or worthies,
this is the mistaken view of the elders of the world,
not the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals' phrasing.
Unlawful words and unverified theories,
the noble person rejects;
how could they be upheld!
Some say:
"Nature has sprouts of goodness,
the mind has the substance of goodness,
how can it not be good?"
Respond to them:
"Not so.
A cocoon has silk,
but a cocoon is not silk;
an egg has a chick,
but an egg is not a chick.
Compare these categories directly,
what doubt is there?"
Heaven endows people with the Six Classics,
those speaking of nature should not differ.
Yet some say nature is good,
some say nature is not yet good,
then what is called good
varies in meaning.
Nature has sprouts of goodness,
acting to love parents,
better than beasts,
then it is called good.
This is Mèngzǐ's statement.
Following the three bonds and five constants,
One who comprehends the principles of the eight virtues,
is loyal, trustworthy, and broadly benevolent,
sincere and fond of propriety,
may then be called good.
This is the goodness of the sage.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"A good person,
I have never been able to meet;
if I could meet someone with constancy, that would suffice."
From this perspective,
what the sage calls goodness
is not easily attained,
it is not merely being better than beasts that is called goodness.
If moving towards the beginnings of goodness compared to beasts could be called goodness,
then why are such good people not seen?
That being better than beasts does not qualify as true goodness
is like knowledge compared to plants—it cannot be called true knowledge.
The nature of the common people may be better than beasts, yet it cannot be named goodness;
the name of knowledge is taken from the sage.
What the sage decrees,
the world takes as standard.
To correct the morning and evening, one looks to the North Star;
to resolve doubts, one looks to the sage.
The sage believed that in an age without kings,
and among untaught people,
none can attain goodness.
So difficult is it to attain goodness,
yet to say that the nature of all people can achieve it
is an error.
Compared to the nature of beasts,
the nature of the people is good;
but compared to the goodness of the human way,
the people's nature falls short.
To acknowledge that the people's nature is better than beasts,
but not to acknowledge what the sage considers good—
in my assessment of what defines nature, I differ from Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ compared downwards to what beasts do,
thus saying nature is already good;
I compare upwards to what the sage considers good,
thus I say nature is not yet good.
Goodness surpasses nature,
the sage surpasses goodness.
The Spring and Autumn Annals emphasizes the origin,
hence it is careful in rectifying names.
If the name does not match the origin,
how can one speak of not yet good or already good?
Chapter 36: On the Reality of Nature
Confucius said:
"If names are not correct,
then speech will not be fluent."
Now to say that nature is already good
is nearly to say that without teaching, it is as it naturally is,
which also does not accord with the way of governance.
Moreover, names are the reality of nature,
reality is the substance of nature.
At the time without teaching,
how could it suddenly be good?
Goodness is like rice,
nature is like the grain plant.
Though rice comes from the plant,
the plant cannot be called rice.
Though goodness comes from nature,
nature cannot be called good.
Rice and goodness
are what humans continue from Heaven and complete externally,
not what is within Heaven's direct doing.
What Heaven does
has its limit and stops there.
What stops within is called Heaven,
what stops outside is called kingly teaching.
Kingly teaching is outside nature,
yet nature cannot but be developed.
Therefore it is said:
Nature has the potential for goodness,
but it is not yet able to be good.
How dare I use elegant words?
This is the actual reality.
What Heaven does
stops at the silkworm cocoon, hemp, and the grain plant.
To make cloth from hemp,
silk from cocoons,
cooked rice from grain,
and goodness from nature—
these are all what the sage continues from Heaven and advances,
not what raw nature and simple substance can achieve,
thus it cannot be called nature.
To correct the morning and evening, one looks to the North Star;
to resolve doubts, one looks to the sage.
What the sage names,
the world takes as standard.
Now examining the sage's words,
originally there is no name 'nature is good',
but there is 'good person'—
'I have never been able to meet one.'
If the nature of all people were already able to be good,
then why are good people not seen?
Considering the meaning of Confucius's words here,
he thought goodness very hard to attain.
Yet Mèngzǐ believed that all people's nature can attain it—
this is an error.
The nature of the sage
cannot be used to name nature;
the nature of the petty-minded
also cannot be used to name nature.
What is named nature is the nature of the average people.
The nature of the average people is like a cocoon or an egg.
An egg needs incubation for twenty days before it can become a chick;
a cocoon needs boiling in hot water before it can become silk;
nature needs gradual training and teaching before it can become good.
Goodness is the result of teaching and training,
not what raw substance can achieve,
thus it is not called nature.
Nature should be understood by its name—
it arises without dependence,
it is innate from birth;
if goodness were innate,
then teaching and training would already not be nature.
Thus, rice comes from grain,
but grain cannot be called rice;
jade comes from the rough stone,
but the rough stone cannot be called jade;
goodness comes from nature,
but nature cannot be called good.
This comparison holds for many things,
yet for nature, some think it does not—
why not understand the category?
The nature of an egg cannot yet make a chick,
the nature of a cocoon cannot yet make silk,
the nature of hemp cannot yet make thread,
the nature of grain cannot yet make rice.
The Spring and Autumn Annals distinguishes the principles of things to rectify their names;
naming things must each follow their true essence,
true to their meaning,
true to their reality,
only then are they named.
Naming a falling star, the five come after;
naming retrograde flight, the six come first—
these are all based on their truth.
The sage is never careless in his words.
Nature is the simple substance of Heaven's endowment;
goodness is the transformation of kingly teaching.
Without the substance,
kingly teaching cannot transform;
without kingly teaching,
the simple substance cannot become good.
To have substance but not use it for goodness in nature—
the name is not correct,
thus it is not accepted.
Chapter 37: On the Feudal Lords
To give birth, nurture, and raise,
to mature and regenerate,
ending and beginning again,
these affairs that benefit and sustain the people are endless;
though Heaven does not speak,
its intention to provide amply is evident.
The ancient sages, seeing Heaven's generous intent towards people,
thus faced south and ruled the world,
necessarily benefiting all.
For what is too distant for the eye to see,
and too hidden for the ear to hear,
then beyond a thousand miles,
they divided land and people,
and established states with rulers,
so that they could see what the Son of Heaven could not see,
hear what he could not hear,
and be summoned for audience and questioning.
The term 'feudal lords' (zhūhóu) is like 'various guardians' (zhū hòu).
Chapter 38: Dialogue on the Five Elements
Prince Xiàn of Héjiān asked Lord Dǒng of Wēnchéng:
"The Classic of Filial Piety says:
'Filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven,
and the righteous conduct of Earth.'
What does this mean?"
He replied:
"Heaven has five phases:
wood, fire, earth, metal, and water.
Wood produces fire,
fire produces earth,
earth produces metal,
metal produces water.
Water corresponds to winter,
metal to autumn,
earth to late summer,
fire to summer,
wood to spring.
Spring governs birth,
summer governs growth,
late summer governs nurturing,
autumn governs harvest,
winter governs storage.
Storage is what winter accomplishes.
Thus, what the father gives birth to,
the son nurtures to growth;
what the father grows,
the son nourishes;
what the father nourishes,
the son brings to completion.
All that the father does,
the son upholds and continues to practice,
not daring to fail in fulfilling the father's intentions,
thus exhausting the way of being human.
Therefore, the five phases are five modes of conduct.
From this perspective,
the father bestows,
the son receives it,
which is the way of Heaven.
Hence it is said:
'Filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven.'
This is what it means."
The Prince said:
"Excellent!
Now that I have heard about the constant principle of Heaven,
I wish to hear about the righteous conduct of Earth."
He replied:
"Earth emits clouds to form rain,
raises vapors to form wind.
Wind and rain are acts of Earth,
yet Earth does not dare claim their merit or name,
but must attribute them to Heaven.
As if following Heaven's command,
thus we speak of Heaven's wind and Heaven's rain,
never saying Earth's wind or Earth's rain.
Though the toil is Earth's,
the credit entirely returns to Heaven.
If not supremely righteous,
who could act thus?
Therefore, subordinates serving superiors,
like Earth serving Heaven,
can be called great loyalty.
Earth is the child of fire.
Among the five phases, none is nobler than earth.
Earth, in relation to the four seasons, has no specific assignment,
not sharing merit or fame with fire.
Wood is named for spring,
fire for summer,
metal for autumn,
water for winter.
The righteousness of loyal ministers,
the conduct of filial sons,
are derived from earth.
Earth is the noblest of the five phases,
its righteousness cannot be surpassed.
Among the five tones, none is nobler than gōng;
among the five flavors, none is finer than sweet;
among the five colors, none is nobler than yellow.
This is what is meant by 'Filial piety is the righteous conduct of Earth'."
The Prince said:
"Excellent!"
Clothing and appearance
are what please the eye;
speech and response
are what please the ear;
likes, dislikes, approaches, and avoidances
are what please the heart.
Thus, when a gentleman's clothing is appropriate and his appearance respectful,
the eye is pleased;
when his speech is reasoned,
and his responses deferential,
the ear is pleased;
when he loves benevolence and depth, and hates shallowness,
approaches the good and avoids the crooked and mean,
the heart is pleased.
Therefore it is said:
"His conduct and intentions are delightful,
his demeanor and actions are admirable."
This is what it means.
