"Heaven as the Origin of Humanity: Chapter Forty-One"
The power to generate cannot create humans;
it is Heaven that creates humans.
That which makes humans human originates from Heaven.
Heaven is humanity's great ancestor,
this is why humans are classified as resembling Heaven above.
The human form
transforms according to heavenly numerical patterns;
human blood and qi
transform according to Heaven's will into benevolence;
human moral conduct
transforms according to heavenly principle into righteousness;
human likes and dislikes
transform according to Heaven's warmth and coolness;
human joy and anger
transform according to Heaven's cold and heat;
human endowment of life
transforms according to Heaven's four seasons.
Human life has responses of joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness,
corresponding to spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
Joy corresponds to spring,
anger to autumn,
happiness to summer,
sorrow to winter.
Heaven's counterpart resides in humans.
Human nature and emotions derive from Heaven.
Therefore it is said 'to receive',
which means 'from Heaven'.
As a ruler of men,
no way is brighter than examining the Heaven within oneself,
as if Heaven were issuing forth,
causing it to issue forth.
Respond to Heaven's issuing of the four seasons and be faithful to what one receives,
then even the governance of Yáo and Shùn could not surpass it.
Such people can be given life or death,
but cannot be made to create chaos.
Therefore it is said:
"Without the Way, do not act;
without the Law, do not speak."
This is what it means.
The Tradition says:
Only the Son of Heaven receives the mandate from Heaven;
the empire receives the mandate from the Son of Heaven;
a state receives the mandate from its ruler.
If the ruler's commands are proper,
then the people will have proper destinies;
if the ruler's commands are perverse,
then the people will have perverse destinies.
Therefore it is said:
"If one man is virtuous,
the myriad people rely on him."
This is what it means.
The Tradition says:
Governance has three aspects:
If father and son are not affectionate,
promote loving kindness;
if great ministers are not harmonious,
encourage respect and observance of rites;
if the common people are not settled,
exert effort in filial and fraternal duties.
Filial and fraternal duties are what settle the common people;
exertion means diligently practicing them,
personally transforming through them.
The numbers of Heaven and Earth
cannot form a year with cold and heat alone,
there must be spring, summer, autumn, and winter;
the way of the sage
cannot achieve governance through authority alone,
there must be education and transformation.
Therefore it is said:
Begin with universal love,
teaching benevolence;
what is difficult to obtain,
the gentleman does not prize,
teaching righteousness.
Even the Son of Heaven must have those he honors,
teaching filial piety;
must have those who precede him,
teaching fraternal duty.
This shows that authority alone is insufficient to rely on,
and the achievement of education and transformation is indeed great!
The "Tradition" says:
Heaven gives them birth,
Earth supports them,
and the Sages educate them.
The ruler is the heart of the people,
and the people are the body of the ruler.
What the heart favors,
the body must find comfort in;
what the ruler favors,
the people are sure to follow.
Therefore, the ruler of the people
values filial piety and fraternal duty and delights in ritual and righteousness,
prizes benevolence and integrity and esteems lightly wealth and profit,
personally attends to these duties from above, and the myriad people listen,
giving rise to goodness below.
Hence it is said:
"The former kings saw that education could transform the people."
This expresses it.
The Meaning of the Five Agents: Chapter Forty-Two
Heaven has the Five Agents:
the first is Wood,
the second is Fire,
the third is Earth,
the fourth is Metal,
the fifth is Water.
Wood is the beginning of the Five Agents,
Water is the end of the Five Agents,
and Earth is the center of the Five Agents.
This is Heaven's sequence.
Wood produces Fire,
Fire produces Earth,
Earth produces Metal,
Metal produces Water,
Water produces Wood;
this is their father-son relationship.
Wood resides on the left,
Metal on the right,
Fire in front,
Water behind,
and Earth in the center;
this is the father-son order,
mutually receiving and arranged.
Thus Wood receives from Water, and Fire receives from Wood,
Earth receives from Fire,
and Metal receives from Earth,
Water receives from Metal.
All that give,
are the fathers;
all that receive,
are the sons;
constantly relying on the father
to employ the son
is the Way of Heaven.
Therefore, when Wood has been born, Fire nourishes it;
when Metal has died, Water stores it;
Fire delights in Wood and nourishes it with yang,
Water overcomes Metal and mourns it with yin;
Earth's service to Fire exhausts its loyalty.
Thus the Five Agents
are the conduct of filial sons and loyal ministers.
Does speaking of the Five Agents mean they act?
Hence the expression is obtained.
The Sages understood this,
so they increased love and reduced severity,
enriched nurturing life and carefully attended to sending off the dead,
following Heaven's system.
As a son welcoming and completing nurture,
like Fire delighting in Wood.
Mourning a father,
like Water overcoming Metal;
serving a ruler,
like Earth revering Heaven;
this may be called having conduct.
The following of the Five Agents
each according to its order;
the offices of the Five Agents
each exerting their abilities.
Thus Wood resides in the east and governs the spring qi,
Fire in the south governing summer qi,
Metal in the west governing autumn qi,
Water in the north governing winter qi.
Hence Wood governs life and Metal governs killing,
Fire governs heat and Water governs cold,
employing people necessarily by their order,
appointing officials necessarily by their ability—
this is Heaven's principle.
Earth resides in the center,
serving as Heaven's moisture.
Earth is Heaven's limbs and sinews.
Its virtue is abundant and beautiful,
not to be named by a single season's affair,
so though there are Five Agents and four seasons,
Earth combines them.
Metal, Wood, Water, and Fire, though each has its duty,
without relying on Earth,
their directions would not be established,
just as sour, salty, pungent, and bitter cannot form flavors without relying on sweetness and richness.
Sweetness is the basis of the five flavors;
Earth is the master of the Five Agents.
The master of the Five Agents is Earth's qi,
just as the five flavors have sweetness and richness;
they cannot but be completed.
Therefore, in the conduct of the Sages,
none is more valued than loyalty—
this refers to the virtue of Earth.
Among human offices, the greatest
is not named by its duty;
the Prime Minister is such;
among Heaven's offices, the greatest
is not named by what it produces;
Earth is such.
Yang is Honored, Yin is Lowly: Chapter Forty-Three
The great numerical cycle of Heaven concludes in ten xún.
Between Heaven and Earth,
all things are fully manifested through ten;
in the work of growth and development,
all is accomplished through ten.
Ten is where the numbers of Heaven culminate.
The ancient sages took this culmination of Heaven's numbers as the basis for numerical order.
Ten signifies renewal and a fresh start,
passed down through generations,
yet people do not reflect on its origin.
Reflecting on its origin,
one sees where Heaven's numbers begin;
seeing where Heaven's numbers begin,
one understands the positions of nobility and baseness, compliance and opposition;
understanding these positions,
the nature of Heaven and Earth becomes evident,
and the treasure of the sages is revealed.
Thus, the yang energy begins to emerge from the earth in the first month,
nurturing and fostering growth above.
By the time its work is accomplished,
it accumulates over ten months.
Humans are also born after ten months,
aligning with Heaven's numbers.
Therefore, the Way of Heaven completes in ten months,
and humans also complete in ten months,
in harmony with the Way of Heaven.
Hence, yang energy emerges from the northeast,
enters the northwest,
arises in early spring,
and concludes in early winter,
and all things respond accordingly.
As yang begins to emerge,
things also begin to appear;
when yang is at its peak,
things are also flourishing;
as yang starts to decline,
things also begin to wane;
things follow yang in their emergence and retreat,
numbers follow yang in their beginning and end;
the governance of the three sage kings
shifted in accordance with yang.
From this, it is evident
that yang is esteemed and yin is disdained.
Therefore, in counting days,
we rely on daytime, not night;
in counting years,
we rely on yang, not yin.
This principle must not be violated.
Thus, in the Spring and Autumn Annals regarding marriage rites,
it honors the Duke of Sòng but not the mother of the Marquis of Jì.
The mother of the Marquis of Jì should be honored but is not,
while the Duke of Sòng should not be but is,
esteeming yang and not yin,
governed by the Way of Heaven.
Men, even if lowly, are all yang;
women, even if noble, are all yin;
within yin, there are further distinctions of yin,
and within yang, further distinctions of yang.
Those above are yang to those below,
those below are yin to those above.
Yīn is like sinking.
What name or possession does it have?
All is unified under yang,
striving diligently yet yielding merit.
Thus, when clouds form and rain falls,
it must descend from above,
called "Heaven's rain."
It dares not claim its origin,
with the superior being good and the inferior bad.
The bad receive it,
the good do not.
The expression of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
along with warmth, coolness, cold, and heat,
are essentially of the same category.
The energy of joy is warmth, corresponding to spring;
the energy of anger is coolness, corresponding to autumn;
the energy of pleasure is great yang, corresponding to summer;
the energy of sorrow is great yin, corresponding to winter.
These four energies
are shared by Heaven and humans,
not something humans can store,
so they can be regulated but not halted.
Regulating them brings order,
halting them brings chaos.
Humans are born of Heaven,
and take transformation from Heaven.
Joyful energy is drawn from spring,
pleasurable energy from summer,
angry energy from autumn,
sorrowful energy from winter,
representing the heart of the four energies.
The responses of the four limbs each have their place,
like the four seasons;
cold and heat cannot be displaced,
just as limbs cannot.
If limbs are moved from their place,
it is called deformity;
if cold and heat are displaced,
it is called a ruined year;
if joy and anger are misplaced,
it is called an age of chaos.
The enlightened king aligns joy with spring,
anger with autumn,
pleasure with summer,
sorrow with winter.
Rulers and subjects follow this
to adopt the Way of Heaven.
Spring's energy is loving,
autumn's is stern,
summer's is joyful,
winter's is sorrowful.
Loving energy gives birth to things,
stern energy completes achievements,
joyful energy nurtures life,
sorrowful energy ends in loss,
such is the will of Heaven.
Therefore, the warmth of spring
is how Heaven loves and generates life;
the coolness of autumn
is how Heaven sternly brings to completion;
the warmth of summer
is how Heaven joyfully nurtures;
the cold of winter
is how Heaven sorrowfully stores away.
Spring governs birth,
summer governs nurture,
winter governs storage,
autumn governs harvest.
In life, irrigate with joy for nurture,
in death, irrigate with sorrow for storage,
as is the way of a dutiful child.
Thus, the cycle of the four seasons
is the way of father and son;
the will of Heaven and Earth
is the righteousness of ruler and minister;
the principles of yin and yang
are the laws of the sages.
Yin is the energy of punishment,
yang is the energy of virtue.
Yin begins in autumn,
yang begins in spring.
"Chūn" (spring) suggests something bustling and vibrant,
"Qiū" (autumn) suggests something desolate and sorrowful.
Bustling and vibrant describes an appearance of joy and pleasure,
desolate and sorrowful describes a state of worry and grief.
Hence, spring brings joy, summer pleasure, autumn worry, winter grief,
grieving death and delighting in life.
Using summer to nurture spring,
using winter to mourn autumn,
is the will of the great person.
Thus, love comes first, sternness later,
delight in life and grief at its end,
as Heaven decrees,
and humans draw from Heaven.
Great virtue and minor punishment.
Therefore, the ruler draws near to what Heaven draws near,
distances from what Heaven distances;
magnifies what Heaven magnifies,
minimizes what Heaven minimizes.
Thus, the numbers of Heaven favor yang, not yin,
emphasize virtue, not punishment.
Punishment cannot be relied upon to govern the world,
just as yin cannot be relied upon to complete the year.
To govern relying on punishment
is called opposing Heaven,
not the Way of the King.
"The King's Way Connects with the Three, Chapter Forty-Four"
The ancient creators of writing,
with three strokes connected through the center,
called it "wáng" (king).
The three strokes represent Heaven, Earth, and Humanity,
while connecting them through the center
signifies penetrating their Dào,
taking the center between Heaven, Earth, and Humanity as the thread to interconnect them—
who but a king could embody this?
Thus, the king alone follows Heaven's bestowals,
dispensing them timely to achieve results,
emulating its mandates to guide the people,
modeling its patterns to initiate affairs,
governing by its Dào to establish laws,
and cultivating its will to return to Rén.
The beauty of Rén lies in Heaven.
Heaven is Rén itself;
it shelters and nurtures all things,
transforming them to life,
nourishing them to maturity,
its tasks never ceasing,
ending only to begin anew,
all ultimately dedicated to serving humanity.
Examining Heaven's intent reveals
boundless, infinite Rén.
Humanity receives its mandate from Heaven;
drawing Rén from Heaven, it becomes rén.
Hence, in receiving Heaven's mandate, humanity honors Heaven's dignity,
maintains the closeness of father, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers,
possesses hearts of loyalty, trust, kindness, and benevolence,
conducts itself with courtesy, righteousness, integrity, and deference,
governs with distinctions of right and wrong, obedience and defiance,
its patterns radiant and profound,
its knowledge vast, abundant, and broad—
only the human Dào can thereby align with Heaven.
Heaven constantly holds love and benefit as its intent,
taking nurturing and growth as its task,
with spring, autumn, winter, and summer all serving this purpose.
The king too should constantly hold love and benefit for all under heaven as his intent,
taking the peace and happiness of the age as his task,
employing likes, dislikes, joy, and anger as needed.
Yet the ruler's likes, dislikes, joy, and anger
are to the world as spring, summer, autumn, and winter;
their warmth, coolness, cold, and heat
bring about change and transformation to achieve results.
When Heaven produces these phenomena,
timely, the year is bountiful;
untimely, the year is poor.
When the ruler emits these four dispositions,
righteous, the age is orderly;
unrighteous, the age is chaotic.
Thus, orderly ages and bountiful years share the same principle,
chaotic ages and poor years share the same principle—
herein lies the correspondence of human principle with the heavenly Dào.
Heaven has cold and heat.
Earth, like soil,
is the ultimate in righteousness.
Therefore, in the Chūnqiū, the ruler is not named for evil,
nor the minister for good;
all goodness is attributed to the ruler,
all evil to the minister.
The minister's righteousness is likened to earth;
thus, those who serve as ministers
look to how earth serves Heaven;
those who serve as sons
look to how soil serves fire.
Though residing at the center,
also ruling for seventy-two days of the year,
assisting fire in harmonizing, nurturing, and growing,
yet not being named—
all credit is merged into fire's achievement,
enabling fire to flourish,
not daring to share the father's merit and beauty—
this is the ultimate in filial piety.
Hence, the conduct of filial sons
and the righteousness of loyal ministers
all emulate earth.
Earth serves Heaven
as the subordinate serves the superior;
earth is Heaven's complement,
yet things lack the principle of conjunction.
Therefore, extrapolating the essence of Heaven and Earth,
operating the categories of yīn and yáng,
distinguishes the principles of compliance and defiance.
Where is it not applied?
In high and low,
great and small,
strong and weak,
worthy and unworthy,
good and evil.
The category of evil belongs entirely to yīn,
the category of good entirely to yáng.
Yáng represents virtue,
yīn represents punishment.
Punishment, though opposing virtue, aligns with it,
also belonging to the category of expediency.
Though called expedient,
all are within the completion of expediency.
Thus, yáng operates through compliance,
yīn operates through defiance;
defiance that moves toward compliance,
compliance that moves toward defiance—
this is yīn.
Therefore, Heaven uses yīn as expediency,
yáng as constancy;
yáng emerges in the south,
yīn emerges in the north;
constancy is used in fullness,
expediency in decline;
herein lies Heaven's manifestation of constancy and concealment of expediency,
prioritizing virtue and subsequent punishment.
Thus it is said:
Yáng is Heaven's virtue,
yīn is Heaven's punishment;
yáng qì is warm, yīn qì is cold;
yáng qì gives, yīn qì takes;
yáng qì is rén, yīn qì is harsh;
yáng qì is lenient, yīn qì is urgent;
yáng qì loves, yīn qì hates;
yáng qì generates, yīn qì kills.
Hence, yáng always occupies the position of substance and operates in fullness,
while yīn always resides in emptiness and operates in decline.
Heaven favors rén and draws near,
detests harshness and keeps distant—
this is the intent of magnifying virtue and minimizing punishment.
Constancy precedes expediency,
honoring yáng and debasing yīn.
Thus yīn,
in summer, enters and resides below,
not permitted to oversee the year's affairs;
in winter, emerges and resides above,
placed in an empty position;
during nurturing and growth, it hides below,
kept far away,
not allowed to act as yáng;
in times of inaction,
it arises in empty places,
made to stand in reserve,
guarding closure and obstruction.
This shows Heaven's proximity to yáng and distance from yīn;
Heaven inherently possesses this,
yet without specific direction,
simply as its own nature.
The ruler stands in the position of life and death,
sharing with Heaven the power to hold the momentum of change,
so that all things respond to Heaven's transformations.
The transformations of Heaven and Earth are like the four seasons.
When the favored wind emerges,
it brings warm qì, generating life in customs;
when the detested wind emerges,
it brings cool qì, bringing death to customs;
joy becomes summer heat,
nurturing growth;
anger becomes winter cold,
causing closure and obstruction.
The ruler uses likes, dislikes, joy, and anger to transform customs,
while Heaven uses warmth, coolness, cold, and heat to transform plants and trees;
timely and appropriate joy and happiness lead to a bountiful year,
untimely and reckless ones lead to a poor year.
Heaven, Earth, and the ruler are one.
Thus, the ruler's likes, dislikes, joy, and anger
are Heaven's warmth, coolness, cold, and heat—
one must carefully consider their timing before emitting them.
Cold in summer's heat,
heat in winter's cold,
will surely make a poor year;
the ruler joyful when he should be angry,
angry when he should be joyful,
will surely create a chaotic age.
Hence, the ruler's great responsibility lies in cautious restraint and internal prohibition,
ensuring that likes, dislikes, joy, and anger are emitted only when righteous,
just as warmth, coolness, cold, and heat are released only in their proper seasons.
The ruler who masters this without error,
so that his likes, dislikes, joy, and anger never err,
like spring, autumn, winter, and summer never exceeding their bounds,
may be said to align with Heaven.
Deeply concealing these four and preventing reckless emission
may be called being Heaven-like.
Tiān Róng Dì Sìshíwǔ (The Countenance of Heaven, Chapter 45)
The Way of Heaven
follows sequence and timeliness,
possesses measure and moderation,
transforms with constancy,
reaches forth with mutual support,
subtle yet extending far,
lofty yet reaching utmost refinement,
unified with minimal accumulation,
broad yet substantial,
empty yet full.
The sage observes Heaven and acts accordingly.
Therefore, in establishing prohibitions and examining the proper expression of likes, dislikes, joy, and anger,
he seeks to align with how Heaven does not emit warmth, coolness, cold, or heat outside their seasons;
in instructing through governance and edicts to transform customs with clarity and subtlety,
he seeks to align with how Heaven inverts and reverts its unity to complete the year;
in shunning superficiality, triviality, ostentation, and emptiness while valuing sincerity, honesty, and faithfulness,
he seeks to align with how Heaven silently, without speaking, accumulates achievements and virtues;
in avoiding favoritism, partiality, and selfishness while praising universal love and shared benefit,
he seeks to align with how Heaven in accomplishing things uses little frost but much dew;
in inwardly reflecting on this and outwardly manifesting it,
one must not be untimely.
The ruler has joys and angers,
which must not be untimely.
Appropriateness is a matter of timeliness,
and timeliness is a matter of righteousness.
Joys and angers, when categorized and aligned,
share the same principle.
Thus, righteousness and unrighteousness
are categories aligned with timeliness,
and joys and angers are the distinct qi of cold and heat.
"Heaven's Discrimination Lies in Humans: Forty-Six"
An objector asks:
"The meeting of yīn and yáng
occurs twice a year.
The meeting in the south occurs at midsummer,
and the meeting in the north occurs at midwinter.
Winter is the qì of loss for things,
so why does their meeting
occur then?"
"As with metal, wood, water, and fire,
each serves its ruling element in following yīn and yáng,
joining forces and working together.
In reality, it is not solely yīn and yáng,
yet yīn and yáng arise through them,
assisting what they rule.
Thus, Shàoyáng arises through wood,
assisting spring's growth;
Tàiyáng arises through fire,
assisting summer's nurturing;
Shàoyīn arises through metal,
assisting autumn's completion;
Tàiyīn arises through water,
assisting winter's storage.
Although yīn combines its qì with water and joins winter,
in reality they differ,
hence water alone involves loss, while yīn does not partake in it.
Therefore, the meeting of yáng and yīn at midwinter
is not about that loss.
Spring embodies the disposition of love,
summer of joy,
autumn of sternness,
winter of sorrow.
Thus, love includes sternness,
joy includes sorrow,
which is the principle of the four seasons.
The calamities of joy and anger,
the righteousness of sorrow and joy,
exist not only in humans,
but also in Heaven;
and the yáng of spring and summer,
the yīn of autumn and winter,
exist not only in Heaven,
but also in humans.
Without the spring qì in humans,
how could there be universal love and accommodation of all?
Without the autumn qì in humans,
how could sternness be established and achievements accomplished?
Without the summer qì in humans,
how could nurturing flourish and joy in life thrive?
Without the winter qì in humans,
how could death be mourned and bereavement comforted?
Without the qì of joy in Heaven,
how could warmth and spring bring forth growth?
Without the qì of anger in Heaven,
how could coolness and autumn bring completion through execution?
Without the qì of joy in Heaven,
how could yáng disperse and summer nurture growth?
Without the qì of sorrow in Heaven,
how could yīn be stirred and winter close and store?
Hence it is said:
Heaven has the actions of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight,
and humans have the qì of spring, autumn, winter, and summer
— this is what is called categorical alignment.
Even a commoner, though lowly,
can perceive the application of virtue and punishment.
Therefore, the movements of yīn and yáng
each last six months,
with the same measure in distance and proximity,
but differing in location.
The movement of yīn
resides in the east during spring,
in the west during autumn,
in the empty right during summer,
in the empty left during winter,
under the emptiness during summer,
above the emptiness during winter,
which are the constant positions of yīn.
The movement of yáng
resides above during spring,
below during winter,
which are the constant positions of yáng.
Yīn shifts four times throughout the year,
while yáng always resides in fullness,
is this not favoring yáng and neglecting yīn,
employing virtue and distancing punishment?
The intent of Heaven
often places yīn in empty positions,
slightly drawing upon it for assistance.
Thus, punishment serves virtue,
yīn assists yáng,
and yáng is the master of the year.
All insects under Heaven follow yáng in their emergence and retreat,
all plants under Heaven follow yáng in their growth and shedding,
the Three Sovereigns under Heaven followed yáng in rectifying the calendar,
all ranks of nobility and baseness under Heaven follow yáng in ordering positions.
The young reside where yáng is scant,
the old reside where yáng is aged,
the noble reside where yáng is flourishing,
the base correspond to where yáng is declining.
'Hidden' refers to not being in the position of yáng,
while those in the position of yáng
are the ministers and sons;
yáng
refers to the ruler and father.
Therefore, the ruler faces south,
taking the position of yáng.
Yáng is noble and yīn is base,
by the decree of Heaven.
The ritual preference for the right
is not favoring yīn,
but respecting the elder yáng and honoring accomplished merit."
"Positions of Yīn and Yáng: Forty-Seven"
Yáng qì begins emerging in the northeast and moves southward,
taking its position;
it turns westward and enters northward,
storing its rest;
yīn qì begins emerging in the southeast and moves northward,
also taking its position;
it turns westward and enters southward,
concealing its service.
Therefore, yáng takes the south as its position,
and the north as its rest;
yīn takes the north as its position,
and the south as its rest.
When yáng reaches its position,
great summer heat occurs;
when yīn reaches its position,
great winter cold freezes;
when yáng reaches its rest,
it enters and transforms within the earth;
when yīn reaches its concealment,
it withdraws from virtue below.
Thus, what emerges in summer to grow above and enters in winter to transform below
is yáng;
what enters in summer to guard the empty earth below and emerges in winter to guard the empty position above
is yīn.
Yáng emerges from fullness and enters fullness,
yīn emerges from emptiness and enters emptiness.
Heaven employs yáng and not yīn,
favors virtue and not punishment,
as is thus.
Therefore, yīn and yáng each emerge once throughout the year.
"The Beginning and End of Yīn and Yáng: Forty-Eight"
The Way of Heaven
cycles from end to beginning.
Thus, the northern direction
is where Heaven ends and begins,
where yīn and yáng converge and separate.
After the winter solstice,
yīn descends and enters westward,
while yáng rises and emerges eastward.
Their points of emergence and entry
are always opposite.
The harmony of their abundance and scarcity
is always mutually compliant.
There is abundance without excess,
scarcity without cessation.
In spring and summer, yáng is abundant and yīn is scarce;
in autumn and winter, yáng is scarce and yīn is abundant.
Their abundance varies without constancy,
yet they never fail to separate and disperse.
Through emergence and entry, they mutually increase and decrease,
through abundance and scarcity, they mutually irrigate and aid.
When abundance overcomes scarcity, the entry doubles;
the entry decreases by one,
while the emergence increases by two.
Heaven initiates with one,
moves and doubles again,
constantly riding the momentum of reverse balance and repeated ascent,
to unite with its kind,
and reciprocate with it.
Thus, their qì intertwine,
and through transformation, they exchange.
In the middle of spring and autumn,
the qì of yīn and yáng merge together.
Mid-spring brings life,
mid-autumn brings decay.
From this, it is seen
that when Heaven initiates, its qì accumulates;
when Heaven abolishes, its qì follows.
Thus, in spring, shàoyáng emerges eastward to join wood,
and together they generate life;
in summer, tàiyáng emerges southward to join fire,
and together they bring warmth.
Is this not each going to its kind and rising together?
Shàoyáng joins wood,
tàiyáng joins fire,
fire and wood correspond,
each assuming its proper place.
Is this not aligning their order?
When it comes to autumn,
shàoyīn arises but cannot follow metal in autumn,
for following metal would harm fire's achievement;
though it cannot follow metal,
it still emerges eastward in autumn,
lowering its position to fulfill its task,
thereby completing the year's work.
Is this not flexibility?
The movement of yīn
always resides in emptiness and cannot occupy substance.
By winter, it halts in void,
and then tàiyáng can go north to join its kind,
and with water, brings cold.
Therefore, the Way of Heaven has order, constancy, and flexibility.
"The Meaning of Yīn and Yáng: Forty-Nine"
The constancy of Heaven's Way
is one yīn and one yáng.
Yáng represents Heaven's virtue,
yīn represents Heaven's punishment.
Tracing the annual course of yīn and yáng,
one observes what Heaven favors and entrusts.
Achieving Heaven's work,
it is still called emptiness,
the substance of emptiness.
Thus, clarity and coolness in the year
are like sour and salty in taste,
merely present and no more.
The governance of the sage
follows accordingly.
Heaven's shàoyīn is used for achievement,
tàiyīn is used for emptiness.
In humans, shàoyīn is used for severity,
while tàiyīn is used for mourning.
Mourning is also emptiness,
emptiness is also mourning.
Therefore, Heaven's Way uses three seasons for growth
and one season for death and mourning.
Death
refers to the withering and falling of all things;
mourning
refers to the sorrow of yīn qì.
Heaven also has qì of joy and anger, a heart of sorrow and pleasure,
corresponding to humans.
Classifying them accordingly,
Heaven and humanity are one.
Spring is the qì of joy,
hence life;
autumn is the qì of anger,
hence decay;
summer is the qì of pleasure,
hence nourishment;
winter is the qì of sorrow,
hence storage;
these four, Heaven and humanity share alike.
They share the same principle and apply it uniformly.
Those who align with Heaven achieve great order,
those who oppose Heaven fall into great chaos.
Therefore, the way of the ruler
lies in clearly recognizing what within oneself aligns with Heaven and applying it,
ensuring that joy and anger emerge only when they accord with righteousness,
just as cold and heat arrive only in their due season.
Make virtue outweigh punishment,
as yáng exceeds yīn.
Thus, when Heaven employs yīn qì,
it takes a little to form autumn,
and the remainder it assigns to winter.
When the sage employs yīn qì,
he takes a little to establish severity,
and the remainder he assigns to mourning.
Mourning is also the winter qì of humans,
hence humanity's tàiyīn
is not used for punishment but for mourning,
while Heaven's tàiyīn
is not used for things but for emptiness.
Emptiness is also mourning,
mourning is also emptiness,
their essence is one,
all being the heart of death and mourning.
"The Emergence, Entry, Ascent, and Descent of Yīn and Yáng: Fifty"
The great numerical principle of Heaven's Way:
Opposing entities cannot emerge simultaneously,
as exemplified by Yīn and Yáng.
In spring, Yáng emerges while Yīn withdraws;
in autumn, Yīn emerges while Yáng withdraws;
in summer, Yáng dominates the right while Yīn the left;
in winter, Yīn dominates the right while Yáng the left.
When Yīn emerges, Yáng withdraws;
when Yáng emerges, Yīn withdraws;
when Yīn is on the right, Yáng is on the left;
when Yīn is on the left, Yáng is on the right.
Therefore in spring both move south,
in autumn both move north,
yet follow different paths;
in summer they cross in front,
in winter they cross behind,
yet operate by different principles.
They proceed together without confusion,
flowing smoothly while maintaining their distinct roles,
this is what is called Heaven's intent.
How then should one act accordingly?
The Way of Heaven
begins approaching the Great Winter,
as Yīn and Yáng each come from one direction,
shifting to the rear.
Yīn comes from the east toward the west,
Yáng comes from the west toward the east,
until the mid-winter month,
when they meet in the north,
merge into one,
called the arrival of the solstice.
Then they separate and depart,
Yīn going to the right,
Yáng going to the left.
That which goes left follows a smooth path,
that which goes right follows a contrary path,
contrary energy ascending leftward,
smooth energy descending rightward,
hence warmth below and cold above.
This shows how in winter Heaven places Yīn on the right and Yáng on the left,
with the superior on the right and the inferior on the left.
When the winter months end,
both Yīn and Yáng return southward,
Yáng returning south emerges at Yín,
Yīn returning south enters at Xū,
these are the apparent positions where Yīn and Yáng begin to emerge from and enter the earth.
By the mid-spring month,
Yáng is due east,
Yīn is due west,
called the spring equinox.
At the spring equinox, Yīn and Yáng are equally balanced,
so day and night are equal and cold and heat are moderate,
as Yīn daily decreases while following Yáng,
and Yáng daily increases and expands,
thus bringing warmth and heat.
When first reaching the height of summer,
they meet in the south,
merge into one,
called the arrival of the solstice.
Then they separate and depart,
Yáng going to the right,
Yīn going to the left.
Going left proceeds from below,
going right proceeds from above,
hence heat above and cold below,
this shows how in summer Heaven places Yáng on the right and Yīn on the left.
The superior is on the right,
the inferior on the left.
When the summer months end,
both Yīn and Yáng return northward.
Yáng returning north enters at Shēn,
Yīn returning north enters at Chén,
these are the apparent positions where Yīn and Yáng begin to emerge from and enter the earth.
By the mid-autumn month,
Yáng is due west,
Yīn is due east,
called the autumn equinox.
At the autumn equinox,
Yīn and Yáng are equally balanced,
so day and night are equal and cold and heat are moderate.
Yáng daily decreases while following Yīn,
Yīn daily increases and expands,
thus by late autumn frost begins,
by early winter cold begins,
with minor snow all things complete their growth,
with great cold all things are fully stored away,
thus Heaven and Earth's work is accomplished.
"The Way of Heaven Does Not Duality: Chapter Fifty-One"
Heaven's constant Way:
opposing entities cannot arise together,
therefore it is called unity.
Being one and not two
is Heaven's operation.
Yīn and Yáng,
being opposing entities,
thus sometimes emerge and sometimes withdraw,
sometimes are on the right and sometimes on the left,
in spring both move south,
in autumn both move north,
in summer they cross in front,
in winter they cross behind,
proceeding together but on different paths,
meeting yet each acting on behalf of the other,
is this not its pattern?
Heaven's Way
has one emerging and one withdrawing,
one resting and one hiding,
its measure is one,
yet their intentions differ.
When Yáng emerges,
it always takes position ahead and assumes annual duties;
when Yīn emerges,
it always takes position behind and guards emptiness;
when Yáng rests,
its work completed above, it hides below;
when Yīn hides,
it cannot approach righteousness but remains distant.
Heaven employs Yáng but not Yīn, prefers virtue over punishment,
thus it is.
Therefore Yáng emerges ahead,
Yīn emerges behind,
revealing the mind that honors virtue and disdains punishment.
Yáng emerges and accumulates through summer,
employing virtue in annual affairs;
Yīn emerges and accumulates through winter,
displacing punishment to empty spaces;
this must be discerned accordingly.
Heaven shows no constancy toward things,
but is constant in its timing.
What is timely and appropriate,
it uniformly acts upon.
Thus it opens one, closes one, raises one, abandons one,
until the season ends,
finally returning to begin again from one.
One means unity.
Thus in Heaven, all in Yīn positions dislike disorder and prefer goodness,
yet cannot hold the primary name,
such is Heaven's Way.
Therefore it remains constantly one and never perishes,
Heaven's Way.
In affairs, whether great or small,
in tasks, whether difficult or easy,
to oppose Heaven's Way
leads to no success.
Thus the eye cannot focus on two sights,
the ear cannot listen to two sounds,
one hand cannot perform two tasks.
With one hand drawing squares,
and the other drawing circles,
none can be accomplished.
Humans attempting trivial and easy things
ultimately cannot succeed,
thus opposing Heaven proves unworkable.
Therefore the ancients, in depicting things and writing,
considered the mind fixed on one center
as loyalty;
holding two centers
as calamity;
calamity being humanity's lack of unity.
Lack of unity is whence calamity arises.
Thus the noble person disdains duality and values unity.
Who among humans lacks goodness?
But goodness not unified
cannot establish one's person.
What governance lacks constants?
But constants not unified
cannot achieve merit.
The Book of Songs says:
"God watches over you,
do not have a divided heart."
These are the words of one who understands Heaven's Way!
"Which is More Predominant, Warmth or Cold: Chapter Fifty-Two"
The Way of Heaven,
brings forth warmth through yang to give life,
and brings forth coolness through yin to bring to completion.
Therefore, without the mild warmth, there can be no growth,
and without the severe cold, there can be no ripening;
this is the essence of the year.
One who understands the mind but does not examine whether mild warmth or severe cold is more prevalent,
will certainly act contrary to Heaven when applying this knowledge.
Acting contrary to Heaven,
even with toil, one will not succeed.
Thus, from the first month to the tenth month,
Heaven's work is completed.
Calculate within this period:
how much time is occupied by yin and yang respectively,
and which is more numerous, the days of mild warmth or severe cold?
From the initial sprouting of things,
to their full maturation,
which is doubled, the descent of dew or frost?
Hence, from mid-spring to autumn,
the qi is warm, gentle, and harmonious.
Then in the last month of autumn, September,
yin begins to outnumber yang,
and at this time, Heaven brings forth severe cold and sends down frost.
Bringing forth severe cold and sending down frost,
while greatly bestowing upon things,
they are already fully formed.
Therefore, September
is when Heaven's work is largely concluded in this month,
and by October, it is entirely finished.
Thus, examining its traces,
and counting the actualities,
the days of clear cold are indeed few.
After the work is fully accomplished,
yin then emerges greatly.
In Heaven's accomplishment of its work,
lesser yin participates while greater yin does not,
with lesser yin inside,
and greater yin outside,
hence frost alights on things,
while snow falls on emptiness,
emptiness meaning merely the ground,
not reaching things.
After the work is fully accomplished,
and before things are reborn,
is when greater yin regularly emerges.
Although called yin,
it also relies on the great yang to aid in transforming its position,
yet it is unaware of what it receives.
Therefore, when a sage king is on the throne,
Heaven covers and Earth supports,
winds command and rains bestow.
The bestowal of rain means distributing virtue evenly,
the command of winds means enforcing orders justly.
The Book of Songs says:
"Without knowledge or awareness,
they follow the rules of the Emperor."
This means being unable to know or recognize,
yet emulating what Heaven does.
Yǔ's floods and Tāng's droughts,
were not constant norms,
but happened to encounter the changes of worldly qi, causing yin and yang to lose balance.
Yáo regarded the people as his children,
and the people cherished Yáo as their parents.
The Book of Documents says:
"After twenty-eight years,
Fàngxūn (Yáo) passed away,
and the people mourned as if for their own parents.
Within the four seas,
all music was silenced for three years."
For three years, yang qi was suppressed by yin,
and yin qi greatly arose,
which is why Yǔ has the reputation of floods.
Jié was the cruel tyrant of the world,
while Tāng was of great virtue in the world,
and the world removed the cruel tyrant to gain great virtue and goodness twice,
this was doubling yang,
hence Tāng has the reputation of drought.
These were all encountered changes,
not the faults of Yǔ or Tāng.
Do not let encountered changes doubt the constants of ordinary life,
then what is upheld will not be lost,
and the correct path will become clearer.
Jī Yì Dì Wǔshísān (Fundamental Meanings Fifty-Three)
All things must have their counterparts.
In a pair, there must be an upper,
there must be a lower,
there must be a left,
there must be a right,
there must be a front,
there must be a rear,
there must be an exterior,
there must be an interior.
Where there is beauty, there must be ugliness,
where there is compliance, there must be opposition,
where there is joy, there must be anger,
where there is cold, there must be heat,
where there is day, there must be night,
all these are their pairings.
The yīn is the counterpart of the yáng,
the husband is the counterpart of the wife,
the son is the counterpart of the father,
the minister is the counterpart of the ruler.
Nothing lacks a counterpart,
and each pairing has its yīn and yáng.
The yáng encompasses the yīn,
the yīn encompasses the yáng;
the husband encompasses the wife,
the wife encompasses the husband;
the father encompasses the son,
the son encompasses the father;
the ruler encompasses the minister,
the minister encompasses the ruler.
The principles of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife,
are all derived from the way of yīn and yáng.
The ruler is yáng,
the minister is yīn;
the father is yáng,
the son is yīn;
the husband is yáng,
the wife is yīn.
The way of yīn does not act alone.
At the start, it cannot initiate independently,
at the end, it cannot claim separate merit,
there is a principle of mutual encompassment.
Therefore, the minister's merit is encompassed by the ruler,
the son's merit is encompassed by the father,
the wife's merit is encompassed by the husband,
the yīn's merit is encompassed by the yáng,
the earth's merit is encompassed by heaven.
What is raised upward,
is also pressed downward;
there is screening to the left,
and drawing to the right;
there is closeness and trust,
and distance and estrangement;
some desire daily increase,
some desire daily decrease.
Increase is used while decreasing its hindrances,
sometimes decreasing little increases much,
sometimes decreasing much increases little.
Little but not to the point of cessation,
much but not to the point of excess.
The two entities, yīn and yáng,
each emerge once throughout the year,
their emergence is singular,
with the same measure of distance but different intentions.
When yáng emerges,
it often hangs in the front and undertakes tasks;
when yīn emerges,
it often hangs in the rear and guards empty space.
This shows that heaven favors yáng and distances yīn,
embracing virtue and not relying on punishment.
Therefore, the principles of benevolence, righteousness, and institutions,
are all taken from heaven.
Heaven acts as the ruler, covering and nourishing,
earth acts as the minister, supporting and carrying;
yáng acts as the husband, giving life,
yīn acts as the wife, assisting;
spring acts as the father, generating life,
summer acts as the son, nurturing it;
autumn acts as death, encoffining,
winter acts as grief, mourning.
The three bonds of the kingly way,
can be sought from heaven.
Heaven emits yáng,
providing warmth to generate life;
earth emits yīn,
providing coolness to complete it.
Without warmth, there is no generation,
without coolness, there is no completion.
Yet considering the proportion of their amounts,
warmth and heat occupy a hundred parts, while coolness and cold occupy one.
The relationship between moral instruction and penalties is like this.
Thus, the sage increases love and reduces severity,
thickens virtue and simplifies punishments,
thereby matching heaven.
Heaven's great number,
necessarily consists of ten xún.
Xún is the number of heaven and earth,
ten completes the full raising,
xún is the achievement of growth,
ten completes the full accomplishment.
Heaven's qì is gradual,
alternating between cold and heat.
Hence, cold does not freeze,
heat does not parch,
because it comes gradually with surplus,
not abruptly or violently.
The Yì jīng says:
"Treading on frost, solid ice comes,
this speaks of gradual progress."
Thus, what is solid above does not skip steps,
indeed it is heaven's doing,
accomplished without active making;
human actions,
should also reach their peak without active making.
In all undertakings,
gradually advance with humility and compliance,
making people's hearts joyful and at ease,
not causing fear in people's hearts,
and without forcing them,
hence it is said:
"The noble person governs people with humanity,
carefully honoring their simplicity."
This refers to that.
The way of the sage,
is identical to heaven and earth,
spreads throughout the four seas,
transforming customs and practices.

The Correspondence of the Four Seasons, Fifty-Fifth
The way of heaven:
spring warmth generates life,
summer heat nurtures it,
autumn coolness kills,
winter cold stores.
Warmth, heat, coolness, cold,
different qì but same function,
all are how heaven completes the year.
The sage aligns governance with heaven's actions,
thus using rewards to correspond to warmth in spring,
using commendations to correspond to heat in summer,
using penalties to correspond to coolness in autumn,
using punishments to correspond to cold in winter.
Rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments,
different actions but same function,
all are how the king accomplishes virtue.
Rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments and spring, summer, autumn, winter,
correspond by category,
like matching tallies.
Therefore it is said:
The king matches heaven,
in his way.
Heaven has four seasons,
the king has four policies,
the four policies are like the four seasons,
interconnected categories,
shared by heaven and humanity.
Rewards are spring,
commendations are summer,
penalties are autumn,
punishments are winter.
Rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments must be complete,
just as spring, summer, autumn, winter must be complete.
Rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments,
must be applied at their proper places,
like warmth, heat, coolness, cold,
must emerge in their proper times.
Rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments each have their correct application,
as spring, summer, autumn, winter each have their time.
The four policies must not interfere with each other,
just as the four seasons must not interfere.
The four policies must not be exchanged in application,
just as the four seasons cannot be exchanged.
Thus, if rewards, commendations, penalties, punishments are not applied in their correct places,
the Chūnqiū criticizes it.
Human Correspondence to Heaven's Numbers, Fifty-Sixth
Heaven's virtue is to bestow,
Earth's virtue is to transform,
Humanity's virtue is righteousness.
The qi of Heaven ascends,
The qi of Earth descends,
Human qi resides between them.
Spring gives birth and summer nurtures growth,
All things thereby flourish;
Autumn brings execution and winter storage,
All things thereby hide away.
Thus nothing is more essential than qi,
Nothing is richer than Earth,
Nothing more divine than Heaven.
Of all beings produced by the essence of Heaven and Earth,
None is more noble than humans.
Humans receive their mandate from Heaven,
Therefore they transcend and have something to rely upon.
Other creatures cannot practice rén and yì,
Only humans alone can practice rén and yì;
Other creatures cannot match Heaven and Earth,
Only humans alone can match Heaven and Earth.
Humans have three hundred sixty joints,
Matching the number of Heaven;
Their physical form, bones, and flesh,
Match the thickness of Earth;
Above they have ears and eyes with acute senses,
Resembling the sun and moon;
The body has hollow orifices and vascular patterns,
Resembling rivers and valleys;
The heart has sorrow, joy, anger, and happiness,
Categories of spiritual qi.
Observing the human body as a whole,
How highly it surpasses other creatures,
And resembles Heaven.
Other creatures obliquely draw upon Heaven's yīn and yáng to survive,
While humans brilliantly possess their own patterns.
Therefore, in the forms of all creatures,
None fail to submit and obliquely follow Heaven and Earth in their course,
But humans stand upright and properly oriented,
Directly facing them.
Thus, those who take little from Heaven and Earth
Are oblique;
Those who take much from Heaven and Earth
Are direct.
This shows how humans are distinguished from creatures and correlate with Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, in the human body,
The head is rounded and dome-like,
Resembling Heaven's appearance;
Hair resembles the stars;
Ears and eyes are sharp and clear,
Resembling the sun and moon;
Nose and mouth breathe,
Resembling wind and qi;
The chest comprehends knowledge,
Resembling divine intelligence;
The abdomen is full or empty,
Resembling all things.
All things are closest to Earth,
So below the waist,
Is Earth.
The images of Heaven and Earth
Take the waist as a belt.
Above the neck,
Spirit and dignity reside,
Illuminating the nature of Heaven's category;
Below the neck,
Is plump and humble,
Comparable to soil;
Feet are spread and square,
Resembling the shape of Earth.
Therefore, in ritual,
The belt and sash must align straight with the neck,
To distinguish the heart.
Above the belt is entirely yáng,
Below the belt is entirely yīn,
Each in its own division.
Yáng is the qi of Heaven,
Yīn is the qi of Earth.
Thus, when yīn and yáng move,
Causing foot ailments in humans,
Or throat ailments to arise,
Then Earth's qi ascends as clouds and rain,
And the images correspond as well.
The correspondences of Heaven and Earth,
The counterparts of yīn and yáng,
Are constantly established in the body,
The body is like Heaven,
Its numbers correlate with it,
Thus destiny is linked with it.
Heaven uses the number of a full year
To form the human body,
Hence the minor joints number three hundred sixty-six,
Counterpart to the days;
The major joints in twelve parts,
Counterpart to the months;
Internally there are five zàng organs,
Counterpart to the five phases;
Externally there are four limbs,
Counterpart to the four seasons;
Sometimes seeing, sometimes closing eyes,
Counterpart to day and night;
Sometimes hard, sometimes soft,
Counterpart to winter and summer;
Sometimes sorrowful, sometimes joyful,
Counterpart to yīn and yáng;
The heart has calculations and considerations,
Counterpart to measures and numbers;
Conduct has moral principles,
Counterpart to Heaven and Earth;
All these are subtly attached to the body,
Born together with the person,
Compared and paired in close harmony.
For those that can be counted,
They correspond in number;
For those that cannot be counted,
They correspond in category.
All should uniformly correspond to Heaven,
As one.
Therefore, display the tangible to reveal the intangible,
Grasp the countable to illuminate the uncountable.
By this, it is said that the Dào should also correspond by category,
Just as its form
Matches through numbers.
Chapter Fifty-Seven: Like Categories Activate Each Other
Now, if water is poured on level ground,
it will avoid the dry parts and move towards the damp;
if fire is applied to a pile of evenly distributed firewood,
it will avoid the damp parts and move towards the dry.
All things avoid what is different from them
and follow what is similar.
Thus, when energies are alike, they converge;
when sounds match, they respond to each other,
a proof that is strikingly clear.
Try tuning a qín and sè and placing them apart:
strike the gōng note on one,
and the other's gōng note will resonate;
strike the shāng note,
and its shāng note will respond.
The five notes resonate and sound on their own,
not due to any deity,
but because such is their inherent principle.
Good deeds attract good kinds,
evil deeds attract evil kinds;
like categories respond and arise together.
Just as when a horse neighs, other horses answer it.
When an emperor is about to rise,
auspicious signs also appear first;
when he is about to fall,
portents of doom also appear beforehand.
Thus, things inherently summon their like:
so the dragon brings rain,
the fan drives away heat,
where armies camp, thorns and brambles grow.
Both good and evil have their origins as fate,
though none know exactly where they lie.
When Heaven is about to bring overcast rain,
ailments in people act up beforehand,
which is the hidden correspondence at work.
When Heaven is about to become overcast and rainy,
it also makes people feel sleepy and lie down,
due to the yīn energy.
Having worries
also makes one lie down,
which is yīn seeking its kind;
having joy
makes one unwilling to sleep,
which is yáng seeking its counterpart.
Water at night
gains several fēn in depth;
when the east wind arrives, wine overflows in vats.
When the sick reach nighttime,
their illnesses worsen;
as dawn approaches, chickens
all crow and press against each other.
Their energy becomes more refined;
thus yáng enhances yáng and yīn enhances yīn,
for the energies of yáng and yīn can indeed augment or diminish by category.
Heaven has yīn and yáng,
and so do humans.
When Heaven and Earth's yīn energy arises,
the yīn energy in humans responds and rises;
when human yīn energy arises,
Heaven and Earth's yīn energy should likewise respond and rise.
The principle is one and the same.
Those who understand this
can summon rain by activating yīn to stir yīn,
or stop rain by activating yáng to stir yáng.
Thus, causing rain is not divine,
yet it seems mysterious,
for the principle is subtle.
Not only can yīn and yáng energies advance or retreat by category,
but even the origins of omens, disasters, and blessings
follow this pattern.
Invariably, one initiates it first,
and things respond and move according to their kind.
Hence, the wise and sagely,
looking inward and listening within,
are called brilliantly sage;
by introspection and inner listening,
they alone know that the root lies in their own hearts.
Thus, when a qín or sè is played striking its gōng note,
another's gōng note resonates in response,
exemplifying things moving by category.
Their movement is through sound and without form,
so if people do not see the form of the movement,
they call it spontaneous sounding.
Moreover, mutual influence without visible form
is termed natural,
but in truth, it is not natural;
there is something causing it to be so.
Things inherently have a reality that drives them,
though the driver is formless.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn states:
"When the Zhōu was about to rise,
a great crimson bird carrying grains in its beak
alighted on the king's roof.
King Wǔ was delighted,
and all the ministers rejoiced.
Duke Zhōu said:
'Splendid!
Splendid!
Heaven shows this to encourage us.'"
Lest one rely solely on it.
"The Fifth Eighth: Mutual Conquest of the Five Phases"
Wood corresponds to the Minister of Agriculture.
If the Minister of Agriculture acts corruptly,
forming cliques and coteries,
obscuring the ruler's clarity,
driving away worthy scholars,
eliminating impartial ministers,
teaching the people extravagance,
consorting with guests and connections,
neglecting to encourage farming,
indulging in gambling and cockfighting,
racing dogs and playing with horses,
disregarding etiquette between young and old,
the great and small preying on each other,
all becoming bandits and thieves,
acting recklessly and beyond reason,
then the Minister of Land should punish him,
as in the case of Duke Huán of Qí.
Pursuing hegemony and employing military force,
he invaded Cài,
which crumbled,
then attacked Chǔ,
and the people of Chǔ surrendered,
thus stabilizing the Central States.
Wood is the official of the ruler;
for wood represents agriculture,
and agriculture represents the people.
If they disobey as if in rebellion,
then order the Minister of Land to punish their leaders—
that is correct.
Hence it is said: Metal conquers Wood.
Fire corresponds to the Minister of War.
If the Minister of War engages in slander,
twisting words and accusations against others,
dividing kin within,
alienating loyal ministers without,
causing sages and worthies to perish one after another,
while slanderers and villains thrive daily,
as with Jìsūn, the senior minister of Lǔ.
Usurping authority and monopolizing power,
diminishing the state's majesty and virtue,
instead fostering negligence and malice,
slandering his officials,
deceiving and confusing his ruler.
When Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
upholding righteousness and enforcing laws,
Jìsūn's influence waned on its own,
the fortifications of Fèi and Hòu were dismantled,
and arms and armor were reduced appropriately.
Fire represents the grand court;
if slanderers and deceivers mislead the ruler,
the enforcer of law should punish them.
The enforcer of law is Water,
hence it is said: Water conquers Fire.
Earth corresponds to the office of the ruler,
assisted by the Minister of Works.
If the Minister of Works is ingratiating,
whatever the ruler does,
he says is acceptable;
whatever the ruler says,
he agrees is good.
Flattering and complying with the ruler's wishes,
forming cliques of followers.
Promoting what the ruler favors,
to gratify his desires,
leading the ruler into depravity,
guiding him toward unrighteousness.
Building grand palaces,
erecting numerous towers and pavilions,
carving and engraving ornate patterns,
ablaze with five colors.
Imposing taxes without limit,
plundering the people's wealth;
conscripting excessive corvée labor,
robbing the people of their time;
undertaking projects without end,
draining the people's strength.
The people, distressed and suffering,
rebel and leave the state,
as with King Líng of Chǔ.
He built the Gānxī Tower,
which after three years remained unfinished,
the people exhausted and rebellious,
leading to his own assassination.
Earth is the office of the ruler;
if the ruler is overly extravagant,
transgressing norms and losing propriety,
the people will rebel.
When the people rebel,
the ruler is left with no recourse.
Hence it is said: Wood conquers Earth.
Metal corresponds to the Minister of the Masses.
If the Minister of the Masses becomes corrupt,
gaining favor with the ruler internally,
and acting arrogantly toward the military externally,
monopolizing power and presuming authority,
executing the innocent,
launching aggressive and cruel campaigns,
engaging in warfare and wrongful seizures,
causing orders to be unenforced,
and prohibitions to be unheeded,
with generals not trusted,
and soldiers not obedient,
leading to weakened military and lost territory,
bringing shame upon the ruler,
then the Minister of War shall execute him.
An example is the State of Chǔ executing its Minister of the Masses, Dé Chén.
Dé Chén repeatedly fought and defeated enemies,
gaining favor with the ruler internally,
but became arrogant and did not care for his subordinates,
so his troops would not obey,
weakening when facing the enemy,
thereby endangering the State of Chǔ,
and the Minister of War executed him.
Metal corresponds to the Minister of the Masses;
if the Minister of the Masses is weak,
unable to command the troops,
then the Minister of War executes him,
hence it is said that Fire overcomes Metal.
Water corresponds to the Minister of Justice.
If the Minister of Justice causes disorder,
being overly courteous in small matters,
using clever words and a pleasing countenance,
accepting petitions and bribes,
showing favoritism and injustice,
delaying orders and hastening executions,
killing the innocent,
then the Minister of Works executes him.
Yíng Dàng is an example.
He served as the Minister of Justice of Qí.
When Tài Gōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
he asked about the essentials of governing the state.
Yíng Dàng replied:
"Simply uphold benevolence and righteousness."
Tài Gōng asked:
"How does one uphold benevolence and righteousness?"
Yíng Dàng replied:
"Benevolence means loving others;
righteousness means respecting the elderly."
Tài Gōng asked:
"How does one love others and respect the elderly?"
Yíng Dàng replied:
"Loving others means
having sons who do not rely on their own labor;
respecting the elderly means
a wife being older and the husband bowing to her."
Tài Gōng said:
"I intended to govern Qí with benevolence and righteousness,
but now you use them to disrupt Qí.
I will stand and execute you,
to stabilize the State of Qí."
Water corresponds to the law-enforcing Minister of Justice.
If the law enforcer shows favoritism and injustice,
punishing people according to the law,
then the Minister of Works executes him,
hence it is said that Earth overcomes Water.
"The Mutual Generation of the Five Phases, Chapter Fifty-Nine"
The qì of Heaven and Earth,
combines into one,
divides into yīn and yáng,
separates into the four seasons,
and arrays as the Five Phases.
Phases mean actions,
and their actions differ,
hence they are called the Five Phases.
The Five Phases correspond to the five offices,
with adjacent phases generating each other and alternating phases overcoming each other.
Thus, following this brings order,
opposing it brings chaos,
and conforming to it establishes law.
The East corresponds to Wood,
the foundation of agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture upholds benevolence,
promoting scholars of classical learning,
guiding them with the ways of emperors and kings,
fostering their virtues,
and correcting their faults.
He holds the compass and gives life,
being warm and moistening below,
knowing the fertility and quality of the land,
establishing affairs and creating rules,
according to the suitability of the land.
Shào Gōng is an example.
He personally went into the southern fields,
observing the people clearing weeds and opening irrigation,
cultivating the five grains,
accumulating surplus,
ensuring each household was well-supplied and people satisfied,
with granaries and storehouses full.
The Minister of War manages the grain.
The Minister of War corresponds to the court;
the court is Fire,
hence it is said that Wood generates Fire.
The South corresponds to Fire,
the court.
The Minister of War upholds wisdom,
promoting wise and sagely scholars,
who understand astronomy above,
and when signs have not yet appeared,
or sprouts have not yet grown,
can clearly foresee the pivot of survival or demise,
the essentials of gain and loss,
the origins of order and chaos,
preventing issues before they arise.
He holds the square and grows,
being utmost loyal, sincere, and benevolent,
assisting his ruler.
Zhōu Gōng is an example;
when King Chéng was young and weak,
Zhōu Gōng served as regent,
executing Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū,
to stabilize the realm.
The realm was thus pacified and secured.
The ruler's office
is the Minister of Works.
The Minister of Works is Earth,
hence it is said that Fire generates Earth.
The Center corresponds to Earth,
the ruler's office.
The Minister of Works upholds trustworthiness,
humbling himself and lowering his stature,
rising early and retiring late,
citing ancient examples,
to encourage the ruler's intent.
Clearly seeing success and failure,
subtly advising and accepting good counsel,
preventing and eliminating evil,
cutting off sources and blocking gaps,
holding the plumb line to regulate all directions,
being utmost loyal, sincere, and trustworthy,
in serving his ruler,
upholding righteousness over personal affection.
Tài Gōng is an example.
He responded to Heaven and adapted to the times,
achieving through might and strong defense.
The Chief Judge is the Minister of the Masses.
The Minister of the Masses is Metal,
hence it is said that Earth generates Metal.
The West corresponds to Metal,
the Chief Judge,
the Minister of the Masses.
The Minister of the Masses upholds righteousness,
where ministers die for their ruler and people die for their fathers,
with kinship having seniority and juniority,
positions having high and low,
each fulfilling their duties unto death,
without overstepping bounds.
He holds the scale and punishes.
In war, not conquering unjustly,
not taking wrongfully,
acting only after righteousness,
being utmost incorruptible and authoritative,
honest, straightforward, firm, and resolute.
Zǐ Xū is an example.
He attacked the guilty,
punished the unrighteous,
thus the people adhered closely,
borders were peaceful,
bandits did not arise,
and with no lawsuits in the cities, kinship was secure.
The law enforcer is the Minister of Justice.
The Minister of Justice is Water,
hence it is said that Metal generates Water.
The North corresponds to Water,
upholding the law,
which is the domain of the Sīkòu.
The Sīkòu values ritual,
where sovereign and ministers have their proper positions,
the elder and younger have their order,
the court has its ranks,
and villages respect seniority.
Rising and bowing in deference,
kneeling and prostrating in homage,
turning and moving with squared precision,
standing bent like a chime stone,
cupping hands as if embracing a drum,
holding the scale impartially—
utmost purity, integrity, and fairness,
accepting no bribes,
heeding no special pleas,
adjudicating cases by the law,
without any partiality:
such was Kǒngzǐ.
As the Lǔ Sīkòu,
he decided lawsuits diligently,
sharing the process with all,
daring not to act arbitrarily.
Thus, the dead bore no grudges,
the living held no resentment,
and all craftsmen worked timely
to produce tools and vessels.
Once tools and vessels were made,
they were supplied to the Sīnóng.
The Sīnóng is the office of agriculture.
The agricultural office corresponds to Wood,
hence it is said Water gives rise to Wood.
"On the Mutual Generation and Conquest of the Five Phases, Section Sixty"
Wood represents spring,
the nature of growth,
the foundation of farming.
Encourage agricultural work,
do not rob people of their farming seasons,
employ corvée labor
for no more than three days a year,
levy a ten percent tax,
and promote scholars versed in the classics.
Relax various prohibitions,
release those lightly imprisoned,
remove delays,
abolish shackles,
open what is closed,
and unblock obstructions.
If kindness extends to plants and trees,
then trees flourish beautifully,
and vermilion grass grows;
if kindness extends to scaly creatures,
then fish thrive greatly,
giant sturgeons and whales do not appear,
and dragons descend.
If the ruler goes out and returns unpredictably,
races dogs and tests horses,
gallops without returning to the palace,
indulges in excessive pleasure,
drowns in wine,
acts wantonly,
neglects governance,
frequently mobilizes labor,
robbing people of their seasons,
plots to increase taxes,
seizing people's wealth,
then people suffer from itchy sores,
feverish bodies,
and painful shins.
The blame falls on Wood,
causing lush trees to wither,
and many wheels made by craftsmen to break.
Poisoned water drowns groups,
draining ponds to catch fish;
blame falls on scaly creatures,
so fish do not thrive,
dragons hide deep,
and whales emerge.
Fire represents summer,
growth and maturation,
the foundation of the court.
Promote the virtuous and worthy,
advance the talented,
so offices are filled by the capable,
and tasks are accomplished with strength,
reward the meritorious,
ennoble the virtuous,
distribute goods and wealth,
relieve the distressed and needy,
rectify borders,
and pacify the four directions.
If kindness extends to people,
then Fire aligns with humans and sweet dew descends;
if kindness extends to feathered creatures,
then birds thrive greatly,
yellow swans appear,
and phoenixes soar.
If the ruler is misled by slander and evil,
estranged from kin within,
alienated from loyal ministers without,
even to killing the heir,
executing the innocent,
banishing loyal ministers,
elevating concubines to wives,
discarding laws and decrees,
letting women govern,
and bestowing rewards improperly,
then people suffer from blood disorders,
swellings,
and blurred vision.
Blame falls on Fire,
causing great drought,
and sure fire disasters;
raiding nests and taking fledglings,
blame falls on feathered creatures,
so birds do not thrive,
wintering ones do not return,
owls caw in flocks,
and phoenixes soar high away.
Earth represents midsummer,
ripening all grains,
the ruler's office.
Follow the rules of palace chambers,
strictly distinguish husband and wife,
and increase kindness to relatives.
If kindness extends to earth,
then the five grains mature and auspicious grains flourish.
If kindness extends to naked creatures (humans),
then the people become close and loyal,
cities are filled and solid,
sages and worthies all advance,
and immortals descend.
If the ruler is fond of debauchery and excess,
has excessive wives and concubines,
violates relatives,
insults fathers and elder brothers,
deceives the people,
builds grand towers and pavilions,
glittering with five colors,
carved and engraved,
then people suffer from heart and abdominal pains, jaundice,
and tongue sores.
Blame falls on Earth,
so the five grains do not mature;
if violently cruel and arbitrary in punishment,
blame falls on naked creatures,
so they do not thrive,
the people rebel and leave,
and sages and worthies are exiled or flee.
Metal represents autumn,
the beginning of the aura of execution.
Raise flags and drums,
grasp staffs and battle-axes,
to punish the treacherous and cruel,
prohibit violence and oppression,
and bring peace and order.
Thus, when mobilizing the masses and raising armies,
it must align with righteousness and principle,
offering sacrifices when departing,
and reorganizing upon return,
training them in drills,
through hunting exercises,
remembering death while alive,
and mindful of danger in peace.
Repair city walls,
mend barriers,
scrutinize all prohibitions,
prepare weapons and armor,
alert all officials,
and punish the lawless.
If kindness extends to metal and stone,
then cool breezes blow;
if kindness extends to furry creatures,
then beasts thrive greatly,
and qílín arrive.
If the ruler is fond of war,
invading and bullying feudal lords,
coveting bribes from cities and towns,
disregarding the lives of the people,
then people suffer from throat coughs,
muscle cramps,
and nasal congestion.
Blame falls on Metal,
so casting congeals and stalls,
freezing solid without forming;
spreading nets on all sides,
burning forests to hunt,
blame falls on furry creatures,
so beasts do not thrive,
white tigers attack recklessly,
and qílín go far away.
Water corresponds to winter,
the ultimate yin in concealment.
It marks the beginning of ancestral temple sacrifices,
revering the seasonal offerings,
and the order of the Di and Xia sacrifices arranging the Zhaomu hierarchy.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven,
while the feudal lords sacrifice to the earth.
Close the city gates,
conduct thorough searches,
adjudicate penalties,
apprehend the guilty,
secure passes and bridges,
and prohibit outward migration.
If kindness extends to water,
sweet springs will emerge;
if kindness extends to shelled creatures,
giant softshell turtles and crocodiles will thrive,
and divine turtles will appear.
If the ruler neglects the ancestral temples,
fails to offer prayers,
abolishes sacrifices,
enforces laws unjustly,
and acts contrary to the natural seasons,
then the people will suffer from edema, distension, paralysis, and blockages in the orifices.
The blame will extend to water,
with mists becoming dense and gloomy,
inevitably leading to great floods,
and water becoming a scourge to the people;
the blame will extend to shelled creatures,
causing turtles to hide deeply,
and softshell turtles and crocodiles to gasp.
"Governing Water and the Five Phases, Sixty-First"
On the winter solstice,
for seventy-two days, Wood is in effect,
its energy dry, turbid, yet clear.
For seventy-two days, Fire is in effect,
its energy harshly yang and red.
For seventy-two days, Earth is in effect,
its energy damp, turbid, and yellow.
For seventy-two days, Metal is in effect,
its energy bleak and white.
For seventy-two days, Water is in effect,
its energy cool, cold, and black.
After seventy-two days, Wood returns to effect.
When Wood is in effect,
practice gentle benevolence,
and relax various prohibitions.
Upon the arrival of the Beginning of Spring,
release those lightly imprisoned,
remove delays,
abolish shackles,
open gates and doors,
clear obstructions,
care for the young and orphaned,
pity the widowed and solitary,
and do not cut down trees.
When Fire is in effect,
rectify boundaries,
and tend to the fields.
Upon the arrival of the Beginning of Summer,
promote the worthy and virtuous,
ennoble the moral,
reward the meritorious,
send envoys to the four directions,
and do not set uncontrolled fires.
When Earth is in effect,
nurture the elderly,
care for the young and orphaned,
pity the widowed and solitary,
bestow honors on the filial and fraternal,
extend kindness and favor,
and do not undertake earthworks.
When Metal is in effect,
repair city walls,
mend fences,
examine all prohibitions,
prepare armor and weapons,
alert all officials,
punish the lawless,
support the elderly,
and do not smelt metal or stone.
When Water is in effect,
close the city gates,
conduct thorough searches,
adjudicate penalties,
apprehend the guilty,
secure passes and bridges,
prohibit outward migration,
and do not breach ponds or dikes.
"Governing Disorder with the Five Phases, Sixty-Second"
If Fire encroaches on Wood,
hibernating insects emerge early,
and thunder occurs prematurely.
If Earth encroaches on Wood,
fetuses die young, eggs spoil,
and birds and insects are often harmed.
If Metal encroaches on Wood,
there will be warfare.
If Water encroaches on Wood,
frost falls in spring.
If Earth encroaches on Fire,
there will be frequent thunder.
If Metal encroaches on Fire,
plants and trees are leveled.
If Water encroaches on Fire,
there is summer hail.
If Wood encroaches on Fire,
the earth shakes.
If Metal encroaches on Wood,
the five grains are damaged,
and calamity follows.
If Water encroaches on Earth,
summer turns cold with frost and rain.
If Wood encroaches on Earth,
naked creatures fail to thrive.
If Fire encroaches on Earth,
there is great drought.
If Water encroaches on Metal,
fish do not flourish.
If Wood encroaches on Metal,
plants and trees regrow.
If Fire encroaches on Metal,
plants and trees bloom in autumn.
If Earth encroaches on Metal,
the five grains do not ripen.
If Wood encroaches on Water,
hibernating creatures do not hide in winter.
If Earth encroaches on Water,
hibernating insects emerge in winter.
If Fire encroaches on Water,
stars fall.
If Metal encroaches on Water,
winter is extremely cold.
"Rescuing Through Changes in the Five Phases, Sixty-Third"
When the five phases undergo abnormal changes,
they should be remedied with virtue,
applied throughout the world,
then calamities will be removed;
if not remedied with virtue,
within three years,
heaven will rain stones.
When wood undergoes changes,
spring brings withering and autumn brings blooming.
In autumn, trees ice over,
in spring, there is excessive rain.
This results from numerous corvée duties,
heavy taxes,
the people becoming impoverished and rebellious,
and many starving persons on the roads.
To remedy this,
reduce corvée duties,
lighten taxes,
release granary grains,
and relieve the distressed and poor.
When fire undergoes changes,
winter is warm and summer cold.
This is due to the ruler being unenlightened,
the good unrewarded,
the evil not demoted,
the unworthy in office,
the worthy in hiding,
leading to disordered cold and heat,
and epidemics among the people.
To remedy this,
promote the worthy and good,
reward the meritorious,
and enfeoff the virtuous.
When earth undergoes changes,
great winds arrive,
damaging the five grains.
This stems from distrusting the benevolent and worthy,
disrespecting fathers and elder brothers,
unrestrained debauchery,
and lavish palaces.
To remedy this,
reduce palace constructions,
eliminate ornate decorations,
promote filial piety and fraternal duty,
and show compassion to the common people.
When metal undergoes changes,
the Bì and Mǎo constellations appear reversed,
three coverings suggest military affairs,
there is much warfare,
many bandits and invaders.
This arises from abandoning righteousness, coveting wealth,
disregarding people's lives,
valuing bribes,
the people pursuing profit,
and much treachery and lawlessness.
To remedy this,
promote the incorrupt,
establish the upright,
conceal military actions and practice civility,
and store away armor and weapons.
When water undergoes changes,
winter is damp with much fog,
spring and summer bring rain and hail.
This is due to lax laws and decrees,
and unenforced punishments.
To remedy this,
be concerned about prisons,
investigate the treacherous and wicked,
punish the guilty,
and search for five days.
"The Five Phases and Five Affairs, Chapter Sixty-Four"
If the ruler shows no courtesy to his ministers,
and his demeanor is not solemn and respectful,
then wood will not bend or straighten,
and summer will have many violent winds.
Wind is the qi of wood,
its sound is jué,
hence it responds with violent winds.
If the ruler's words are not followed,
then metal will not obey transformation,
and autumn will have many thunderclaps.
Thunderclaps are the qi of metal,
its sound is shāng,
hence it responds with thunderclaps.
If the ruler's vision is unclear,
then fire will not flame upward,
and autumn will have much lightning.
Lightning is the qi of fire,
its sound is zhǐ,
hence it responds with lightning.
If the ruler's hearing is not acute,
then water will not moisten downward,
and spring and summer will have heavy rainstorms.
Rain is the qi of water,
its sound is yǔ,
hence it responds with rainstorms.
If the ruler's mind is intolerant,
then crops will not ripen,
and autumn will have much thunder.
Thunder is the qi of earth,
its sound is gōng,
hence it responds with thunder.
The five affairs:
first is demeanor,
second is speech,
third is vision,
fourth is hearing,
fifth is thought.
What does this mean?
These five affairs
are what humans receive from heaven,
and what the ruler cultivates to govern the people.
Thus the ruler, acting for the people,
in governance must be enlightened,
standards must be upright.
The ruler's demeanor is called reverent;
reverent means respectful.
Speech is called accordant;
accordant means it can be followed.
Vision is called clear;
clear means knowing the worthy and unworthy,
distinguishing black from white.
Hearing is called acute;
acute means hearing matters and discerning their meaning.
Thought is called tolerant;
tolerant means nothing is unaccommodating.
Reverence creates solemnity,
accordance creates order,
clarity creates wisdom,
acuteness creates planning,
tolerance creates sageliness.
What does this mean?
Reverence creates solemnity,
meaning if the ruler truly possesses an inner attitude of reverence,
