then all under heaven will be solemn.
Accordance creates order,
meaning the ruler's words can be followed,
clearly correct and put into practice,
then all under heaven is well-governed.
Clarity creates wisdom,
wisdom means knowledge,
if the ruler is clear,
then the worthy are advanced,
the unworthy are dismissed,
all under heaven know the good and are encouraged by it,
know the evil and are shamed by it.
Acuteness creates planning,
planning means deliberating on affairs,
if the ruler is acute,
then he hears matters and plans with his ministers,
thus affairs are not misplanned.
Tolerance creates sageliness,
sageliness means establishing,
if the ruler's mind is broad and all-embracing,
then he can sagely establish and set forth,
and affairs each attain their proper place.
If the ruler can be reverent, then there is solemnity,
solemnity then attains spring qi,
thus solemnity governs spring.
Spring—yang qi is subtle,
all things are soft and pliable,
movable and transformable.
At this time, yin qi acts as a thief,
thus the ruler is respectful.
Respectful, he does not discuss yin affairs,
then all things flourish and grow,
and wood can bend and straighten.
If spring practices autumn governance,
then plants and trees wither;
if it practices winter governance,
then there is snow;
if it practices summer governance,
then there is destruction.
If spring loses proper governance, then.
If the ruler can govern, then righteousness is established,
righteousness established then autumn qi is attained,
thus order governs autumn.
Autumn qi begins the killing,
the ruler carries out minor punishments,
if the people do not offend, then ritual and righteousness are accomplished.
At this time, yang qi acts as a thief,
thus the ruler assists with official oversight matters,
then all things mature and ripen.
In autumn,
plants and trees do not bloom gloriously,
metal obeys transformation.
If autumn practices spring governance,
then there is blooming;
if it practices summer governance,
then there is tall growth;
if it practices winter governance,
then there is falling.
If autumn loses proper governance,
then in spring, great winds do not cease,
and thunder does not sound.
If the king is capable of wisdom,
he then knows good and evil;
knowing good and evil,
he attains the summer qi.
Hence, the wise ruler governs summer.
Summer
is when yang qi begins to flourish,
and all things show signs of growth.
If the king does not obscure clarity,
then the Way does not retreat or become blocked.
After the summer solstice,
the great heat rises,
and all things flourish, nurture, and bear potential.
The king fears that his clarity may not discern the worthy from the unworthy,
clearly distinguishing white from black.
At this time, cold becomes a thief,
so the king assists with acts of reward and bestowal,
after which summer grasses and trees do not frost,
and fire blazes upward.
If summer follows spring governance,
there will be winds;
if it follows autumn governance,
there will be floods;
if it follows winter governance,
there will be withering.
If summer fails in governance,
then winter will not freeze ice,
the five grains will not be stored,
and the great cold will not dissipate.
If the king makes no errors in strategy,
then he attains the winter qi,
hence the strategist governs winter.
Winter
is when yin qi begins to flourish,
and grasses and trees must die.
If the king can hear affairs
and carefully strategize and consider them,
then there will be no invasions or attacks.
Without invasions, attacks, or killings,
the dead will not hold grudges,
and the living will not bear resentment.
After the winter solstice,
the great cold descends,
and all things hide below.
At this time, heat becomes a thief,
so the king assists with urgent and decisive matters,
as water moistens and flows downward.
If winter follows spring governance,
there will be steam;
if it follows summer governance,
there will be thunder;
if it follows autumn governance,
there will be drought.
If winter fails in governance,
then in summer, grasses and trees will not bear fruit,
frost will fall,
and the five grains will swiftly wither.
"Discourse on Suburban Sacrifice Sixty-Five"
People say:
vinegar dispels smoke,
owl feathers remove dimness,
lodestone attracts iron,
flint produces fire,
silkworms spin silk indoors,
yet strings break in the hall,
grains ripen in the fields,
yet millet is lacking in the granary,
elm trees grow in Yān,
while orange and trifoliate orange trees die in Jīng.
These ten things
are all strange and marvelous,
not what humans can anticipate.
If things that are not anticipated by humans yet exist,
since they already do,
could it be that auspicious or ominous fortunes, benefits or harms, arise from such sources,
without any strangeness,
unforeseen by humans,
in this manner?
Such things are to be feared.
Confucius said:
"The noble person has three fears:
fear of the Mandate of Heaven,
fear of great men,
and fear of the words of sages."
How could it be that they cause no harm to humans,
yet Confucius and his followers feared them?
From this, it is evident that Heaven must be feared and revered,
just as the ruler must be served with caution.
Not serving the ruler with caution
brings manifest calamities;
not fearing and revering Heaven
brings hidden disasters.
Hidden disasters show no signs,
as if they occur naturally.
Hence it is said:
Majestic as Heaven,
its calamities need not be immediately confronted,
silent and without sound,
hidden and without form.
From this perspective,
the difference between Heaven's calamities and the ruler's punishments
lies in their hidden or manifest nature.
Otherwise, in their arrival upon humans,
they are scarcely different.
Confucius equated them,
saying both are to be feared.
The heart of Heaven and Earth's divine spirits
and the truth of human affairs' success or failure
are inherently unseen by anyone,
only the sage can perceive them.
The sage sees what others cannot see,
thus the words of the sage are also to be feared.
How then can the suburban sacrifice be abandoned?
The suburban sacrifice is what humans hold most sacred.
Abandoning what the sage held most sacred,
while good and bad fortunes, benefits and harms lie in the unseen and imperceptible,
even if one has already suffered greatly from it,
how could one know the cause?
Therefore, it is said:
When inquiring of the sage,
ask what he did, not why he did it.
Asking why he did it,
one will never see the reason,
so it is better not to ask.
Ask what he did and do it,
what he did not do, do not do;
this is to share the substance with the sage,
what fault could there be?
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not err, do not forget,
follow the old statutes."
The old statutes are the established patterns of the former sages;
following them
means each has its proper adherence.
This speaks of the established patterns of the former sages:
even if one cannot deeply see and know their principles in detail,
one still does not know the merit of their beautiful reputation.
Now, the meaning of the suburban sacrifice to Heaven
is what the sages thus spoke of.
"Meaning of the Suburban Sacrifice Sixty-Six"
The meaning of the suburban sacrifice:
The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is that the king sacrifices to Heaven once a year at the suburban altar,
and four times at the ancestral temple.
The ancestral temple sacrifices are based on the changes of the four seasons,
while the suburban sacrifice is based on the beginning of the new year.
The sages had reasons to initiate this,
for the sacrifice must be performed personally.
Heaven is the lord of all spirits,
and what the king holds in highest honor.
Because of honoring Heaven as supreme,
therefore, at the start of the year when the calendar changes,
the suburban sacrifice is held at its beginning.
The suburban sacrifice must be on the first xīn day of the first month,
meaning to honor the most revered at the start of the year's affairs.
Each calendar change begins with the suburban sacrifice;
the suburban sacrifice initiates it,
embodying the principle of prioritizing the honored,
the way of revering Heaven.
"Suburban Sacrifice Sixty-Seven"
The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals states,
when a state has a great mourning,
it suspends sacrifices to the ancestral temples,
but does not stop the suburban sacrifice,
for one dares not abandon the rites of serving Heaven and Earth due to the mourning for one's parents.
The mourning for parents,
being the utmost in grief and sorrow,
still does not warrant abandoning the suburban sacrifice;
what then could be sufficient to abolish it?
Therefore, in the rites it is also said:
"Those in mourning do not perform sacrifices,
except for sacrificing to Heaven, which is carried out despite the mourning."
Thus, the ancients' reverence for Heaven and the importance they placed on the suburban sacrifice to Heaven
were as profound as this.
Nowadays, officials and scholars do not investigate thoroughly,
but say:
"The multitude of people are largely poor,
some even suffering from hunger and cold;
is the suburban sacrifice appropriate?"
How mistaken are these words!
The Son of Heaven serves Heaven as his parent,
and nurtures the myriad people as his children.
If the people are not all fed,
and thus one should not sacrifice to Heaven,
that would be like children not having food,
and thus not feeding their parents.
No words could be more contrary to reason than this,
showing how far they have strayed from the rites.
The noble should come before the humble;
who is nobler than the Son of Heaven?
The Son of Heaven is titled the Son of Heaven.
How can one bear the title of Son of Heaven
yet not perform the rites of the Son of Heaven?
The Son of Heaven must not fail to sacrifice to Heaven,
no different from how a person cannot fail to feed his father.
Therefore, the sage kings of old
regarded this as the most important of all ceremonies,
and previous kings all emphasized it,
serving with utmost sincerity and reverence
to worship Heaven.
Yet when it came to the Qín dynasty, they alone neglected and abandoned it;
how greatly they failed to follow the established regulations!
Heaven is the supreme sovereign of all spirits.
If the service to Heaven is not complete,
even serving a hundred spirits would be of no benefit.
How can this be explained?
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize
those who sacrifice to earthly spirits.
Confucius said:
"If you have offended against Heaven,
there is none to whom you can pray."
This is the principle.
Hence, it has not been seen that the state of Qín received blessings from Heaven like the state of Zhōu did.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only this King Wén,
with cautious reverence,
brightly served the Lord above,
and thus secured abundant blessings."
Abundant blessings do not refer to the person,
but to the achievements,
meaning the blessings bestowed by Heaven.
The Tradition says:
"The descendants of the Zhōu state were many and worthy,
flourishing to the extent that twin pregnancies occurred,
four births yielding eight sons,
all outstanding gentlemen and heroes."
This was how Heaven prospered the Zhōu state,
not something the Zhōu state could achieve by itself.
Now Qín, like Zhōu, holds the position of Son of Heaven,
yet their manner of serving Heaven differs from that of Zhōu.
Taking the suburban sacrifice as the beginning of all sacrifices,
at the start of the year,
one must first offer to Heaven on the first Xīn day of the first month,
then dare to offer to Earth,
embodying the principle of honoring the noble first.
Whether it is performed at the beginning of the year or not performed at all
makes a vast difference.
If the blessings of Heaven seem unremarkable,
the reason for long neglecting the sacrifice
is not due to a clear recognition of its propriety and intentional omission,
but because officials in charge of rites often have doubts,
unable to clearly understand its appropriateness.
Now, I firmly believe that whether it is appropriate or not
can be determined by introspection.
Yáo said to Shùn:
"The celestial order rests upon your person."
This means examining oneself to understand Heaven.
If one has a son,
who would not wish for his son to perform the rites of a son?
The sage rectifies names,
and names do not arise without reason.
The Son of Heaven is the son of Heaven.
Measuring Heaven by oneself,
why would one not desire his son to perform the rites of a son?
Now, being the Son of Heaven,
yet neglecting to sacrifice to Heaven,
how would Heaven necessarily favor him?
It is heard that:
when the world is peaceful and harmonious,
then disasters do not arise.
Now that disasters occur,
it shows the world is not yet peaceful and harmonious.
The reason the world is not peaceful and harmonious
is that the teachings and influence of the Son of Heaven are not implemented.
The Book of Songs says:
"With virtuous conduct evident,
the four quarters follow him."
"Evident" means conspicuous;
when a king has clearly manifest virtuous conduct in the world,
then all directions respond,
and his influence spreads beneficially.
Therefore it is said:
be generous with rewards,
strict with punishments,
and swift with laws and decrees.
"The Four Sacrifices - Sixty-eighth"
In ancient times, there were four sacrifices per year.
The four sacrifices
were based on what ripened in the four seasons,
to sacrifice to one's ancestors and parents.
Thus, spring was called cí,
summer yuè,
autumn cháng,
winter zhēng.
This means not missing the season
to honor ancestors with sacrifice.
Missing the season without sacrifice
means failing in the way of a filial child.
Cí is for beginning to eat leeks in the first month;
yuè is for eating wheat in the fourth month;
cháng is for tasting millet in the seventh month;
zhēng is for offering new rice in the tenth month.
This is the constant of Heaven,
the principle of Earth.
Filial sons and daughters-in-law follow the timing of Heaven
and utilize the benefits of Earth.
Having received the mandate and become king,
one must first sacrifice to Heaven,
then undertake kingly affairs,
as with King Wén's campaign against Chóng.
The Book of Songs says:
"Majestic is our king,
on left and right they hold the jade tablets.
Holding the tablets reverently,
befitting the elite officers."
This refers to King Wén's suburban sacrifice.
The following lines say:
"Swiftly move the boats on the Jīng River,
many oarsmen row them.
The king of Zhōu is on the march,
the six armies follow him."
This refers to King Wén's campaign against Chóng.
The earlier lines speak of holding jade tablets,
the later of attacking Chóng,
showing that King Wén first performed the suburban sacrifice and then launched the campaign.
King Wén, upon receiving the mandate, performed the suburban sacrifice,
and after the sacrifice, attacked Chóng.
The people of Chóng
were suffering under a tyrannical ruler,
not yet having received the virtuous influence of the sage,
yet King Wén had already performed the suburban sacrifice.
How can it be said that one cannot perform the suburban sacrifice before virtuous influence has spread?
"Suburban Sacrifice - Sixty-ninth"
For one who is a son and does not serve his father,
no one in the world would consider it acceptable.
Now, being the son of Heaven and not serving Heaven,
how is this different?
Therefore, the Son of Heaven, at the beginning of each year,
must first perform the suburban sacrifice to honor Heaven,
before daring to act on earth,
fulfilling the rites of a son;
whenever about to raise an army,
must first perform the suburban sacrifice to announce it to Heaven,
before daring to launch a campaign,
following the way of a son.
King Wén received the Mandate of Heaven and ruled the world,
first performing the suburban sacrifice before daring to act,
and then raising an army to attack Chóng.
The Odes say:
"Luxuriant are the cluster-beams and oaks,
which we cut and pile.
Majestic is the king,
to whom all hasten.
Majestic is the king,
with his attendants bearing jade tablets.
Holding the tablets high,
the elite are well-suited."
This is the text for the suburban sacrifice.
The following lines say:
"Like boats on the Jīng River,
rowed by many oarsmen.
The king of Zhōu sets forth,
and the six armies follow."
This is the text for the campaign.
The following lines say:
"King Wén received the Mandate,
achieving these military feats.
After attacking Chóng,
he built the city of Fēng."
Through these verses,
it is seen that King Wén, upon receiving the Mandate, performed the suburban sacrifice,
and only after the sacrifice did he attack Chóng.
At the time of attacking Chóng,
how could the people have suffered hardship!
During the time of King Xuān of Zhōu,
there was a great drought in the world,
and the harvest was extremely poor,
causing the king great worry.
The Odes say:
"Vast is the Milky Way,
shining and revolving in the sky.
The king said:
'Alas!
What fault have the people of today?
Heaven sends down chaos and disaster,
famine repeatedly befalls.
No deity is left un-sacrificed to,
nor are the sacrificial animals spared.
The jade discs and tablets are all used up,
yet none will listen to me!
The drought is too severe,
oppressive and blazing.
I have not ceased the sacrifices,
from the suburban altar to the ancestral temple.
Offering above and burying below,
no deity is left un-honored.
Hòu Jì cannot save us,
and Shàngdì does not descend.
Devastation spreads over the land,
why must it fall upon me?'"
King Xuān believed he was not as capable as Hòu Jì,
and not aligned with Shàngdì,
hence this disaster occurred.
Faced with this disaster,
he became more fearful and reverently served Heaven.
If Heaven did not grant this family,
how could this family be established as the Son of Heaven?
To be established as the Son of Heaven,
Heaven must grant this family.
Heaven granting this family means
Heaven employs this family.
Heaven employing this family means
this family is granted by Heaven,
and sent by Heaven.
Heaven has already granted it,
Heaven has already employed it,
so how could it be disconnected from Heaven?
Why?
Therefore, in the Spring and Autumn Annals, whenever the suburban sacrifice is discussed,
it never criticizes the ruler's virtue as insufficient for the suburban sacrifice.
But when the suburban sacrifice is omitted and mountains and rivers are sacrificed to instead,
disrupting the order of sacrifices,
and violating the rites,
it is inevitably criticized.
From this perspective,
one who does not sacrifice to Heaven
should not sacrifice to minor deities either.
The suburban sacrifice requires divination first;
if inauspicious,
one dares not perform it.
For sacrifices to the hundred deities, divination is not used,
but for the suburban sacrifice alone, it is divined,
because the suburban sacrifice is the most important.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize sacrifices during mourning,
but do not criticize the suburban sacrifice during mourning.
The suburban sacrifice does not avoid mourning,
and if even mourning is not avoided,
how much less other matters?
The suburban sacrifice text says:
"Oh, majestic Heaven above,
shining upon the earth below.
Gathering the spirits of the land,
sending down sweet winds and rain.
For all living beings."
It speaks not for itself,
but for all living beings,
so that humanity may appeal to Heaven without blame.
Heaven bears no blame,
and with respectful and submissive words,
it should be pleasing.
The above are the nine lines of the suburban sacrifice text.
Nine lines represent the number of Yang.
Shùn Mìng Dì Qī Shí
The father is the heaven of the son,
and heaven is the father's heaven.
To be born without heaven
has never existed.
Heaven is the ancestor of all things,
and without heaven, nothing comes into being.
Solitary yīn does not generate life,
solitary yáng does not generate life;
only when yīn and yáng interact with heaven and earth does life emerge.
Hence it is said:
A child of the father may be honored,
while a child of the mother may be humble;
the honored receive honorable titles,
the humble receive humble titles.
Thus, those whose virtue equals heaven and earth
are supported by the supreme heaven as its sons,
and are titled the Son of Heaven.
Next are the five ranks of nobility to honor them,
all taking the names of states or fiefs.
Those without virtue between heaven and earth
are assigned to provinces, states, or common people;
the worst are not even entitled to state or fief names.
They are severed from kinship ties,
alienated from human relations,
and called obscure thieves.
They have no name, surname, or clan between heaven and earth,
the lowest among the lowly.
The highest in honor possess ultimate virtue,
towering and unsurpassable;
the lowest in baseness,
sink into obscurity with no further depth.
The Spring and Autumn Annals arrange positions in order of humility and honor,
clearly visible in sequence.
Even the dim-witted and foolish
cannot fail to see this clearly.
The vegetables, melons, and fruits of the earth,
the cultivated rice, wheat, millet, and sorghum,
when vegetables grow and grains ripen,
after long consideration of auspicious days,
preparing sacrificial offerings,
fasting, abstaining, and bathing,
purifying and showing reverence,
they sacrifice to their ancestors, fathers, and mothers.
Filial sons and daughters-in-law do not let the time pass by;
they dwell in love and respect,
act with deference and humility,
and thus nearly avoid offense.
Even the offense of Prince Qìngfù should not be tied to the state;
for the sake of kinship, it was concealed,
yet in the state of Qí, Zhòngsūn,
was stripped of his princely kinship.
Thus, those who commit great crimes and do not follow heaven's mandate
are all forsaking their heavenly bonds.
Humans, in relation to heaven,
receive mandate through the Way;
in relation to others,
they receive mandate through words.
Those not aligned with the Way
are cut off by heaven;
those not aligned with words
are cut off by humans.
Ministers and sons greatly receive mandates from their ruler;
upon taking leave and crossing borders,
only in cases of peril to the altars of soil and grain or the state
may they speak out and act to secure them,
as in alliances.
The Son of Heaven receives mandate from heaven,
feudal lords from the Son of Heaven,
sons from their fathers,
servants and concubines from their masters,
wives from their husbands.
All who receive mandates
hold their superiors as heaven;
thus, it may be said they receive mandate from heaven,
or not from heaven.
If the Son of Heaven cannot uphold heaven's mandate,
he is deposed and called a duke,
as with the descendants of former kings.
If dukes and marquises cannot uphold the Son of Heaven's mandate,
they are stripped of titles and cannot assume position,
as with Marquis Shuò of Wèi.
If a son does not follow his father's command,
he faces the crime of being punished by an elder,
as with Crown Prince Kuǎikuì of Wèi.
If a minister does not follow his ruler's command,
even if well-intentioned,
it is termed rebellion,
as with Zhào Yǎng of Jìn entering Jìnyáng in rebellion.
If a concubine does not follow her master's command,
it is like the attendant bride arriving first.
If a wife does not follow her husband's command,
she is severed,
as when the husband does not speak of involvement.
It is said:
Those who do not obey and follow heaven
bear such crimes.
Confucius said:
"Stand in awe of the Mandate of Heaven,
stand in awe of great men,
stand in awe of the words of the sages."
When sacrificing to the gods of soil and grain, ancestral temples, mountains, rivers, and spirits,
if not done in the proper way,
there may be no disaster or harm.
But when sacrificing to heaven is not accepted,
the divination does not follow,
the sacrificial ox's mouth is injured,
or mice gnaw its horns.
Some say the ox is eaten,
some say it dies after eating,
some eat and live,
some die without being eaten,
some change the divination and the ox dies,
some divinate and its horns are eaten.
Transgressions have depth and shallowness, thickness and thinness,
and disasters vary in simplicity and severity,
which must be examined.
Like the changes in the suburban sacrifice,
they adapt to disasters and change accordingly,
responding naturally without forced action.
To see the changes in all affairs and the naturalness of the unknown—
can words suffice?
This shows what is to be feared.
Is it not heaven alone that exclusively metes out punishment and severance?
Ministers killing rulers,
sons killing fathers—
over thirty such cases,
and the lesser ones are even more numerous.
From this perspective,
is it not the Mandate of Heaven and great men that are to be feared?
Over fifty states have perished,
all due to not standing in awe.
How much more so for those who do not fear great men,
usurping punishment,
leading to the ruler's destruction—
how long can they last?
Duke Xuān of Lǔ violated the words of the sages,
altering the ancient and changing the constant,
and disaster immediately followed.
Should not the words of the sages be treated with caution?
These three objects of awe,
though different in focus, lead to the same end;
thus the sames regard them alike,
all stating they are to be feared.
Response on Suburban Sacrifice Affairs, Seventy-First
The Commandant of Justice, your subject Tāng, ventures at the risk of death to state:
"Your subject Tāng, in accordance with the imperial decree,
has inquired of the former Chancellor of Jiāoxī, Zhòngshū, regarding the suburban sacrifice."
Your subject Zhòngshū replied:
"What I have heard is that among the rites of the Son of Heaven in ancient times,
none was more important than the suburban sacrifice.
The suburban sacrifice was always held on the first xīn day of the first month,
in order to place it ahead of all other spirits and give it the foremost position.
According to the rites, during the three-year mourning period,
one does not sacrifice to one's ancestors but dare not omit the suburban sacrifice.
The suburban sacrifice is more important than the ancestral temple,
for Heaven is more revered than humans.
The 'Royal Regulations' state:
'The ox for sacrificing to Heaven and Earth has horns the size of a silkworm cocoon or a chestnut,
the ox for the ancestral temple has horns a hand's breadth,
the ox for guests has horns a foot long.'
This means that the more virtuous the act, the more humble the sacrificial animal.
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
'When Lǔ sacrificed to Duke Zhōu,
a white bull was used.'
The color white signifies the value of purity.
'The imperial sacrificial animal is kept in the cleansing stable for three months.'
The value of the sacrificial animal lies in its fatness and cleanliness,
not in its large size.
In all methods of raising sacrificial animals,
the essential point is merely fatness and cleanliness.
If foals and calves cannot yet digest fodder and grain,
it is best to let them suckle from their mothers."
Your subject Tāng respectfully asked Zhòngshū:
"When Lǔ sacrificed to Duke Zhōu using a white bull,
was this not contrary to ritual?"
Your subject Zhòngshū replied:
"It was in accordance with ritual."
Your subject Tāng asked:
"The Son of Heaven of Zhōu used a pure red bull,
while the various lords used animals of mixed colors.
Since Duke Zhōu was one of the various lords,
how could he be accorded the use of a pure-colored animal?"
Your subject Zhòngshū replied:
"When King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
still in swaddling clothes.
Duke Zhōu continued the enterprise of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
completing the work of the two sages.
His virtue permeated Heaven and Earth,
his beneficence covered all within the Four Seas.
Therefore, King Chéng, being worthy, honored him.
The Book of Songs says:
'There is no virtue that goes unrewarded.'
Thus King Chéng had Duke Zhōu sacrificed to with a white bull,
which was neither of the same color as that of the Son of Heaven above,
nor the same as that of the various lords below.
In my humble opinion, this was a ritual to repay virtue."
Your subject Tāng asked Zhòngshū:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven,
the various lords sacrifice to Earth.
Why then did Lǔ perform the suburban sacrifice?"
Your subject Zhòngshū replied:
"Duke Zhōu tutored King Chéng,
enabling King Chéng to attain sagehood.
No achievement is greater than this.
Duke Zhōu was a sage,
qualified to sacrifice to the Way of Heaven.
Therefore, King Chéng ordered Lǔ to perform the suburban sacrifice."
Your subject Tāng asked Zhòngshū:
"When Lǔ sacrificed to Duke Zhōu, a white bull was used.
What was used for their suburban sacrifice?"
Your subject Zhòngshū replied:
"For the suburban sacrifice, Lǔ used a pure red bull.
The color of the Zhōu dynasty was red,
and since Lǔ performed the suburban sacrifice by order of the Son of Heaven,
they used a red bull."
Your subject Tāng asked Zhòngshū:
"In sacrificing at the ancestral temple, sometimes a duck is used in place of a wild duck.
A duck is not a wild duck;
is this permissible?"
Zhòngshū replied:
"A duck is not a wild duck,
nor is a wild duck a duck.
I have heard that when Confucius entered the Grand Temple,
he asked about everything,
showing the utmost caution.
Your Majesty examines affairs personally,
fasting, bathing, and purifying yourself
to attend to the ancestral temple,
with great reverence and care.
How then can you substitute a wild duck for a duck, or a duck for a wild duck?
When name and reality do not correspond,
and you use this to serve the Grand Temple,
is it not inappropriate?
In my humble opinion, it should not be done.
Your subject, with teeth worn like those of a dog or horse,
has been granted retirement,
and lives in a humble lane.
Yet Your Majesty has graciously sent a minister of the ninth rank to inquire about court affairs.
Your subject is ignorant and unlearned.
I am truly inadequate to receive your brilliant decree
and respond to your great questions.
Your subject Zhòngshū ventures at the risk of death to present this."
"Presenting Gifts: Chapter Seventy-Two"
In all presentations of gifts:
the Son of Heaven uses aromatic wine,
dukes and marquises use jade,
high officials use lambs,
great officers use wild geese.
The wild goose has characteristics resembling those of an elder:
an elder, being above the people,
must orderly have those who follow before and after,
and must gracefully maintain ranked order.
Therefore, great officers use it as a gift.
The lamb has qualities that resemble Heaven.
The Way of Heaven
relies on the Yang and not the Yin;
the Way of the King
relies on virtue and not punishment,
in accordance with Heaven.
The lamb has horns but does not use them,
equipped but not employing them,
resembling one who loves benevolence;
when held it does not cry out,
when killed it does not lament,
resembling one who dies for righteousness;
when the lamb feeds from its mother,
it always kneels to receive milk,
resembling one who knows ritual.
Thus, the word for sheep (yáng) is akin to auspiciousness (xiáng)!
Therefore, high officials use it as a gift.
Jade resembles the gentleman.
The Master said:
"If a man does not say 'What shall I do? What shall I do?'
I can do nothing with him."
Thus, one who conceals his illness cannot get a good doctor,
and the sage avoids one who is ashamed to ask,
considering him one who distances himself from achievement and courts disaster,
and thus has nothing.
Jade is perfectly pure yet does not hide its flaws;
if there are blemishes within,
they are sure to show on the outside.
Therefore, the gentleman does not conceal his shortcomings.
What he does not know, he asks;
what he cannot do, he learns:
this is taken from jade.
The gentleman compares himself to jade.
Jade is moist yet not defiled,
this is benevolence and utmost purity;
sharp-edged yet not injurious,
this is righteousness and doing no harm;
hard yet not brittle,
it passes through without being stained.
It looks like an ordinary stone,
spreads out like rock,
its form is like stone,
scratched yet cannot be set ablaze,
pure white as undyed silk and不接受污,
jade embodies all these qualities.
Therefore, dukes and marquises use it as a gift.
Aromatic wine resembles the sage:
pure in benevolence, utterly unadulterated,
and possessing the value of knowledge.
What is selected from the self becomes entirely virtuous words,
what is manifested in affairs becomes entirely enriching moisture.
Accumulating beauty, the wine's fragrance
penetrates to Heaven.
Aromatic wine also takes the essence of a hundred spices,
gathers their finest parts,
combines them into one,
and conveys their scent,
its vapor reaching to Heaven.
Its pure, unadulterated nature, without selection,
is one with the sage.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven uses it as a gift.
And each is used to serve the superior accordingly.
By observing the meaning of the gifts,
one can see how they serve.
"In Praise of Mountains and Rivers: Chapter Seventy-Three"
The mountains, lofty and precipitous,
towering and majestic,
stand firm without collapsing or crumbling,
resembling men of benevolence and purpose.
Confucius said:
"With the establishment of mountain and river deities,
treasures and resources multiply,
tools and utensils find their use,
the crooked and straight align,
the larger ones can become palaces, towers, and pavilions,
the smaller ones can serve as boats, carts, and rafts.
The larger ones are all suitable,
the smaller ones all find their place,
wield an axe and they are chopped,
swing a sickle and they are cut.
The living dwell upon them,
beasts lie subdued,
the dead are buried within,
yet they claim no merit for their many deeds,
thus the gentleman draws analogy from them.
Moreover, accumulating earth to form a mountain
causes no loss;
achieving its height
brings no harm;
attaining its greatness
incurs no deficit.
Narrow at the top,
broad at the base,
enduring in stability,
with no后世 departures or arrivals,
solemn and alone it stands,
such is the virtue of the mountain.
The Book of Songs says:
'Behold that Southern Mountain,
its rocks so towering and steep;
illustrious is the Grand Tutor Yǐn,
the people all look up to you.'
This is what it means."
As for water, from its source it gushes and flows torrentially,
unceasing day and night,
resembling the strong;
filling hollows before advancing,
resembling the upholders of balance;
following crevices downward,
leaving no small gap untouched,
resembling the perceptive;
tracing valleys without losing its way,
sometimes traversing ten thousand miles yet surely arriving,
resembling the wise;
blocked by barriers yet remaining clear,
resembling those who know destiny;
entering turbid,
emerging pure and clean,
resembling the adept at transformation;
plunging into chasms a thousand ren deep without hesitation,
resembling the courageous;
all things are overwhelmed by fire,
yet water alone overcomes it,
resembling the martial;
all gain it and live,
lose it and die,
resembling the virtuous.
Confucius, standing by a river, said:
"What passes away is like this,
never ceasing day or night."
This is what it means.
"Seeking Rain, Section Seventy-Four"
In spring drought, seek rain.
Order the towns and villages to, on a water day, instruct the people to pray to the community god,
with each household making offerings at their doors.
Do not cut down famed trees,
nor fell trees in the mountains and forests.
Expose the shamans to the sun,
gather the crippled.
On the eighth day,
outside the east gate of the town, erect an open altar on all sides,
eight chi square,
and set up eight dark green silks.
The deity is Gònggōng,
offer to it eight live fish and dark wine,
along with clear wine and dried meat.
Choose shamans who are pure of conduct and eloquent in speech to perform the invocations,
who fast for three days,
wear dark green clothes,
first bow twice,
then kneel to present the offerings,
after presenting,
bow twice again,
then rise.
The invocation says:
"Heaven gave birth to the five grains to nourish the people,
now the five grains suffer from drought,
fear they may not mature,
respectfully we present clear wine and dried meat,
bow twice to beg for rain.
May rain generously pour down."
Offer sacrifices and pray,
on a jiǎ-yǐ day, make one large azure dragon,
eight zhàng long,
placed in the center;
and seven small dragons,
each four zhàng long,
in the east.
All facing east,
spaced eight chi apart.
Eight young boys,
all fasting for three days,
wear blue-green clothes and dance.
The field overseer also fasts for three days,
wears blue-green clothes and stands by.
In all village shrines,
connect to the ditches outside the lanes,
catch five frogs,
and place them alternately in the shrines,
in a pond eight chi square,
two chi deep,
put water and frogs in it.
Prepare clear wine and dried meat,
the invocator fasts for three days,
wears dark green clothes,
bows and kneels,
presents the invocation as before.
Take a three-year-old rooster and a three-year-old pig,
and burn them at the open shrine on all sides.
Order the closing of the south gates of the town and lanes,
place water outside them.
Open the north gate,
prepare one old boar,
place it outside the north gate of the lane.
Also place one boar in the market,
upon hearing drum sounds,
all burn the pigs' tails,
take human bones and bury them,
open mountain streams,
pile firewood and burn it.
Clear blocked roads and bridges that are impassable,
dredge the waterways.
If fortunate to obtain rain,
repay with one pig,
wine, salt, and millet as sufficient,
use茅 grass for mats,
do not break them.
In summer, seek rain.
Order the towns and villages to, on a water day,
have households worship the stove god.
Do not undertake earthworks,
instead dredge wells with water,
expose cauldrons on the altar,
place mortars and pestles on the paths.
On the seventh day,
erect an open altar on all sides outside the south gate of the town,
seven chi square,
and set up seven red silks.
The deity is Chīyóu,
offer to it seven red roosters and dark wine,
along with clear wine and dried meat.
The invocator fasts for three days,
wears red clothes,
bows, kneels, and presents the invocation as in the spring ritual.
On a bǐng-dīng day, make one large red dragon,
seven zhàng long,
placed in the center.
Also make six small dragons,
each three zhàng five chi long,
in the south.
All facing south,
spaced seven chi apart.
Seven strong men,
all fasting for three days,
wear red clothes and dance.
The minister of works overseer also fasts for three days,
wears red clothes and stands by.
Dig to connect the ditches outside the lanes.
Catch five frogs,
place them alternately in the lane shrines,
in a pond seven chi square,
one chi deep.
Wine and dried meat,
the invocator fasts,
wears red clothes,
bows, kneels, and presents the invocation as before.
Take a three-year-old rooster and a boar,
burn them at the open shrine on all sides.
Open the yin and close the yang as in spring.
In late summer, pray to the mountain tombs to assist.
Order the towns to relocate the market once,
outside the southern gate of the town.
For five days, prohibit men from entering the market.
Families worship the central roof deity.
Do not undertake earthworks,
gather shamans by the market,
and build a canopy for them.
Erect a four-directional altar in the center,
plant five yellow silks.
The deity is Hòujì,
offer to it five mother animals and dark wine,
prepare clear wine and dried meat.
Appoint a named invocator to fast for three days,
wearing yellow clothes.
All as in the spring sacrifice.
On a Wù or Jǐ day, make one large yellow dragon,
five zhǎng long,
placed in the center.
Also make four small dragons,
each two and a half zhǎng long,
in the south,
all facing south,
spaced five chǐ apart.
Five men,
all fasting for three days,
wear yellow clothes and dance with them.
Another five men,
also fasting for three days,
wear yellow clothes and stand by them.
Also connect ditches outside the village to the community altar,
catch frogs,
dig a pond five chǐ square,
one chǐ deep,
all else as before.
"Shénnóng's Rain Prayer,"
on the nineteenth day,
if no rain on Wù or Jǐ days,
command to make a yellow dragon,
also a large dragon,
danced by community members,
with Jì officials standing by.
Also says:
young boys from the east dance it,
strong men from the south, soaked people from the west, and northerners dance it.
In autumn, expose shamans for up to nine days,
do not light fires,
do not smelt metal vessels,
families worship the gate.
Erect a four-directional altar outside the western gate of the town,
nine chǐ square,
plant nine white silks.
The deity is Shàohào,
offer to it nine paulownia wood fish and dark wine,
prepare clear wine and dried meat.
Wear white clothes.
All else as in spring.
On a Gēng or Xīn day, make one large white dragon,
nine zhǎng long,
placed in the center.
Make eight small dragons,
each four and a half zhǎng long,
in the west.
All facing west,
spaced nine chǐ apart.
Nine widowers,
all fasting for three days,
wear white clothes and dance with them.
The Sīmǎ also fasts for three days,
wears white clothes and stands by them.
Frogs,
pond nine chǐ square,
one chǐ deep.
All else as before.
In winter, dance dragons for six days,
pray to famous mountains to assist.
Families worship the well,
do not block water.
Erect a four-directional altar outside the northern gate of the town,
six chǐ square,
plant six black silks.
The deity is Xuánmíng,
offer to it six black dog pups and dark wine,
prepare clear wine and dried meat.
The invocator fasts for three days,
wears black clothes,
the ritual like in spring.
On a Rén or Guǐ day, make one large black dragon,
six zhǎng long,
placed in the center.
Also make five small dragons,
each three zhǎng long,
in the north.
All facing north,
spaced six chǐ apart.
Six elders,
all fasting for three days,
wear black clothes and dance with them.
The Wèi official also fasts for three days,
wears black clothes and stands by them.
Frogs and pond,
all as in spring.
In all four seasons, choose a water day,
make dragons,
must use pure soil for them,
build a canopy,
complete the dragons and then release them.
In all four seasons, on a Gēngzǐ day,
order officials and commoners, husbands and wives, to stay together.
The general principle of rain prayer:
men should hide,
women should harmonize and be joyful.
The "Shénnóng Book" also says:
"Open sacred mountains and deep pools,
pile firewood,
beat drums at night,
make noise and burn it,
to counter the drought."
"Stopping Rain, Seventy-fifth"
When rain is excessive,
order towns on an earth day,
block water channels,
close roads,
cover wells,
prohibit women from entering the market.
Order counties, villages, and hamlets to sweep below the community altar.
If the county has a magistrate, assistant, or three or more officials,
appoint one invocator;
if the village has a manager or three or more officials,
appoint one invocator;
if the hamlet has three or more elders,
appoint one invocator,
all fast for three days,
each wearing seasonal clothes.
Prepare one piglet,
sufficient millet, salt, and fine wine,
sacrifice to the community altar.
Beat drums for three days,
then the invocator bows twice first,
kneels to present the plea,
after presenting,
bows twice again,
then rises.
The invocator says:
"Alas!
Heaven produces the five grains to nourish people,
now excessive rain falls too much,
the five grains do not harmonize.
Respectfully offer fat livestock and clear wine,
to petition the community spirit,
may you stop the rain,
relieve the people's suffering,
do not let yin extinguish yang.
If yin extinguishes yang,
it disobeys Heaven.
Heaven's constant intent
is to benefit people,
people wish to stop the rain,
dare to report to the community."
Drum without singing,
stop when finished.
The general rite for stopping rain:
women should hide and stay secluded,
men should harmonize and be joyful,
open yang and close yin,
shut water and open fire.
Bind the community altar ten times with red silk threads.
Wear red clothes and red headbands.
Cease after three days.
In the eighth month of the twenty-first year, on the day Jiǎshēn,
the new moon.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Jiāngdū Chancellor Dǒng Zhòngshū notified the Interior Minister and Commandant:
"The continuous rain has persisted too long,
fearing it may harm the five grains,
we urge to stop the rain."
The ritual to stop rain
involves suppressing the yīn and promoting the yáng.
A document was sent to seventeen counties,
eighty outlying districts,
and all capital officials below one thousand shí rank,
those with spouses in office,
were all to send their wives home.
Women were not allowed to go to the market,
the market wells were not to be approached,
covered,
and not to be leaked.
Drums were beaten and sacrifices offered at the earth altar.
The prayer said:
"The rain has been too abundant,
the five grains are not in harmony,
we reverently present fat sacrifices,
to plead with the earth spirit,
may the earth spirit graciously stop the rain,
remove the people's suffering,
do not let yīn extinguish yáng.
If yīn extinguishes yáng,
it would be contrary to Heaven's will.
Heaven's intent is always to benefit the people,
we wish to stop the rain.
Dare we report."
Drums were beaten and sacrifices offered at the earth altar,
all uniformly on the day Xīnhài,
upon receipt of the document, act immediately,
the county earth altar's magistrates and chiefs,
assistants, commandants, and officials,
the village and town earth altar custodians,
neighborhood officers, heads, and residents all came out,
proceeding to the earth altar,
dined and then concluded.
Three days and then stop.
If not reaching three days,
the sky clears greatly, also stop.
"Sacrificial Principles Seventy-six"
The five grains are the nature of food,
what Heaven bestows upon humans,
in the ancestral temple, what is produced in the four seasons is offered,
receiving the bounty and presenting it in the ancestral temple,
is the nature of reverence,
thus it is appropriate in sacrifice.
The sacrifices in the ancestral temple,
are the utmost in material richness.
In spring, offer bean contents,
in summer, offer basket contents,
in autumn, offer vessel contents,
in winter, offer mound contents.
Bean contents are chives,
which begin to grow in spring;
basket contents are wheat,
the initial harvest of summer;
vessel contents are millet,
the first to ripen in autumn;
mound contents are rice,
which fully matures in winter.
Beginning growth, thus called 'cí',
praising its management;
summer simplicity, thus called 'yuè',
valuing the initial offering;
first ripe, thus called 'cháng',
cháng means sweet;
fully mature, thus called 'zhēng',
zhēng means abundant.
Presenting what is received from Heaven in the four seasons,
is the highest sacrifice,
valuing Heaven's gift,
and honoring the ancestral temple.
Confucius, upon receiving his lord's gift, would sacrifice it,
how much more so for Heaven's gifts.
Within a year,
Heaven's gifts come four times,
upon arrival, they are offered,
this is why the ancestral temple has four sacrifices annually.
Thus the noble person never fails to eat the new harvest,
when the new Heaven's gift arrives,
must first present it,
then take to eat,
this is the heart of honoring Heaven and revering the ancestral temple.
Honoring Heaven is beautiful righteousness,
revering the ancestral temple is great ritual.
This is what the sage carefully observes.
Not seeking abundance but purity,
not greedy for frequency but respectful reverence.
The noble person's sacrifice,
personally attends to it,
expresses the sincerity of their heart,
exhausts the way of reverence and purity,
to approach the most honored,
thus the spirits enjoy it.
Enjoying it thus,
can then be called capable of sacrifice.
Sacrifice is discernment,
it means bringing goodness to the spirits.
Goodness reaches what cannot be heard or seen,
thus it is called discernment.
I, because of the name by which they are enjoyed,
thus sacrifice not in vain,
how could it not be discernment!
Sacrifice means connection.
Only through sacrifice can one see the unseen.
Seeing the unseen's visibility,
then one knows the Mandate of Heaven and the spirits.
Knowing the Mandate of Heaven and the spirits,
then one understands the meaning of sacrifice.
Understanding the meaning of sacrifice,
then one values sacrificial matters.
Confucius said:
"If I do not participate in the sacrifice,
it is as if the spirits are present."
Valuing sacrificial matters,
is like serving the living.
Thus the sage towards the spirits,
fears them and dares not deceive,
trusts them but does not rely solely,
serves them but does not depend entirely.
Relying on their impartiality,
they reward the virtuous;
grateful for their lack of partiality,
they bestow blessings upon people.
As seen in the "Book of Songs" it says:
"Ah, you noble persons,
do not constantly rest in comfort.
Quietly fulfill your duties,
love this uprightness.
The spirits, hearing this,
will grant you great blessings."
The upright receive blessings,
the crooked do not receive blessings,
this is the rule.
Taking the "Book of Songs" as the model for the world.
What is not modeled?
Its words are straightforward and weighty,
with repeated sighs,
wanting people to reflect on their meaning.
Yet people still do not reflect,
how forgetful they are!
Confucius said:
"The weightiness of the writing,
the repetition of the words.
Alas!
Cannot but examine carefully.
Within them must be something beautiful."
This refers to that.
"Following the Way of Heaven Seventy-seven"
Following the Way of Heaven,
to nourish one's body,
is called the Way.
Heaven has two harmonies to form two centers,
the year is established within them,
and their use is endless.
Thus, the center in the north combines with yīn,
and things begin to stir below;
the center in the south combines with yáng,
and nourishment begins to flourish above.
Those stirring below
cannot grow without the harmony of the east,
which is mid-spring.
Those nourished above
cannot mature without the harmony of the west,
which is mid-autumn.
Thus, the beauty and flaws of heaven and earth
lie in the two harmonies,
from which the two centers derive and accomplish their tasks.
Therefore, harmony—the east gives birth and the west brings maturity,
the eastern harmony births,
initiating from the north;
while the western harmony matures,
nourishing growth in the south;
initiation
does not exceed what harmony cannot birth;
nourishment and growth do not exceed what harmony cannot mature.
Maturity comes from harmony,
birth must be harmonious;
beginning from the center,
ending must be centered;
the center is where all things under heaven start and end,
and harmony
is what heaven and earth use to generate and complete.
No virtue is greater than harmony,
and no way is more correct than the center,
the center is the perfect principle of heaven and earth,
guarded by the sages,
The Book of Songs says:
"Neither rigid nor soft,
governing with ease."
Is this not referring to centrality and harmony?
Therefore, those who can govern the world with centrality and harmony
have greatly flourishing virtue;
those who can nourish their bodies with centrality and harmony
attain the utmost longevity.
The method for men and women
follows yīn and yáng.
Yáng energy arises in the north,
peaks in the south,
and at its peak unites with yīn.
Yīn energy arises in mid-summer,
peaks in mid-winter,
and at its peak unites with yáng.
Without peaking, there is no union,
thus in ten months they peak together once,
and in a full year unite twice.
Heaven and earth have enduring rhythms,
taking this as constant,
thus first follow this internally,
nourishing the body to completeness,
so that men do not firm their masculinity without household,
and yīn does not unite without reaching peak abundance.
Hence the body becomes refined and bright,
resistant to decay and firm,
long-lived without fault,
this is the Way of heaven and earth.
Heaven's energy first peaks in masculinity then emits essence,
thus its essence is firm;
earth's energy peaks in femininity then transforms,
thus its transformation is excellent.
Therefore, the union of yīn and yáng,
in winter joins the north and things stir below,
in summer joins the south and things stir above.
The great stirrings above and below
all occur after the solstices.
In cold, it freezes ice and cracks earth;
in heat, it scorches sand and melts stones.
The essence of energy reaches this point,
thus in the transformations of heaven and earth,
spring energy births and all things emerge,
summer energy nourishes and all things grow,
autumn energy kills and all things die,
winter energy stores and all things hide.
Therefore, only the essence of heaven and earth's energy
enters and exits without form,
and nothing fails to respond,
this is the ultimate reality.
The noble person follows what is valued.
Heaven and earth's yīn-yáng correspond to men and women,
human men and women correspond to yīn-yáng.
Yīn-yáng can also be called men and women,
men and women can also be called yīn-yáng.
The constant of heaven and earth,
reaching the center of the east,
greatly nourishes what is born,
reaching the center of the west,
greatly matures what is nourished,
four initiations in a year,
all endeavors must reach the center.
What the center does
must achieve harmony,
thus it is said harmony is essential.
Harmony is heaven's correctness,
the balance of yīn and yáng,
its energy is most excellent,
where things are born.
Truly choosing harmony
is to greatly receive heaven and earth's offerings.
The Way of heaven and earth,
though there may be disharmony,
must return to harmony,
thus actions succeed;
though there may be lack of center,
must stop at the center,
thus actions do not fail.
Therefore, yáng's movement
starts from the center of the north,
and stops at the center of the south;
yīn's movement
starts from the center of the south,
and stops at the center of the north.
The ways of yīn and yáng differ,
but upon peaking, both stop at the center,
their beginnings all start from the center.
The center is the great pivot of heaven and earth,
where the sun and moon reach and turn back,
the peak of length and shortness,
cannot exceed the center,
this is heaven and earth's design.
Combining harmony and disharmony,
center and lack of center,
using them timely,
all to achieve merit.
Thus, there is no time not timely,
this is the Way of heaven and earth.
Following heaven's Way,
rhythm is heaven's regulation,
yáng is heaven's expansiveness,
yīn is heaven's urgency,
the center is heaven's function,
harmony is heaven's achievement.
Lifting up heaven and earth's Way,
beauty lies in harmony,
thus in the birth of things,
all value energy and welcome nourishment.
Mèngzǐ said:
"I am good at nourishing my vast, flowing energy."
Meaning actions must end with propriety,
and the heart naturally rejoices,
often using yáng to generate its intent.
Gōngsūn's nourishment of energy says:
"If internally stored too full, energy does not flow;
too empty, energy is insufficient;
heat dominant then energy □;
cold dominant then energy □;
overworked then energy does not enter;
over-idle then energy stagnates;
anger then energy rises;
joy then energy scatters;
worry then energy runs wild;
fear then energy cowers.
All these ten
are harms to energy,
all arising from lack of centrality and harmony.
Thus, the noble person when angry returns to center,
and comforts oneself with harmony;
when joyful returns to center,
and restrains with correctness;
when worried returns to center,
and relaxes with intent;
when fearful returns to center,
and fills with essence."
Thus, centrality and harmony must be returned to in this way.
Therefore, when the noble person's Way is complete,
energy flourishes and rises.
All energy follows the heart.
The heart is the ruler of energy,
how could energy not follow?
Thus, those who follow the Way under heaven
all say the inner heart is the root.
Therefore, the reason benevolent people often live long
is no greed externally and inner purity,
hearts peaceful and harmonious without losing centrality and correctness,
taking heaven and earth's beauty to nourish their bodies,
thus they are both abundant and orderly.
The reason cranes live long
is no stagnant energy within,
thus they eat ice;
the reason monkeys live long
is they like to stretch their extremities,
thus energy spreads in all directions.
Heaven's energy often descends to bestow on earth,
thus those following the Way also draw energy from the feet;
heaven's energy often moves without stagnation,
thus those following the Way also do not stagnate energy.
If not regulated,
even if full, it is not empty.
Therefore, the noble person nourishes and harmonizes it,
regulates and models it,
Remove excessive indulgence,
adopt collective harmony.
High terraces receive abundant sunlight,
spacious chambers harbor excessive shade—
both distance from the harmonious balance of heaven and earth.
Thus the sage refrains from such extremes,
adhering only to moderation.
The standard measure is eight chǐ for humans,
with four chǐ as its center;
the gōng note is the sound of the center,
sweetness is the flavor of the center,
and four chǐ is the measurement of the center.
Therefore, in the rituals of the Three Sovereigns,
flavors all esteemed sweetness,
sounds all valued harmony.
Positioning oneself thus allows gradual alignment with the way of heaven and earth,
for their principles are of the same kind,
distinguished only by the same vital breath.
To emulate heaven is to emulate human distinctions.
The way of heaven
brings yin forward in autumn and winter,
and withdraws it in spring and summer.
Thus, the ancients welcomed brides at frost descent,
and reduced intimacy when ice melted—
drawing close with yin,
distancing with yang.
The vital breath of heaven and earth
avoids extreme fullness,
and does not intermingle yin and yang recklessly.
Hence, the nobleman highly cherishes his breath and moderates chamber activities,
to embody heaven's way.
Breath is harmed not by abundant circulation,
but by untimeliness and defiance of heaven.
Not aligning with the comings and goings of yin and yang
is called untimeliness;
indulging desires without regard to heavenly cycles
is called defiance of heaven.
The nobleman cultivates his person,
daring not to oppose heaven.
Thus, the newly wedded engage in chamber activities once every ten days,
middle-aged double that interval,
those beginning to decline double the middle-aged,
those mid-decline double the beginning decline,
and the greatly declined take months for what the newly wedded do in days—
thus aligning with the rhythms of heaven and earth.
This is the general outline.
The essence lies in ensuring no encounter during peak abundance.
Sparing in spring and abstaining in summer
is called not distancing from heaven and earth's cycles.
People all know to cherish their clothing and food,
but not their heavenly breath.
The heavenly breath in humans
is weightier than clothing and food.
When clothing and food are exhausted,
there may still be intervals,
but when breath ends, life terminates.
Thus, the greatest aspect of nurturing life
lies in cherishing breath.
Breath follows spirit to form,
spirit follows intent to emerge.
What the heart directs is called intent;
when intent is labored, spirit is disturbed;
when spirit is disturbed, breath diminishes;
when breath diminishes, longevity is hard to achieve.
Therefore, the nobleman restrains desires and halts evils to calm intent,
calms intent to tranquilize spirit,
tranquilizes spirit to nurture breath.
With abundant breath and order,
the greatest means of nurturing the body is attained.
Ancient Daoists have said:
"To avoid being overwhelmed,
firmly preserve one's virtue."
This means that if spirit does not leave the form,
then breath fills the interior abundantly,
enabling endurance of hunger and cold.
Harmony and joy are the external ease of life,
essence and spirit are the internal fullness of life;
external ease is not equal to internal fullness,
let alone external injuries?
Resentment, anxiety, sorrow, and hatred
are injuries to life;
harmony, delight, and encouragement of goodness
are nourishment for life.
The nobleman is cautious in small matters to avoid great failures,
walks the path of centrality and correctness,
lets his voice resonate with vitality,
keeps his breath and intent peaceful and harmonious,
dwells in contentment and joy—
this may be called nurturing life.
In all methods of nurturing life,
none is more essential than breath.
Therefore, the rulers of the world,
this thing alone dies.
What is edible
indicates its flavor benefits humans;
what is not eaten
shows it removes filth and harms without waiting for autumn.
During times of great withering among things,
when all things perish,
this thing alone lives.
What is edible
should be eaten more,
for heaven provides it to benefit humans,
uniquely generating it for them;
what is inedible,
should be stored more.
Heaven took pity on the central plains,
thus producing winter wheat,
which ripens mid-year.
The nobleman observes the peculiarities of things
to seek heaven's intent,
which becomes greatly evident.
Thus, men and women utilize their prime,
select the finest flavors and scents,
reside in harmonious places,
balance labor and leisure,
avoid extremes of cold and warmth,
prevent overindulgence in hunger or fullness,
measure desires and aversions by principle,
align movement and stillness with inherent nature,
halt joy and anger at the mean,
return worry and fear to correctness—
this central harmony constantly resides in their persons,
called greatly attaining heaven and earth's peace.
Those who greatly attain heaven and earth's peace
have their longevity extended and prolonged;
those who do not attain heaven and earth's peace
have their longevity impaired and shortened.
The endowment of shortness or length
is what humans receive from heaven.
Thus, lifespans have short and long,
nurturing has gains and losses,
and when the end comes,
generally it must correspond,
from this none can escape.
Hence, the word for longevity (shòu) is like correspondence (chóu).
Though the people under heaven are numerous,
each must correspond to their manner of life,
and their longevity or brevity stems from their own conduct.
Those who practice the way of endurance
have longevity corresponding to endurance;
those who practice the way of non-endurance
have longevity corresponding to non-endurance.
The conditions of endurance and non-endurance
each correspond to their lifelong conduct;
as now follows later,
it cannot be overcome,
thus it is said:
Longevity is correspondence.
Therefore, what humans practice themselves
actually adds to or detracts from their longevity.
Those whose conduct is leisurely yet enjoy long life
have destiny adding to it;
those whose conduct is upright yet have short life
have destiny detracting from it.
To doubt human gains and losses
based on heaven's destiny's additions and subtractions
is great delusion.
Thus, if heaven lengthens it but humans impair it,
the length is reduced;
if heaven shortens it but humans nurture it,
the shortness is increased.
Those who shorten heaven's gift are all humans;
are humans not heaven's successors?
If heaven gives its essence and humans do not continue it,
how can they stand alone!
"The Movement of Heaven and Earth - Chapter 78"
The way of Heaven and Earth is beautiful,
thus in spring one dons light clothing,
in summer dwells in dense shade,
in autumn avoids the killing wind,
in winter avoids heavy dampness,
seeking harmony.
Clothing should be frequently washed,
appetite should be kept slightly hungry.
The body should be regularly exercised,
without prolonged idleness,
while residing in one's abode.
All things between Heaven and Earth,
thrive by following their natural abundance and are born,
perish when oppressed by what overcomes them,
as seen in the changes of the four seasons.
Thus, the water energy of winter,
shifts eastward to spring and wood is born,
riding on its abundance.
The life of spring,
reaches west to metal and dies,
oppressed by what overcomes it.
What is born of wood,
perishes when it reaches metal;
what is born of metal,
perishes when it reaches fire.
What is born in spring cannot pass through autumn,
what is born in autumn cannot pass through summer,
such is the law of Heaven.
The flavors of food and drink,
each arriving at their season,
also have what overcomes them,
and what they cannot overcome,
a principle that must be carefully observed.
The four seasons have different energies,
each energy has its appropriate match,
where appropriateness lies,
the things of that season excel.
Observe what excels in each season and nurture it accordingly,
mix and consume what is excellent in the same season,
all these are what is appropriate.
Thus, shepherd's purse is excellent in winter,
while mustard matures in summer,
from this, one can see what is suitable to consume in winter and summer.
Winter belongs to water energy,
shepherd's purse has a sweet taste,
what excels by riding on water energy,
is because sweetness overcomes cold.
The word "jì" for shepherd's purse,
means to cross great waters.
Summer belongs to fire energy,
mustard has a bitter taste,
what matures by riding on fire energy,
is because bitterness overcomes heat.
Heaven does not speak,
but expresses its intent through things,
things that do not live and die at the same time as others,
must be deeply examined,
for this is how Heaven communicates with humans.
Thus, the maturity of shepherd's purse conveys sweetness,
the maturity of mustard conveys bitterness.
The noble person examines things and heeds their messages carefully,
so when it is not the time to eat shepherd's purse,
they avoid all sweet things entirely,
until mustard matures.
What Heaven alone causes to mature in its season,
the noble person alone adopts in that season,
this is what is suitable for winter and summer.
In spring and autumn, mix things for harmony,
while in winter and summer, adopt what is appropriate for the season,
then one may attain the beauty of Heaven and Earth,
and harmonize with the four seasons.
The general principle in selecting flavors,
is to follow what is excellent in each season,
thus not straying far from Heaven's way.
Therefore, when all things are greatly born,
and all creatures come to life,
it is difficult,
not to cherish their lives,
this is to save them from hardship;
promoting glory and honor,
praising their goodness,
this is to aid clarity;
receiving the mandate to spread kindness,
assisting in forming noble persons,
this is to aid transformation;
when achievements are completed and tasks accomplished,
attributing virtue to the superior,
this is to uphold righteousness.
Thus, the earth, understanding its principle, is the mother of all things,
the minister, understanding his duty, is the steward of the state.
A mother must not be untrustworthy,
a steward must not be disloyal.
If the mother is untrustworthy, grasses and trees suffer root damage,
if the steward is disloyal, treacherous ministers endanger their ruler.
Root damage leads to loss of branches and leaves,
the ruler endangered leads to loss of the state.
Therefore, those who serve the earth must expose its form,
those who serve as ministers must display their true feelings.
The ruler of a state,
is like the heart in a body.
Residing deep in the palace,
as the heart is hidden in the chest;
supremely noble without equal,
as the spirit of the heart has no match.
Appointing officials and elevating scholars,
valuing the clear and bright over the heavy and turbid,
as the body values the eyes over the feet;
employing all ministers without favoritism,
as the four limbs each have their duties;
internally, there are four assistants,
as the heart has the liver, lungs, spleen, and kidneys;
externally, there are numerous officials,
as the heart has the body with its orifices;
亲近圣人贤士,

superiors and inferiors support and comply with each other,

achieving great peace through non-action,

attracting yellow dragons and phoenixes,

allows the body to be whole;

the inferior suffers the harm,
as when ears and eyes are not clear and hands and feet are injured;
if ministers are disloyal and the ruler perishes,
as when the body acts recklessly and the heart is lost.
Therefore, the relationship between ruler and minister,
is like that between heart and body;
the heart must be firm,
the ruler must be virtuous;
the body must be compliant,
ministers must be loyal.
What enables the heart to be whole,
is the strength of the body;
what enables the ruler to be secure,
is the merit of the ministers.

dwelling deep in seclusion,

measuring abilities to confer offices,

drawing the worthy near to himself,

examining actual achievements,
ranking performances from best to worst,

advancing the meritorious,

if the ruler is not steadfast, treacherous ministers will disrupt his offices.

if ministers are disordered, the ruler is lost.
Thus, for Heaven, it is essential to solidify its vital force,
for the ruler, it is essential to strengthen his governance,

providing food and drink,

upholding integrity and dying for righteousness.
represents the four seasons.
But in human governance,

This is called obstruction,

When joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure reach their time and wish to emerge,

They should flow directly without obstruction,

Heaven completes a year before cycling through these four once,

Moreover, when Heaven wishes to benefit humans,

Removing filth does not wait for a season,
how much more so for purging corrupt men!

"The Source of Majesty and Virtue, Chapter Seventy-Nine"
Heaven possesses harmony and virtue,
balance and authority,
the intention of mutual acceptance,
and the principles of governance,
which must be carefully examined.
Spring represents Heaven's harmony,
summer represents Heaven's virtue,
autumn represents Heaven's balance,
winter represents Heaven's authority.
The order of Heaven
must begin with harmony before manifesting virtue,
must begin with balance before manifesting authority.
This shows that without harmony, one cannot display the virtue of rewards and celebrations,
without balance, one cannot display the authority of punishments and penalties.
It further reveals that virtue arises from harmony,
authority arises from balance.
Without harmony, there is no virtue;
without balance, there is no authority;
this is the way of Heaven,
which the enlightened perceive through this.
Though I may feel joy and delight,
I must first harmonize my heart to seek what is appropriate,
then bestow rewards to establish virtue.
Though I may feel indignation and anger,
I must first calm my heart to seek what is just,
then impose punishments to establish authority.
One who can always act thus
is called possessing heavenly virtue,
and one who practices heavenly virtue
is called a sage.
A ruler,
occupying the position of utmost virtue,
wielding the power of life and death,
transforms the people.
The people follow their ruler
as plants and trees respond to the four seasons.
Joy and anger correspond to cold and heat,
authority and virtue correspond to winter and summer.
Winter and summer embody the union of authority and virtue,
cold and heat pair with joy and anger.
Joy and anger have their time to be expressed appropriately,
cold and heat also have their time to emerge fittingly,
their principle is one and the same.
To refrain from joy when it is due
is like having summer without heat;
to refrain from anger when it is due
is like having winter without cold;
to withhold virtue when it is due
is like having the season of summer without its character;
to withhold authority when it is due
is like having the season of winter without its nature.
Joy, anger, authority, and virtue must not be expressed without proper alignment,
just as cold, heat, winter, and summer must not appear out of their due time,
hence the importance of carefully discerning the beginnings of good and evil.
How can this be verified?
The Spring and Autumn Annals gathers good deeds without omitting the small,
collects evil deeds without sparing the great,
conceals yet does not hide,
condemns yet does not neglect,
using right and wrong,
correct principles to praise and blame.
The expression of joy and anger,
the application of authority and virtue,
all hit their mark appropriately,
comparable to how cold, heat, winter, and summer never miss their timing.
Thus, it is said that the sage matches Heaven.
"Chapter 80: Acting in Accord with Heaven"
The qi of yin and yang,
exists in heaven above,
and also in humans.
In humans, it manifests as likes and dislikes, joy and anger;
in heaven, as warmth and coolness, cold and heat.
They emerge and enter, ascend and descend, move left and right, forward and backward,
flowing smoothly without ceasing,
never stagnating or becoming obstructed.
In humans,
they should also flow without stagnation,
just as the four seasons proceed in orderly fashion.
The cessation and movement of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure
are what heaven endows as human nature and destiny.
When the time comes and they desire to manifest their responses,
this is also heaven's response,
no different from warmth, coolness, cold, and heat arriving at their due times and manifesting.
If one were to retain virtue and wait for spring and summer,
or retain punishment and wait for autumn and winter,
this would have the name of following the four seasons,
but in reality, it would contradict the constant principles of heaven and earth.
What is in humans is also of heaven,
so how can one long retain heaven's qi,
causing it to stagnate,
preventing it from circulating properly?
Therefore, heaven produces grains that rot by yín,
and grows wheat in autumn,
announcing the removal of filth and continuing what is lacking.
The purpose of achieving success and continuing what is lacking
is to provide for humans.
Heaven's production has great constants,
yet in its circulation,
there are also harmful elements;
those that are removed and executed
are dealt with urgently, not waiting for the season—
this is heaven's will.
The sage receives this and governs accordingly:
thus, in spring, he cultivates benevolence and seeks goodness;
in autumn, he cultivates righteousness and seeks out evil;
in winter, he cultivates punishment to achieve purity;
in summer, he cultivates virtue to achieve leniency.
This is how to accord with heaven and earth,
and embody yin and yang.
However, while seeking goodness,
if he encounters evil, he does not release it;
while seeking out evil,
if he encounters goodness, he immediately acts upon it;
while achieving purity,
if he encounters great goodness, he immediately promotes it;
while achieving leniency,
if he encounters great evil, he immediately removes it.
This imitates how heaven, at the time of generating life, also has destruction,
and at the time of destruction, also has life.
Thus, intentions follow heaven and earth,
and urgency or leisure imitate yin and yang.
However, in human affairs, what should be carried out
encounters no obstruction;
moreover, being forbearing toward others
and compliant with heaven,
the ways of heaven and humans are both upheld—
this is called holding to the mean.
Heaven does not use spring to give life to humans
and autumn to kill them.
What should live is called life;
what should die is called death;
it is not that the responsibility for killing things is arbitrarily assumed
by spiritual intelligence;
the rise of chaotic ages
is also broadly like this,
all following the transformations of heaven and earth,
to complete or destroy things,
relying on the resources of yin and yang,
to carry out what they do.
Thus, if one commits evil, it exceeds human effort and harms achievement,
and the fault lies with oneself.
Between heaven and earth,
there is the qi of yin and yang
that constantly permeates humans,
just as water constantly permeates fish.
What distinguishes it from water
is that it is visible or invisible,
so subtle and pervasive.
Thus, humans dwelling between heaven and earth
are like fish separated from water—
it is the same.
There is no gap,
as if qi were more fluid than water.
Water compared to qi
is like mud compared to water.
Thus, between heaven and earth,
it seems empty but is substantial,
and humans are constantly permeated in this subtle flow,
while the qi of order and chaos
circulates and intermingles with it.
Therefore, when human qi is harmonious,
the transformations of heaven and earth are beautiful;
if mixed with evil, the flavor is ruined—
this is the principle of change in things.
Inferring from the categories of things,
using the easy to understand the difficult,
their nature can be grasped.
The qi of order and chaos,
the winds of evil and uprightness,
are what mix with the transformations of heaven and earth;
born from transformation, they in turn mix with transformation,
connected with movement.
The Spring and Autumn Annals record the ways of worldly affairs;
some document heaven,
whether completely or incompletely,
is the responsibility of the king.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven is difficult to rely upon,
and it is not easy to be king."
This refers to this.
The king must not fail to understand heaven.
Understanding heaven
is difficult even for the poets.
Heaven's intent is hard to see,
and its way is hard to comprehend.
Therefore, clarify the positions of yang and yin, entry and exit, substance and emptiness,
to observe heaven's will.
Distinguish the root and branch, compliance and opposition, small and large, broad and narrow of the five phases,
to observe heaven's way.
Heaven's will is benevolent,
and its way is righteous.
The ruler of men,
in giving and taking, life and death,
should each accord with righteousness,
like the four seasons;
in appointing officials and setting up officers,
must do so based on their abilities,
like the five phases;
loving benevolence and hating cruelty,
employing virtue and distancing punishment,
like yin and yang.
This is called being able to match heaven.
Heaven—its way nurtures the myriad things,
and the king nurtures the people.
The greatness of the ruler
is a triad with heaven and earth;
the distinction between likes and dislikes
follows the principle of yin and yang;
the expression of joy and anger
is analogous to cold and heat;
the duties of offices
follow the meaning of the five phases.
In this way, he endures between heaven and earth,
expansive.
