"Heaven, Earth, Yīn, Yáng, Chapter Eighty-One"
Heaven, earth, yīn, yáng, wood, fire, earth, metal, water,
making nine,
and with humans, ten,
completes heaven's numbers.
Thus, numbers stop at ten,
and writing ends with ten,
all derived from this.
Why does the sage value them?
They begin with heaven
and end with humans.
Beyond this are called things,
things being what are cast aside from what is valued,
and not included within.
From this, it is seen that humans transcend above all things
and are the most valued under heaven.
Humans, below, nurture all things,
above, join with heaven and earth;
thus, the reasons for order and chaos,
the qi of movement, stillness, compliance, and opposition,
affect the transformations of yīn and yáng,
and stir within the four seas.
Things difficult to understand are like the divine,
it cannot be said otherwise.
Now, thrown to the ground, they die or are injured without leaping to aid,
thrown into mud, they interact closely,
thrown into water, they interact but drift farther.
From this, it is observed
that the more fluid things are, the more easily they stir and shake.
Now, the fluidity of qi transformation
is not merely like water.
And if the ruler allows endless movements among the masses,
thus often the qi of order and chaos
interferes with the transformations of heaven and earth, leading to disorder.
When the world is orderly and the people harmonious,
intentions are calm and qi upright,
then the transformations of heaven and earth are refined,
and the beauty of all things arises.
When the world is chaotic and the people discordant,
intentions are perverse and qi adverse,
then the transformations of heaven and earth are harmed,
and qi produces disasters.
Therefore, the virtue of an orderly world
moistens plants and trees,
its beneficence flows to the four seas,
achieving merit.
Names are used to distinguish things.
For the intimate, they are weighty;
for the distant, light;
for the noble, ornate;
for the humble, plain;
for the near, detailed;
for the far, brief;
literary expression does not conceal true feelings,
clear feelings do not omit refinement,
people's hearts follow without opposition,
past and present connect without confusion:
this is the meaning of names.
Men and women are like the Dào.
In human life, distinctions speak of ritual and righteousness,
the origin of names and titles arises from human affairs.
Not complying with the heavenly Dào
is called unrighteousness;
examining the distinction between heaven and humans,
observing the differences between the Dào and destiny,
one can understand the principles of ritual.
Seeing good, one cannot but like it;
seeing bad, one cannot but dislike it;
likes, dislikes, rejections, and acceptances cannot be firmly held without,
hence there is the human Dào.
The human Dào is what humans follow, finding joy without disorder, returning without weariness.
All things bear names as they are born;
the sage names them based on their images.
Yet they can be changed,
all following righteousness,
thus rectifying names to clarify righteousness.
'Thing' is a general name,
all are names,
yet things have private names;
this is a thing,
not that thing.
Therefore, it is said:
All things move without form—
that is intention;
have form without changing—
that is virtue;
joyful without disorder, returning without weariness—
that is the Dào.
Within the four seas,
the qi of yīn and yáng intermingles,
mixing with heaven and earth.
Hence, it is said:
Since it is said the king joins heaven and earth,
if he joins heaven and earth,
then he transforms,
how could it be only the essence of heaven and earth!
The king also joins and intermingles with them;
in order, he intermingles with the transformations of heaven and earth with upright qi;
in chaos, with evil qi;
in chaos,
like elements benefit each other,
unlike elements harm each other—such is the principle,
leaving no doubt.

the qì of movement, stillness, compliance, and opposition,
can augment or diminish the transformations of yīn and yáng
and stir upheaval within the Four Seas.
Things difficult to understand are like spirits,
but this cannot be denied.
Now, when thrown on the ground, things die or are injured without helping each other rise;
when thrown into mud, they interact closely;
when thrown into water, they interact but drift farther apart.
From this, it is observed
that the more fluid things are, the more easily they stir and shift.
Now, the fluidity of qì transformations
is not merely like water.
And if the ruler allows endless movements among the masses,
then the qì of order and chaos
will intermingle with the transformations of Heaven and Earth, leading to disorder.
When the world is orderly and the people harmonious,
with intentions calm and qì upright,
then the transformations of Heaven and Earth are refined,
and the beauty of all things arises.
When the world is chaotic and the people rebellious,
with intentions perverse and qì adverse,
then the transformations of Heaven and Earth are harmed,
and qì gives rise to disasters.
Therefore, the virtue of an orderly age
moistens plants and trees,
its blessings flow to the Four Seas,
surpassing the achievements of spirits.
The origins of a chaotic age are also widespread.
Thus,
all rely on the transformations of Heaven and Earth
to complete or ruin things,
utilizing the resources of yīn and yáng
to enable their actions,
so that evil deeds waste human effort and harm achievements,
and reputation suffers accordingly.
Between Heaven and Earth,
there are yīn and yáng qì
that constantly immerse humanity,
just as water constantly immerses fish.
The difference from water
lies only in being visible or invisible,
so subtle is it.
Thus, humanity dwelling between Heaven and Earth
is like fish separated from water—
the principle is the same.
The seamlessness is like qì, yet more fluid than water.
Comparing water to qì
is like comparing mud to water.
Therefore, between Heaven and Earth,
it appears empty but is substantial,
and humanity is always immersed in this subtlety,
with the qì of order and chaos
flowing and intermingling with it.
Thus, when human qì is harmonious,
the transformations of Heaven and Earth are beautiful;
if mixed with evil, the flavor spoils—
this is the principle of change in things.
Inferring from categories of things,
using the easy to understand the difficult,
their essence can be grasped.
The qì of order and chaos,
the winds of evil and uprightness,
are what intermingle with the transformations of Heaven and Earth.
Born from transformations yet in turn mingling with them,
they are linked to fate.
The Spring and Autumn Annals illustrate the ways of the world's affairs,
recording Heaven's actions,
whether complete or incomplete—
this is the responsibility of the king.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven is difficult to rely upon,
and it is not easy to be king."
This refers to this.
The king must not fail to understand Heaven.
Understanding Heaven
is difficult even for the poets.
Heaven's intent is hard to perceive,
its way hard to fathom.
Therefore, clarify the positions of yáng and yīn, entry and exit, substance and emptiness,
to observe Heaven's will.
Distinguish the roots and branches, compliance and opposition, small and large, broad and narrow of the Five Phases,
to observe the way of Heaven.
Heaven's will is benevolent,
its way is righteous.
The ruler,
in granting and taking, giving life and executing,
must align each with righteousness,
like the four seasons;
in appointing officials and establishing posts,
must base it on ability,
like the Five Phases;
in loving benevolence and hating cruelty,
employing virtue and avoiding punishment,
like yīn and yáng.
This is called being able to match Heaven.
Heaven, in its way, nurtures all things,
and the king nurtures humanity.
The greatness of the ruler
lies in aligning with Heaven and Earth;
the distinction between likes and dislikes
follows the principle of yīn and yáng;
the expression of joy and anger
compares to cold and heat;
the duties of offices
reflect the meaning of the Five Phases.
Thus, he nurtures between Heaven and Earth,
influences within the Four Seas,
mingles the qì of yīn and yáng,
and intertwines with Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, it is said:
Since the king aligns with Heaven and Earth,
if he aligns with them,
then he transforms.
How could it be only the essence of Heaven and Earth?
The king also aligns and mingles with them:
in order, he mingles the upright qì with the transformations of Heaven and Earth;
in chaos, he mingles the evil qì with the transformations of Heaven and Earth.
This is the principle that like benefits like and unlike damages each other—
there is no doubt about it.
The Application of Heaven's Way, Chapter Eighty-Two
Heaven's way applies,
Earth's way transforms,
Humanity's way is righteousness.
The sage sees the beginning and knows the root—
this is the height of refinement,
grasping one to respond to ten thousand—
this is the essence of order.
To stir the root without calming the branches,
to accept the beginning without declining the end—
benefit is the root of theft,
recklessness is the start of chaos.
To be at the start of chaos,
to stir the root of theft,
and yet expect the people to be calm—
this is impossible.
Therefore, the noble person does not speak without ritual,
does not act without ritual.
Lust without ritual leads to dissipation,
eating and drinking without ritual lead to conflict,
and dissipation and conflict lead to chaos.
Thus, ritual embodies emotions and prevents chaos.
The people's emotions cannot restrain their desires
without measuring them by ritual.
Let the eyes see proper colors,
the ears hear proper sounds,
the mouth taste proper flavors,
the body follow the proper path—
this is not to seize their emotions,
but to pacify them.
Change is called emotion;
even holding different things,
if the nature remains the same,
it is called internal.
The change of changing changes
is called external.
Thus, even with emotion,
it does not explain nature.
Therefore, it is said:
External things moving nature
are like the spirit not staying guarded.
Accumulated habits and gradual influences
are subtle among things.
They enter people unknowingly,
become habitual and forgotten, then act,
seeming constant like nature—
this must be examined.
Pure knowledge and light thoughts lead to clear reasoning;
restraining desires and following proper conduct lead to moral order;
taking admonition and restraint as abode,
and ritual and righteousness as the path, leads to cultured virtue.
Thus, utmost sincerity discards things without changing with them,
personal magnanimity avoids conflict without following customs,
the crowd's strength cannot penetrate,
shedding the turbid and filthy,
embracing the principles of fate and application,
moving with all things without losing oneself—
this is the heart of the sage.
A Sū Yù Edition: The Application of Heaven's Way, Chapter Eighty-Two
The Way of Heaven bestows,
the Way of Earth transforms,
the Way of Humankind embodies righteousness.
The sage perceives the subtle signs and thereby knows the root,
such is the ultimate of refinement;
grasping the one to respond to the myriad,
such is the order of categorization.
Those who disturb the root do not know how to calm the branches,
those who accept the beginning cannot refuse the end.
Profit is the root of theft,
recklessness is the start of chaos.
To be at the start of chaos,
and stir the root of theft,
yet desire the people to be calm,
is unattainable.
Thus, the noble person does not speak without ritual,
does not act without ritual.
Fondness of beauty without ritual leads to dissipation,
eating and drinking without ritual leads to contention,
dissipation and contention result in chaos.
Ritual embodies emotions and prevents chaos.
People's emotions cannot control their desires,
so they are made to measure by ritual.
The eyes gaze upon proper colors,
the ears listen to proper sounds,
the mouth tastes proper flavors,
the body follows the proper path—
this is not to seize their emotions,
but to pacify their emotions.
Change is called emotion,
even if holding different things, the nature remains so;
thus it is said to be internal.
The change of changing changes
is called external.
Therefore, even with emotion,
it does not equate to the nature's explanation.
Hence it is said:
External things moving the nature,
are like the spirit not being guarded.
Accumulated habits gradually erode,
they are subtle aspects of things.
They enter people unknowingly,
through habituation and forgetting become actions,
constant as if nature,
and must not be unexamined.
Pure knowledge and light thoughts lead to clear contemplation,
moderating desires and following proper conduct yield moral order,
taking remonstrance and restraint as abode,
and ritual-righteousness as the path, then cultural virtue is achieved.
Therefore, utmost sincerity discards things without changing with them,
personally broad and contention-free without conforming to customs,
the crowd's strength cannot penetrate.
Shedding the cocoon from turbid filth,
embracing the principles of fate and bestowal,
migrating with the myriad things without losing oneself—
this is the heart of the sage.
Names are used to distinguish things.
The intimate are emphasized,
the distant are lightened,
the noble are adorned,
the humble are plain,
the near are detailed,
the far are brief.
Literary expressions do not conceal feelings,
clear feelings do not omit adornment,
the human heart follows without opposition,
past and present connect without disorder—
this is the meaning of names.
Male and female are like the Way.
In human life, distinctions speak of ritual-righteousness,
the origin of names and titles arises from human affairs.
Not following the Way of Heaven
is called unrighteousness;
examining the distinction between Heaven and humanity,
observing the differences in the Way and fate,
one can understand the discourse of ritual.
Seeing good, one cannot but like it,
seeing bad, one cannot but dislike it;
liking, disliking, approaching, avoiding—
if unable to hold firm,
thus the Way of Humanity exists.
The Way of Humanity is what people follow to be joyful without disorder,
to return without weariness.
The myriad things bear names and come to life,
the sage names them according to their images.
Yet they can be changed,
all with righteousness to follow,
hence correcting names to clarify righteousness.
Things are grand names,
all are names,
yet things have private names—
this thing,
not that thing.
Therefore it is said:
The myriad things move without form—
that is intention;
formed without changing—
that is virtue;
joyful without disorder, returning without weariness—
that is the Way.
